🔄 CORE WORKFLOW — init · plan · apply · destroy
terraform initInitialize directory, download providers
terraform init -upgradeUpgrade provider/module versions
terraform planShow execution plan (no changes)
terraform plan -out=FILESave plan for later apply
terraform applyShow plan + prompt + apply
terraform apply -auto-approveApply without prompt (CI/CD)
terraform apply -replace=XDestroy & recreate resource X
terraform destroyDestroy all managed resources
terraform destroy -target=XDestroy only resource X
✅ VALIDATION & FORMATTING
terraform fmt -recursiveFormat all .tf files recursively
terraform fmt -checkCheck formatting (CI gate)
terraform validateCheck syntax validity
terraform consoleInteractive HCL expression REPL
📋 STATE MANAGEMENT — output · state · import
terraform outputShow all output values
terraform output -jsonOutput values as JSON
terraform state listList all resources in state
terraform state show ADDRShow single resource details
terraform state mv SRC DSTMove resource within state
terraform state rm ADDRRemove from state (keep resource)
terraform import ADDR IDImport existing resource into state
🛠️ WORKSPACES & MAINTENANCE
terraform workspace listList all workspaces
terraform workspace new NAMECreate a new workspace
terraform workspace select NAMESwitch to workspace
terraform taint ADDRMark resource for recreation
terraform untaint ADDRRemove taint mark
terraform force-unlock LOCK_IDRelease stuck state lock ⚠️
terraform graph \| dot -Tpng >g.pngVisualize dependency graph
terraform providersShow required providers

🟢 Part 1: Foundation — What is Infrastructure as Code?Chapters 1-3

Chapter 1: What is Terraform? (The Big Picture)

Before diving into HCL syntax and terraform apply, let's understand why Terraform exists, what problems it solves, and how it transforms infrastructure management. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django + Kubernetes project to make every concept concrete.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours📖 Conceptual🎯 Big Picture

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why manual infrastructure deployment is slow, expensive & error-prone
  • ✅ What Infrastructure as Code (IaC) really means and why it's revolutionary
  • ✅ How Terraform compares to CloudFormation, Pulumi, Ansible, and Bicep
  • ✅ The 6 killer features that make Terraform the industry standard
  • ✅ How Terraform fits into the anihpj/jobpost project workflow
  • ✅ 10 essential Terraform terms you must know for the exam
🎓 Exam Relevance
Domain 1: Resource LifecycleFoundation ALL DOMAINS
Understanding "Why" Matters on the Exam

While Chapter 1 concepts aren't directly tested in hands-on labs, understanding the declarative model (you declare WHAT, Terraform figures out HOW) is essential for every exam task. The state file, plan/apply workflow, dependency graph, and resource addressing all build on this foundation. Internalize these concepts now — they'll make every later chapter easier.

1.1 The Problem Terraform Solves

Imagine you've built anihpj — a Django app with a jobpost module listing jobs filtered by Skills, Location, and Author. It works perfectly on your laptop. But how do you run it in production so thousands of users can access it reliably?

📖 Key Term: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

Infrastructure as Code is the practice of managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable definition files rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools. Terraform is the leading IaC tool — treating your cloud infrastructure the same way developers treat application code: versioned, tested, and automated.

The Pain of Manual Infrastructure

Before IaC, deploying infrastructure meant clicking through cloud consoles, running manual SSH commands, and hoping nothing went wrong. Each environment was a snowflake — unique, fragile, and impossible to reproduce.

😰 Deploying anihpj WITHOUT Terraform
  • 🔴 AWS Console: Click, click, click... 200+ manual steps to create VPC, subnets, EC2, RDS, EKS
  • 🔴 Forget one security group rule = broken application
  • 🔴 Staging ≠ Production = configuration drift between environments
  • 🔴 Onboarding a new developer: "Here's a 50-page wiki, good luck"
  • 🔴 Disaster recovery: "Rebuild everything from memory"
  • 🔴 Who changed what? No version history for infrastructure
The IaC Revolution — A Tale of Two Deployments
  SCENARIO: Deploying anihpj/jobpost to AWS for a new customer

  👤 MANUAL DEPLOYMENT (Before IaC)              🤖 TERRAFORM DEPLOYMENT (With IaC)
  ─────────────────────────────────────          ──────────────────────────────────
  Day 1: VPC, subnets, route tables                Minute 1:  git clone anihpj/infra
         → 6 hours, 47 clicks,                                terraform init
           forgot NAT gateway                     Minute 3:  terraform plan
  Day 2: EC2, Docker, nginx                                 (preview EVERYTHING)
         → 4 hours, SSH session lost              Minute 5:  terraform apply
  Day 3: RDS PostgreSQL, security groups          Minute 20: ☕ Coffee break
         → 3 hours, wrong SG = no connection      Minute 25: ✅ DONE!
  Day 4: EKS, kubectl, deploy app                           VPC + EKS + RDS + S3
         → 8 hours, 3 failed attempts                        + IAM ALL created!
  Day 5: Debug, tweak, pray. Go live.                        kubectl get pods →
         → "How do I recreate this??"                        jobpost RUNNING!

  TOTAL: 5 DAYS | ~$1,500 cost                    TOTAL: 25 MINUTES | ~$10 cost
  RESULT: ❌ Snowflake, no docs                    RESULT: ✅ Versioned, repeatable
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🎯 SAME RESULT — 288× FASTER, 150× CHEAPER, INFINITELY BETTER

💡 The Core Insight

Terraform doesn't just save time — it fundamentally changes HOW you think about infrastructure. Instead of "I need to click through 47 screens to set up a VPC," you think "I need a VPC with these properties" — and Terraform figures out the rest. This shift from procedural to declarative thinking is the foundation of modern DevOps.

Why Manual Infrastructure Fails — The Snowflake Server Problem

Every manually-built server is a snowflake — unique, fragile, and impossible to perfectly reproduce. Here's why this matters:

🔄
Configuration Drift

You patch production server but forget staging. A month later, code that works in staging fails in production because the environments have diverged. Terraform eliminates drift by enforcing the SAME configuration everywhere.

📝
No Documentation

Infrastructure knowledge lives in someone's head. When they leave, nobody knows how to rebuild. With Terraform, the .tf files ARE the documentation — self-documenting infrastructure that anyone can read.

🔍
No Audit Trail

Who changed the security group last week? With manual changes, you'll never know. Terraform + Git gives you a complete version history of every infrastructure change — who, what, when, and why.

💸
Slow Recovery

AWS region goes down? With manual infrastructure, recovery means rebuilding from scratch. With Terraform, you run the same code in a different region — disaster recovery in minutes, not days.

1.2 Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Defined

📖 Official Definition

"Define your infrastructure in configuration files that you can version, reuse, and share — just like application code." In plain English: You write files describing what infrastructure you want (a VPC, an EKS cluster, a database), and Terraform makes it happen — correctly, consistently, every time.

Declarative vs Imperative — The Key Difference

This is THE most important concept in Terraform. With imperative tools (like Ansible or shell scripts), you say HOW to do something. With declarative tools (like Terraform), you say WHAT you want.

🔧 IMPERATIVE (Ansible, scripts)

You specify every step:

  • 1. Create VPC
  • 2. Create subnet
  • 3. Launch EC2
  • 4. Install Docker
  • 5. Configure K8s...

❌ "How to do it" — If step 3 fails, you're in an unknown state.

📋 DECLARATIVE (Terraform)

You state the desired end result:

resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" }
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id }

✅ "What I want" — Terraform figures out the correct order and handles failures.

Declarative Thinking is Tested Throughout the Exam

Every Terraform exam task follows this pattern: you're told WHAT infrastructure to create (not HOW). Your job is to write the correct .tf configuration. Terraform handles the ordering, parallelism, and error recovery. The exam tests whether you can express infrastructure requirements declaratively in HCL.

🏗️ The Construction Blueprint Analogy

Think of Terraform like an architectural blueprint for a building:

📐
Blueprint (.tf files)

You draw the blueprint specifying what the building should look like — number of floors, room sizes, materials. You don't specify HOW to pour concrete or WHERE to place scaffolding.

🏗️
Construction Crew (Terraform)

Terraform is the construction crew that reads your blueprint and figures out HOW to build it — in what order, with what tools, handling any problems along the way.

📋
Inspection Report (terraform plan)

Before building, you get an inspection report showing exactly what will be built, modified, or demolished. You approve it before any work begins.

📸
Progress Photo (State File)

The state file is like a progress photo — it shows what's already been built, so the crew knows what exists and what still needs to be done.

💡 Key Insight

If the blueprint says "3 floors" and a storm knocks down floor 2, the construction crew (Terraform) notices the difference between the blueprint (desired state) and reality (actual state), and rebuilds floor 2 automatically. This is self-healing infrastructure — the core promise of Terraform.

Key Terraform Terminology — Your First 10 Words

TermWhat It MeansExample
ProviderPlugin that talks to a cloud APIaws, azure, kubernetes
ResourceSomething you create in the cloudaws_vpc, aws_eks_cluster
Data SourceRead existing cloud informationdata.aws_ami.ubuntu
State FileJSON map of real↔config resourcesterraform.tfstate
ModuleReusable group of resourcesmodule "vpc" { ... }
PlanPreview of changes BEFORE applyingterraform plan
ApplyExecute changes to match configterraform apply
BackendWhere state is stored (S3/GCS)S3 bucket + DynamoDB
WorkspaceIsolated state for different envsdev / staging / prod
HCLHashiCorp Configuration Language.tf files

1.3 Why Terraform Over Other IaC Tools?

The IaC landscape has many tools. Each solves a different problem. Here's how they compare:

ToolTypeMulti-CloudState MgmtLanguageMaturity
TerraformProvisioning✅ YES!✅ RichHCL (declarative)✅ 10yr
CloudFormationProvisioning❌ AWS only✅ GoodYAML/JSON✅ 12yr
PulumiProvisioning✅ YES✅ GoodPython/TS/Go/C#🟡 6yr
AnsibleConfig Mgmt✅ YES❌ NoneYAML (imperative)✅ 12yr
BicepProvisioning❌ Azure only✅ GoodBicep DSL🟡 3yr
CrossplaneControl Plane✅ YES✅ K8s nativeYAML🟡 4yr

Terraform's 6 Killer Features

🗺️
Multi-Cloud

One language (HCL) deploys to AWS, GCP, Azure, K8s, and more. Write once, deploy anywhere. anihpj uses AWS for compute, S3 for storage — all in one config.

📋
State File

Terraform tracks every resource it creates. The state file is the single source of truth — it knows what exists, what changed, and what needs updating.

🔮
Plan Preview

terraform plan shows you exactly what WILL change BEFORE it changes. No surprises. No "oops, I deleted production." THE safety feature.

🔗
Dependency Graph

Creates resources in the correct order automatically. VPC before subnet, EKS before deployment. Parallelizes independent resources for speed.

📦
Modules

2,000+ reusable modules on the registry. Build a VPC module once, reuse in dev/staging/prod. Like LEGO blocks for infrastructure.

🔌
2,000+ Providers

AWS, GCP, Azure, K8s, Helm, GitHub, Datadog, Cloudflare... Any API can become a Terraform provider. The ecosystem is massive.

How Terraform Compares to Writing Scripts

Many beginners ask: "Why not just write a Python script that calls AWS APIs?" Here's why that doesn't work at scale:

🐍 Custom Script Approach
  • Write 500 lines of Python to create VPC, subnets, EC2
  • Handle errors manually (what if subnet creation fails midway?)
  • Track what was created — build your own "state" system
  • What if someone changed the security group manually? Script doesn't know
  • New team member: "Which script? What parameters?"

Result: You've accidentally built a bad version of Terraform

⚡ Terraform Approach
  • Write 50 lines of HCL describing desired state
  • Terraform handles errors, retries, and ordering automatically
  • State file tracks everything — Terraform knows if drift occurred
  • Manual changes detected on next terraform plan
  • New team member: git clone && terraform apply

Result: Battle-tested, community-supported, production-ready

1.4 Terraform in the anihpj Project — End-to-End Overview

Throughout this guide, we'll use the anihpj/jobpost project — a Django application deployed on Kubernetes (EKS). Here's the complete infrastructure that Terraform will build:

Anihpj Infrastructure — Built Entirely by Terraform
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    ☁️ AWS CLOUD (us-east-1)                          │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐       │
  │  │     VPC      │  │  EKS Cluster   │  │   RDS (Postgres) │       │
  │  │  10.0.0.0/16 │  │  anihpj-k8s    │  │   jobpost-db     │       │
  │  │  pub + priv  │  │  3 worker nodes│  │   db.t3.medium   │       │
  │  │  subnets     │  │  t3.medium     │  │   Multi-AZ       │       │
  │  └──────────────┘  └────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘       │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐       │
  │  │   ALB/NLB    │  │      S3        │  │   ElastiCache    │       │
  │  │  jobpost.io  │  │   backups +    │  │   Redis cache    │       │
  │  │  TLS cert    │  │   static files │  │   session store  │       │
  │  └──────────────┘  └────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘       │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ALL defined in ~500 lines of Terraform (.tf) files:                │
  │  main.tf | variables.tf | outputs.tf | terraform.tfvars | providers.tf│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

By the end of this guide, you'll be able to deploy this entire stack with a single terraform apply command. Every chapter builds toward this goal incrementally — from your first S3 bucket to a full production-grade Kubernetes deployment.

⚠️ When NOT to Use Terraform

Terraform is powerful but not always the right tool. Consider alternatives when:

  • Simple, static infrastructure: A single EC2 instance that never changes — Terraform adds unnecessary complexity
  • Application configuration: Use Ansible, Chef, or Puppet for configuring software INSIDE servers (Terraform is for infrastructure, not app config)
  • Kubernetes-only workloads: If you ONLY use K8s, consider GitOps tools (ArgoCD, Flux) plus Crossplane for infrastructure
  • Multi-step workflows: Terraform is declarative, not procedural. Complex multi-step orchestration may need tools like Airflow or Temporal
Q1

What is the primary difference between declarative and imperative infrastructure management?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Declarative specifies WHAT you want (the desired end state), while imperative specifies HOW to achieve it (the exact steps).

📖 Explanation

Terraform is declarative: you write resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" } and Terraform figures out how to create it. Ansible is imperative: you write steps like "create VPC, then subnet, then EC2." Declarative is safer because you don't need to handle failures between steps — Terraform handles that automatically.

  DECLARATIVE (Terraform)              IMPERATIVE (Ansible/Shell)
  ─────────────────────                ─────────────────────────
  You say: "I want a VPC                You say: "Step 1: Create VPC
           with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16"                Step 2: Create subnet
                                                 Step 3: Launch EC2
  Terraform figures out:                         Step 4: Configure Docker"
    1. Check if VPC exists              If Step 2 fails → unknown state
    2. Create if missing                Must handle EVERY error path
    3. Update if drifted                Script must be idempotent
    4. Parallelize dependencies

  ✅ RESULT: Same every time            ❌ RESULT: Depends on script quality
Q2

What file does Terraform use to track the mapping between your configuration and real-world resources?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

The state file (terraform.tfstate).

📖 Explanation

The state file is a JSON document that maps resources in your .tf files to real cloud resources (e.g., aws_vpc.main → vpc-abc123). Without state, Terraform can't know what exists. State also tracks resource attributes, dependencies, and metadata. State should ALWAYS be stored remotely (S3, GCS, TFC) — never only on a local machine.

  STATE FILE ANATOMY (terraform.tfstate):
  {
    "version": 4,
    "terraform_version": "1.7.0",
    "serial": 42,              ← Incremented on every apply
    "lineage": "uuid-abc123",   ← Unique ID for this state
    "resources": [{
      "mode": "managed",
      "type": "aws_vpc",        ← Maps to resource type in .tf
      "name": "main",           ← Maps to resource name in .tf
      "provider": "provider[\"registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws\"]",
      "instances": [{
        "attributes": {
          "id": "vpc-abc123",   ← REAL cloud resource ID
          "cidr_block": "10.0.0.0/16",
          "arn": "arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789:vpc/vpc-abc123"
        }
      }]
    }]
  }

  .tf FILE → STATE FILE → CLOUD RESOURCE
  aws_vpc.main → vpc-abc123 → Actual AWS VPC
Q3

Which tool is best for multi-cloud infrastructure provisioning with state management?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Terraform — it's the only tool that combines multi-cloud support, rich state management, plan preview, and a dependency graph.

📖 Explanation

CloudFormation is AWS-only. Bicep is Azure-only. Ansible has no state management (it's configuration management, not provisioning). Pulumi is the closest competitor but has a smaller ecosystem. Terraform's unique combination of multi-cloud + state + plan + graph makes it the industry standard for IaC provisioning.

  IaC TOOL COMPARISON MATRIX:
  ┌──────────────┬───────────┬────────┬───────┬──────────┐
  │ Tool         │ Multi-    │ State  │ Plan  │ Language │
  │              │ Cloud     │ Mgmt   │Preview│          │
  ├──────────────┼───────────┼────────┼───────┼──────────┤
  │ Terraform    │ ✅ YES   │ ✅ YES │ ✅ YES│ HCL      │
  │ CloudFormation│ ❌ AWS   │ ✅ YES │ ✅ YES│ YAML/JSON│
  │ Pulumi       │ ✅ YES   │ ✅ YES │ ✅ YES│ TS/Py/Go │
  │ Ansible      │ ✅ YES   │ ❌ NO  │ ❌ NO │ YAML     │
  │ Bicep        │ ❌ Azure │ ✅ YES │ ✅ YES│ Bicep    │
  │ Crossplane   │ ✅ YES   │ ✅ K8s │ ❌ NO │ YAML     │
  └──────────────┴───────────┴────────┴───────┴──────────┘

  WINNER: Terraform = Multi-Cloud + State + Plan + Graph
Q4

What command shows you what Terraform WILL change BEFORE making any actual changes?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform plan

📖 Explanation

terraform plan is THE most important safety feature in Terraform. It compares desired state (.tf files) with actual state (state file after refresh), and shows exactly what will be created (+), destroyed (-), updated in-place (~), or replaced (-/+). You should ALWAYS run plan before apply — it's your last chance to catch mistakes.

  PLAN OUTPUT LEGEND:
  ┌──────┬────────────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │Symbol│ Meaning                    │ Risk     │
  ├──────┼────────────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │  +   │ CREATE new resource        │ ✅ Safe  │
  │  -   │ DESTROY resource           │ ⚠ Check  │
  │  ~   │ UPDATE in-place            │ ✅ Safe  │
  │ -/+  │ REPLACE (destroy+create)   │ 🔴 DATA LOSS │
  │ <=   │ READ data source (no-op)   │ ✅ Safe  │
  └──────┴────────────────────────────┴──────────┘

  Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy.

  # aws_s3_bucket.logs will be created
  + resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
      + bucket = "anihpj-logs"
      + arn    = (known after apply)
    }

  # aws_instance.web will be replaced (AMI changed!)
  -/+ resource "aws_instance" "web" {  ← DANGER: forces replacement
        ~ ami = "ami-old" → "ami-new"
      }
Q5

What is a Terraform provider?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

A plugin that translates HCL configuration into API calls for a specific service (AWS, GCP, Azure, K8s, etc.).

📖 Explanation

When you write resource "aws_s3_bucket" "name" { ... }, the AWS provider translates that into actual S3 API calls. Each provider is a separate binary downloaded during terraform init. Provider versions are pinned in .terraform.lock.hcl. There are 2,000+ providers on registry.terraform.io.

  PROVIDER ARCHITECTURE:

  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
  │ HCL .tf  │────▶│  TERRAFORM   │────▶│ PROVIDER │
  │  FILES   │     │    CORE      │     │  PLUGIN  │
  └──────────┘     └──────────────┘     └────┬─────┘
                                             │
  terraform {                          ┌─────▼──────┐
    required_providers {               │  CLOUD API │
      aws = {                          │  (AWS S3,  │
        source  = "hashicorp/aws"      │   EC2, EKS)│
        version = "~> 5.0"            └────────────┘
      }
    }
  }

  provider "aws" {
    region = "us-east-1"    ← Provider CONFIG block
  }

  resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {  ← Uses AWS provider
    bucket = "anihpj-assets"
  }

  🔑 Provider = TRANSLATOR: HCL → Cloud API calls
  🔑 Downloaded at terraform init into .terraform/providers/
  🔑 Version locked in .terraform.lock.hcl
Q6

Why is Terraform's plan feature considered a critical safety mechanism?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Plan shows exactly what will change before any changes are made — preventing accidental destruction of production resources.

📖 Explanation

Without plan, you'd be running blind — applying changes without knowing what will be created, modified, or destroyed. Plan shows + (create), - (destroy), ~ (update), and -/+ (replace). If you see -/+ next to an RDS database, you know it will be DESTROYED and RECREATED — meaning data loss! Plan lets you catch this before it happens.

  PLAN AS A SAFETY GATE:

  ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │ .tf     │───▶│ terraform│───▶│ REVIEW  │───▶│ terraform│
  │ FILES   │    │  plan    │    │ OUTPUT  │    │  apply   │
  └─────────┘    └──────────┘    └────┬────┘    └──────────┘
                                      │
                              ┌───────▼────────┐
                              │ SAFETY CHECK:  │
                              │ -/+ on RDS?    │──▶ STOP! Data loss!
                              │  ~ on SG only? │──▶ Safe, proceed
                              │  + 5 resources?│──▶ Verify costs
                              └────────────────┘

  WITHOUT PLAN:  apply → "Why is my database gone?!"
  WITH PLAN:     plan → "-/+ on RDS = recreate → STOP"
Q7

What does HCL stand for, and what files use it?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

HashiCorp Configuration Language. Used in .tf files.

📖 Explanation

HCL is Terraform's domain-specific language designed to be both human-readable and machine-friendly. It's declarative (you say WHAT, not HOW), supports variables, functions, and expressions. HCL files use the .tf extension. Terraform also supports JSON (.tf.json) but HCL is preferred for readability.

  HCL SYNTAX ANATOMY:

  # BLOCK TYPE    # BLOCK LABELS
  ┌─────────┐    ┌────────────────┐
  │resource │ "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  └─────────┘    └────────────────┘
    # ARGUMENTS ─────────────────────┐
    bucket = "anihpj-assets"    ← string
    tags = {                     ← map/object
      Environment = "prod"
      Project     = "anihpj"
    }
    force_destroy = true         ← boolean

    # NESTED BLOCK ─────────────────┐
    versioning {
      enabled = true
    }
  }

  BLOCK TYPES:  resource | data | variable | output |
                locals | terraform | provider | module

  FILE EXTENSIONS:
  .tf        → HCL (human-friendly)
  .tf.json   → JSON (machine-generated)
  .tfvars    → Variable values
  .tftpl     → Template files (templatefile function)
Q8

What is configuration drift and how does Terraform help prevent it?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Configuration drift is when environments diverge from each other or from their intended configuration. Terraform detects drift during terraform plan (stage 3: Refresh) by comparing actual state with desired configuration.

📖 Explanation

Example: Someone manually changes a security group rule in the AWS Console. Next time you run terraform plan, Terraform queries AWS (Refresh), discovers the manual change doesn't match the .tf file, and shows a plan to revert it. You can then terraform apply to fix the drift, or update the .tf file to match the new desired state.

  DRIFT DETECTION & REMEDIATION FLOW:

  ▸ DAY 1: terraform apply
    ┌─────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐
    │ .tf     │────▶│ terraform│────▶│ AWS: SG  │
    │ port:80 │     │  apply   │     │ port:80  │ ✅ MATCH
    └─────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘

  ▸ DAY 2: Manual change in AWS Console
    ┌─────────┐     ┌──────────┐
    │ .tf     │     │ AWS: SG  │
    │ port:80 │     │ port:443 │ ⚠ DRIFT!
    └─────────┘     └──────────┘

  ▸ DAY 2: terraform plan (detects drift)
    ┌─────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
    │ .tf     │────▶│ REFRESH  │────▶│ PLAN OUTPUT:     │
    │ port:80 │     │ queries  │     │ ~ port: 443→80   │
    └─────────┘     │ AWS API  │     │ (revert to match) │
                    └──────────┘     └──────────────────┘

  ▸ REMEDIATION OPTIONS:
    A) terraform apply        → Reverts drift (back to port 80)
    B) Update .tf to port:443 → Accepts the change
Q9

Where should Terraform state be stored for team collaboration?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

In a remote backend — such as S3 (with DynamoDB locking), GCS, Azure Storage, or Terraform Cloud.

📖 Explanation

Local state (terraform.tfstate on your laptop) means only YOU can run Terraform. Remote state enables team collaboration, provides state locking (preventing simultaneous applies), and encrypts state at rest. The most common pattern: S3 bucket for state + DynamoDB table for locking.

  REMOTE STATE BACKENDS:

  # S3 + DynamoDB (AWS — most common)
  terraform {
    backend "s3" {
      bucket         = "anihpj-terraform-state"
      key            = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
      region         = "us-east-1"
      dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"   ← Prevents concurrent applies
      encrypt        = true                ← Server-side encryption
    }
  }

  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │ Developer│    │ Developer│    │    CI/CD │
  │  Alice   │    │   Bob    │    │  Pipeline│
  └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘
       │               │               │
       └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                       │
              ┌────────▼────────┐
              │   S3 BUCKET     │  ← Shared state file
              │   (state)       │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
              ┌────────▼────────┐
              │ DYNAMODB TABLE  │  ← Lock: only ONE apply at a time
              │ (terraform-locks)│
              └─────────────────┘

  ⚠ LOCAL STATE:  terraform.tfstate on laptop → ONLY you can apply
  ✅ REMOTE STATE: S3 bucket → WHOLE TEAM can collaborate
Q10

You have a manually-created S3 bucket. How do you bring it under Terraform management?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Use terraform import aws_s3_bucket.name bucket-name, then write matching .tf configuration.

📖 Explanation

Import writes the resource into state but does NOT generate the .tf file. Steps: (1) Write an empty resource block, (2) Run terraform import, (3) Run terraform plan to see the diff, (4) Update your .tf to match the imported state, (5) Run plan again — should show "No changes."

  IMPORT WORKFLOW — 5-STEP RECIPE:

  EXISTING: S3 bucket "my-legacy-bucket" (created manually 2023)
  GOAL:     Manage it with Terraform WITHOUT recreation

  STEP 1: Write skeleton resource block
  ─────────────────────────────────────
  # main.tf
  resource "aws_s3_bucket" "legacy" {
    bucket = "my-legacy-bucket"  ← Must match EXACT bucket name
  }

  STEP 2: Import into state
  ─────────────────────────
  $ terraform import aws_s3_bucket.legacy my-legacy-bucket
  # aws_s3_bucket.legacy: Importing...
  # Import successful! Resources added to state.

  STEP 3: Discover actual config via plan
  ───────────────────────────────────────
  $ terraform plan
  # Shows DIFF between your skeleton .tf and actual bucket
  # Example: ~ versioning (wants to disable, but bucket has it enabled)
  #         ~ tags (missing in .tf, exists on bucket)

  STEP 4: Update .tf to match reality
  ───────────────────────────────────
  resource "aws_s3_bucket" "legacy" {
    bucket = "my-legacy-bucket"
    versioning { enabled = true }     ← Added to match reality
    tags = { Environment = "prod" }   ← Added to match reality
  }

  STEP 5: Verify sync
  ──────────────────
  $ terraform plan
  # No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
  # ✅ Now managed by Terraform!

  ⚠ KEY GOTCHA: terraform import does NOT generate .tf code.
     You MUST write/update the .tf manually.

2.1 The Terraform Core Engine

What actually happens when you type terraform apply? It's not magic — it's an 8-stage pipeline that transforms your .tf files into real cloud resources.

Terraform Apply — Complete Lifecycle Anatomy
  STAGE         WHAT HAPPENS                                    TIME
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. PARSE      Reads ALL .tf files in working directory.       < 1 sec
     .tf FILES  Validates HCL syntax.

  2. LOAD       Reads terraform.tfstate from local disk or      < 2 sec
     STATE      remote backend (S3/GCS/TFC).

  3. REFRESH    Queries cloud APIs for EVERY resource in        5-60 sec
     STATE      state. Detects drift (manual changes outside    (depends on
                Terraform).                                     # resources)

  4. BUILD      Creates dependency graph (DAG). Determines      < 1 sec
     GRAPH      parallel vs sequential execution order.

  5. PLAN       Compares desired (.tf) vs actual (state).       1-30 sec
                Generates diff: +create/-destroy/~update/-/+replace

  6. SHOW       Displays plan to user. User types "yes" or      Interactive
     PLAN       "no" to confirm.

  7. APPLY      Executes API calls to cloud providers in        30 sec -
                correct order. Creates/updates resources.       20 min

  8. UPDATE     Writes new state file with resource IDs,        < 1 sec
     STATE      attributes, and metadata.
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⏱️  Total: 1-25 minutes (EKS cluster creation: ~15 min)
  🔑 Stage 3 (Refresh) is why terraform plan gets slower over time

2.2 Providers — The Bridge to Cloud APIs

A provider is a plugin that translates HCL into API calls for a specific service. When you write resource "aws_s3_bucket", the AWS provider translates that into actual S3 API calls.

How a Provider Works — From HCL to Cloud API
  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │  HCL IN  │───▶│TERRAFORM │───▶│   AWS    │───▶│  AWS S3  │
  │  .tf FILE│    │  CORE    │    │ PROVIDER │    │   API    │
  │          │    │          │    │          │    │          │
  │ resource │    │ "I need  │    │ Translate│    │ POST /   │
  │ "aws_s3_ │    │  to      │    │ HCL→API  │    │ buckets  │
  │ bucket"  │    │  create  │    │ calls    │    │ {name:   │
  │ "anihpj_ │    │  an S3   │    │          │    │ "anihpj_ │
  │ assets"  │    │  bucket" │    │          │    │ assets"} │
  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘

  🔑 The provider is the TRANSLATOR between HCL and cloud APIs
  🔑 Each provider is a SEPARATE binary (downloaded at terraform init)
  🔑 Provider version is PINNED in .terraform.lock.hcl

The Provider Registry

The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) hosts 2,000+ providers. Each provider is versioned and documented. Providers are downloaded automatically when you run terraform init.

🔑 Provider Authentication — How Terraform Talks to AWS

Providers need credentials to authenticate with cloud APIs. For AWS, Terraform checks these sources in order:

  1. Environment variables: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
  2. Shared credentials file: ~/.aws/credentials (created by aws configure)
  3. IAM role: EC2 instance profile or EKS IRSA (most secure — no static credentials!)
  4. Provider block: provider "aws" { access_key = "..." } (⚠️ avoid — hardcodes secrets)

The exam may test: "Where should provider credentials be stored?" Answer: environment variables or IAM roles — NEVER hardcoded in .tf files!

Anihpj's Providers

Our anihpj project uses 8 providers working together:

☁️
AWS

EKS, RDS, S3, VPC, IAM — the core cloud infrastructure

☸️
Kubernetes

Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets on EKS

⎈
Helm

Install Prometheus, Grafana, ingress-nginx via Helm charts

🐳
Docker

Build and push jobpost Docker images

🔐
TLS

Generate TLS certificates for HTTPS

🎲
Random

Generate unique IDs, names, and passwords

📁
Local

Manage local files (kubeconfig, scripts)

🐙
GitHub

Manage repositories, teams, and CI/CD

2.3 The Dependency Graph

Terraform builds a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) from your configuration. This graph determines the order resources are created — and which can be created in parallel for maximum speed.

Anihpj Dependency Graph — 4-Level Resource Ordering
  LEVEL 1: FOUNDATION (runs FIRST)
  ┌──────────┐
  │   VPC    │  aws_vpc.main (10.0.0.0/16)
  └────┬─────┘
       │
  LEVEL 2: NETWORK (AFTER VPC, ALL IN PARALLEL)
  ┌────┴────┬────────────┬────────────┐
  ▼         ▼            ▼            ▼
  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │Pub-1a│ │Pub-1b│ │Priv  │ │ NAT GW   │
  │subnet│ │subnet│ │subnet│ │(elastic) │
  └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ └────┬─────┘
     └────────┼────────┼──────────┘
              ▼        ▼
  LEVEL 3: COMPUTE (AFTER subnets + NAT, PARALLEL)
     ┌────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
     │ EKS Cluster│ │  RDS (PG)    │
     │ anihpj-k8s │ │ jobpost-db   │
     └─────┬──────┘ └──────┬───────┘
           ▼               ▼
  LEVEL 4: APPLICATION (LAST, AFTER compute)
     ┌──────────────────────────────┐
     │  K8s Resources (namespace,   │
     │  deployment, service, ingress│
     └──────────────────────────────┘

  🔑 PARALLEL: Level 2 subnets all deploy SIMULTANEOUSLY
  🔑 SEQUENTIAL: Each level waits for ALL previous to finish
  🔑 terraform graph | dot -Tpng > graph.png (visualize as PNG!)

Why the Dependency Graph Matters

The dependency graph isn't just an optimization — it's what makes Terraform safe. Here's why:

🛡️
Safe Ordering

Terraform will NEVER try to create an EKS cluster before the VPC exists. The graph guarantees correct ordering — even if you list resources in the "wrong" order in your .tf files.

⚡
Maximum Parallelism

Resources that don't depend on each other are created simultaneously. With the default -parallelism=10, Terraform can create 10 independent resources at once — dramatically faster than sequential execution.

🔍
Failure Isolation

If one subnet creation fails, resources that DON'T depend on that subnet continue unaffected. Only dependent resources are blocked — partial success is better than total failure.

📊
Visualization

Run terraform graph | dot -Tpng > graph.png to generate a visual dependency graph. This is invaluable for understanding complex infrastructure and debugging ordering issues.

2.4 Resource Addressing — How Terraform Names Things

Every resource, variable, and output in Terraform has an address — a unique path you use to reference it. Understanding addressing is critical for writing correct Terraform configurations.

Resource Addressing — Complete Reference
  PATTERN                     EXAMPLE                  RETURNS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE         aws_vpc.main.id          vpc-abc123
  TYPE.NAME.all.ATTRIBUTE     aws_instance.web[*].ip   ["i-1","i-2"]
  module.NAME.OUTPUT          module.vpc.vpc_id        vpc-abc123
  data.TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE    data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id   ami-xyz
  TYPE.NAME[INDEX]            aws_instance.web[0]      First one
  TYPE.NAME["KEY"]            aws_instance.web["dev"]  "dev" instance
  var.NAME                    var.environment          "production"
  local.NAME                  local.common_tags        {Project=..}
  path.module                 path.module              "./modules/vpc"
  path.root                   path.root                "."
  path.cwd                    path.cwd                 (working dir)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  DEPENDENCY TYPES:
  IMPLICIT: Terraform figures it out (use resource references)
    resource "aws_instance" "web" {
      subnet_id = aws_subnet.public.id  ← CREATES dependency
    }

  EXPLICIT: You tell Terraform (use depends_on)
    resource "null_resource" "cleanup" {
      depends_on = [aws_instance.web]  ← MUST wait for this
    }

  ⚠️  EXAM GOTCHA: Most dependencies should be IMPLICIT.
     Use depends_on ONLY when Terraform can't infer the link.
Q1

What are the 8 stages of the terraform apply lifecycle?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Parse .tf → Load State → Refresh State → Build Graph → Plan → Show Plan → Apply → Update State.

📖 Explanation

Stage 3 (Refresh) queries cloud APIs for every resource in state — this is why terraform plan gets slower as you add more resources. Stage 4 (Build Graph) creates a DAG to determine execution order. Stage 7 (Apply) is the only stage that actually makes changes to cloud infrastructure.

  TERRAFORM APPLY — 8-STAGE PIPELINE:

  STAGE 1          STAGE 2          STAGE 3          STAGE 4
  ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐
  │ PARSE  │─────▶│ LOAD   │─────▶│REFRESH │─────▶│ BUILD  │
  │ .tf    │      │ STATE  │      │ STATE  │      │ GRAPH  │
  │ files  │      │ (local/│      │ (query │      │ (DAG)  │
  │        │      │ remote)│      │ clouds)│      │        │
  └────────┘      └────────┘      └────┬───┘      └───┬────┘
       < 1s            < 2s        5-60 sec          < 1s
                                        │               │
  STAGE 8          STAGE 7          STAGE 6          STAGE 5
  ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐
  │ UPDATE │◀─────│ APPLY  │◀─────│ SHOW   │◀─────│  PLAN  │
  │ STATE  │      │ (API   │      │ PLAN   │      │ (diff) │
  │ (write)│      │ calls) │      │ (user  │      │        │
  │        │      │        │      │confirm)│      │        │
  └────────┘      └────────┘      └────────┘      └────────┘
       < 1s      30s-20min       Interactive      1-30 sec

  🔑 Only Stage 7 (Apply) touches cloud infrastructure
  🔑 Stage 3 is why plan gets SLOWER over time (more API calls)
  🔑 Stage 4 enables PARALLEL creation of independent resources
Q2

How does Terraform determine the order in which resources are created?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

By building a Dependency Graph (DAG) from resource references in the configuration.

📖 Explanation

Terraform analyzes all .tf files and builds a Directed Acyclic Graph. Resources that reference each other create edges in the graph (e.g., subnet_id = aws_subnet.public.id creates a dependency). Resources with no dependencies can be created in parallel (up to -parallelism=10 by default).

  DEPENDENCY GRAPH (DAG) — ANIHPJ EXAMPLE:

  LEVEL 1 (first)        LEVEL 2 (parallel)     LEVEL 3 (last)
  ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────────┐
  │ aws_vpc  │─────────▶│ subnet-1a│─────────▶│aws_instance  │
  │ .main    │     ┌───▶│ (public) │     ┌───▶│  .web[0]     │
  └──────────┘     │    └──────────┘     │    └──────────────┘
                   │    ┌──────────┐     │    ┌──────────────┐
                   ├───▶│ subnet-1b│─────┤───▶│aws_instance  │
                   │    │ (public) │     │    │  .web[1]     │
                   │    └──────────┘     │    └──────────────┘
                   │    ┌──────────┐     │
                   └───▶│  subnet  │─────┘
                        │ (private)│
                        └──────────┘

  IMPLICIT DEPENDENCY (from code):
  resource "aws_instance" "web" {
    ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
    subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public["a"].id  ← Creates edge in DAG
    vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id]
  }
  # Terraform infers: subnet + SG before instance

  EXPLICIT DEPENDENCY (rare):
  depends_on = [aws_instance.web]  ← Use only when Terraform can't infer
Q3

What is the difference between implicit and explicit dependencies?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Implicit: Terraform infers from resource references. Explicit: You use depends_on.

📖 Explanation

Implicit: subnet_id = aws_subnet.public.id — Terraform knows subnet must exist before EC2. Explicit: depends_on = [aws_instance.web] — used when Terraform can't infer the dependency (e.g., a null_resource that runs a script after EC2 creation). Best practice: prefer implicit dependencies.

  IMPLICIT vs EXPLICIT:

  ✅ IMPLICIT (preferred — 95% of cases):
  resource "aws_instance" "web" {
    subnet_id = aws_subnet.public.id     ← Terraform INFERS dependency
  }
  # Terraform: "subnet.id is referenced → create subnet first"

  ⚠ EXPLICIT (use sparingly — 5% of cases):
  resource "null_resource" "post_deploy" {
    depends_on = [aws_instance.web]      ← YOU declare dependency
    provisioner "local-exec" {
      command = "curl http://${aws_instance.web.public_ip}/health"
    }
  }
  # Use when: Terraform CANNOT see the dependency in code

  COMMON EXPLICIT DEPENDENCY SCENARIOS:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Scenario                    │ Why depends_on needed    │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Run script after deploy     │ No HCL reference to      │
  │                             │ null_resource from EC2   │
  │ IAM policy → S3 bucket      │ Policy references ARN    │
  │ (circular if implicit)      │ but bucket needs policy  │
  │ Cross-module ordering       │ Module A doesn't ref     │
  │ (no shared outputs)         │ Module B's resources     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q4

How do you reference a specific resource's attribute in Terraform?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Using the pattern TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE (e.g., aws_vpc.main.id).

📖 Explanation

Other addressing patterns: module.NAME.OUTPUT for modules, data.TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE for data sources, var.NAME for variables, local.NAME for locals. For resources using count, use index: aws_instance.web[0]. For for_each, use key: aws_instance.web["dev"].

Q5

Where does Terraform download providers from, and when?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

From registry.terraform.io during terraform init.

📖 Explanation

terraform init reads the required_providers block, downloads the specified providers, and creates .terraform.lock.hcl to pin exact versions for reproducible builds. Providers are cached locally in .terraform/providers/. Always run terraform init -upgrade when you need newer provider versions.

Q6

What happens during the Refresh stage of terraform apply?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Terraform queries cloud APIs for every resource in state to detect drift — changes made outside Terraform.

📖 Explanation

Refresh (Stage 3) calls cloud APIs to get the current state of every managed resource. If someone manually changed a security group, Refresh detects the difference. This is why terraform plan gets slower over time — more resources = more API calls during Refresh. Use -refresh=false to skip (faster but risky).

Q7

What is the parallel execution limit for resource creation, and how do you change it?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Default: 10 parallel operations. Change with -parallelism=N flag.

📖 Explanation

terraform apply -parallelism=20 creates up to 20 resources simultaneously. Increasing parallelism speeds up large deployments but may hit cloud API rate limits. Resources that depend on each other are always created sequentially regardless of parallelism setting.

Q8

How do you reference a module's output value?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Using module.NAME.OUTPUT (e.g., module.vpc.vpc_id).

📖 Explanation

Module outputs are the primary way modules share data. Example: if your VPC module outputs vpc_id, you reference it as module.vpc.vpc_id. This creates an implicit dependency — the consuming resource waits for the module to complete. Module outputs appear in terraform output and can be used by other modules.

Q9

Where should provider credentials (AWS access keys) be stored?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

In environment variables or IAM roles — NEVER hardcoded in .tf files.

📖 Explanation

Priority order: (1) AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID env vars, (2) ~/.aws/credentials file, (3) IAM role (EC2 instance profile / EKS IRSA), (4) provider block (⚠️ avoid). Hardcoding credentials in .tf files exposes them in Git history and state files. Always use the credential chain.

Q10

What command visualizes the Terraform dependency graph as an image?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform graph | dot -Tpng > graph.png

📖 Explanation

terraform graph outputs the dependency graph in DOT format. Piping to dot (from Graphviz) renders it as a PNG image. This is invaluable for understanding complex infrastructure — you can visually verify that resources will be created in the correct order and identify unnecessary dependencies.

  GRAPH VISUALIZATION PIPELINE:

  $ terraform graph | dot -Tpng > anihpj-graph.png

  DOT OUTPUT (what terraform graph produces):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ digraph {                                  │
  │   "[root] aws_vpc.main" [label=aws_vpc]   │
  │   "[root] aws_subnet.public" [label=...]  │
  │   "[root] aws_vpc.main" ->                │
  │     "[root] aws_subnet.public"             │
  │   "[root] aws_subnet.public" ->            │
  │     "[root] aws_instance.web"              │
  │ }                                          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  INSTALL GRAPHVIZ:
  macOS:  brew install graphviz
  Linux:  apt install graphviz
  Win:    choco install graphviz

  ALSO USEFUL — terraform graph -type=plan:
  # Shows only resources that WILL change (shorter output)
  $ terraform plan -out=plan && terraform graph -type=plan plan

3.1 Installation (macOS, Linux, Windows, Docker)

🍎 macOS (Homebrew)

Terminal
brew tap hashicorp/tap
brew install hashicorp/tap/terraform
terraform version
# → Terraform v1.8.x on darwin_amd64

🐧 Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)

Terminal
wget -O- https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/hashicorp.gpg] https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com $(lsb_release -cs) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/hashicorp.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install terraform

PowerShell

Terminal
docker run -it --rm -v $(pwd):/workspace hashicorp/terraform:latest plan
✅ Verify Your Installation

Run terraform version — you should see the version number and platform. Also install terraform-docs (optional): brew install terraform-docs — auto-generates README from your .tf files.

3.2 The Terraform CLI — Commands You'll Use Daily

These 6 commands form the core workflow you'll use every day:

CommandPurposeWhen to Use
terraform initInitialize directory, download providers, configure backendFirst command in any project
terraform fmtFormat .tf files consistentlyBefore every commit
terraform validateCheck syntax validityBefore plan (CI gate)
terraform planPreview changes (NO changes made)Before EVERY apply
terraform applyCreate/update infrastructureAfter reviewing plan
terraform destroyTear down everythingCleanup dev environments
Complete Workflow — Anihpj Terminal Session
  $ cd anihpj/terraform/envs/dev

  $ terraform fmt -recursive -check      # ✅ Format check
  $ terraform validate                    # ✅ Syntax OK

  $ terraform init                        # Download providers
  Initializing provider plugins...
  - Installing hashicorp/aws v5.40.0...
  Terraform has been successfully initialized!

  $ terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan      # Preview changes
  # aws_vpc.main will be created
  # aws_subnet.public["us-east-1a"] will be created
  Plan: 23 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

  $ terraform apply plan.tfplan          # Make it real!
  aws_vpc.main: Creating... → Complete! [vpc-0abc...]
  Apply complete! Resources: 23 added.

  $ kubectl get pods -n jobpost          # 🎉 anihpj is LIVE!
  NAME                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  jobpost-7d4f8-abcde   1/1     Running   0          2m

3.3 Your First Terraform Project — Hello anihpj!

Let's create your first Terraform resource: an S3 bucket for anihpj's static assets. In about 15 lines of code, you'll create real cloud infrastructure.

main.tf
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws"; version = "~> 5.0" }
  }
}
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "anihpj_assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-static-assets-${random_id.bucket_suffix.hex}"
  tags = {
    Name = "anihpj-static-assets"; Environment = "dev"
    Project = "anihpj"; App = "jobpost"; ManagedBy = "terraform"
  }
}
resource "random_id" "bucket_suffix" { byte_length = 4 }

# WORKFLOW: init → fmt → validate → plan → apply → destroy
⚡ S3 Bucket Names Must Be Globally Unique

The random_id resource adds a random suffix to avoid name collisions. S3 bucket names are globally unique across ALL AWS accounts. Without the random suffix, your terraform apply would fail because someone else already used "anihpj-static-assets".

What Just Happened? — Understanding the Magic

Let's trace exactly what happened when you ran those commands:

terraform init

Read main.tf, discovered you need the aws and random providers, downloaded them from registry.terraform.io, and created .terraform.lock.hcl to pin their versions.

terraform plan

Compared your desired state (main.tf) with actual state (nothing exists yet — this is your first run). Determined: "I need to create 2 resources: aws_s3_bucket + random_id."

terraform apply

First created random_id.bucket_suffix (instant), then used its value to create aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets with a globally unique name. Wrote both resources to terraform.tfstate.

What if you run terraform apply again?

Terraform checks state, sees the bucket already exists, compares with .tf — no changes needed. Output: "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration." This is idempotency — running the same command twice produces the same result.

3.4 Project Structure — Organizing .tf Files for anihpj

A well-organized Terraform project is essential for maintainability. Here's the recommended structure for anihpj:

Anihpj Terraform Project Structure
  anihpj/terraform/
  ├── main.tf              # Primary resource definitions
  ├── variables.tf          # Input variable declarations
  ├── outputs.tf            # Output value definitions
  ├── terraform.tfvars      # Variable values (GITIGNORE if secrets!)
  ├── providers.tf          # Provider configuration + aliases
  ├── versions.tf           # Terraform & provider version constraints
  ├── backend.tf            # Remote state configuration (S3 + DynamoDB)
  ├── .terraform.lock.hcl   # AUTO-GENERATED — locks provider versions
  ├── modules/              # Reusable Terraform modules
  │   ├── vpc/              #   VPC + subnets + NAT + route tables
  │   ├── eks/              #   EKS cluster + node groups + IAM
  │   └── rds/              #   RDS PostgreSQL + parameter groups
  └── envs/                 # Environment-specific configurations
      ├── dev/              #   Development (t3.small, 1 node)
      ├── staging/          #   Staging (t3.medium, 2 nodes)
      └── prod/             #   Production (t3.large, 3+ nodes)
🔑 File Names Are Just Convention

Terraform reads ALL .tf files in the working directory and merges them into one configuration. The file names (main.tf, variables.tf, etc.) are human conventions — not requirements. You could put everything in stuff.tf and Terraform would work fine. But DON'T do that — the convention exists for a reason: readability and maintainability.

What Each File Does — Anihpj File Map

FilePurposeExample Content
main.tfPrimary resource definitionsaws_eks_cluster, aws_db_instance
variables.tfDeclare input variables (type, default, validation)variable "environment" { type = string }
outputs.tfExpose values after applyoutput "eks_endpoint" { value = ... }
terraform.tfvarsAssign values to variables (GITIGNORE if secrets!)environment = "production"
providers.tfConfigure cloud providers + aliasesprovider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }
versions.tfPin Terraform + provider versionsrequired_version = ">= 1.5.0"
backend.tfRemote state configuration (S3 + DynamoDB)backend "s3" { bucket = "..." }
.terraform.lock.hclAUTO-GENERATED: locks provider versions for reproducible builds. Git TRACK this file!DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY

Environment Separation — Why dev/staging/prod Are Separate Directories

Notice that envs/dev/, envs/staging/, and envs/prod/ are separate directories, each with their own state. This is intentional blast-radius isolation:

🛡️
Blast Radius Isolation

If you accidentally run terraform destroy in dev, only dev is destroyed. Production is completely unaffected — separate state, separate directory.

🔧
Different Configurations

Dev uses t3.small with 1 EKS node. Production uses t3.large with 3+ nodes. Same module code, different variable values per environment.

👥
Independent Lifecycles

Deploy to dev 5× daily, production once weekly. Separate state = separate lifecycles — no cross-contamination.

🔐
Access Control

Developers can apply to dev. Only SREs can apply to production. Enforced at the directory/state/bucket level.

💡 Use tfenv for Version Management

Install tfenv to switch between Terraform versions: brew install tfenv → tfenv install 1.8.5 → tfenv use 1.8.5. Different projects may need different versions. The exam has a specific version pre-installed.

Q1

What is the correct order of the core Terraform workflow?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform init → terraform fmt → terraform validate → terraform plan → terraform apply

📖 Explanation

Init downloads providers and configures the backend. Fmt formats code consistently. Validate checks syntax. Plan previews changes (ALWAYS before apply). Apply makes real changes. This workflow is used in 80% of exam hands-on tasks.

  CORE WORKFLOW PIPELINE:

  ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐
  │  INIT  │──▶│  FMT   │──▶│ VALIDATE │──▶│  PLAN  │──▶│ APPLY  │
  └───┬────┘   └───┬────┘   └────┬─────┘   └───┬────┘   └───┬────┘
      │            │             │             │            │
  Download     Standardize    Catch syntax   Preview      Execute
  providers    HCL style      errors early   changes      changes
  config bknd  (-check CI)    (no API calls) (safety!)   (real API)

  $ terraform init -upgrade           # Download providers
  $ terraform fmt -recursive -check   # Check formatting (CI gate)
  $ terraform validate                # Syntax check (fast!)
  $ terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan   # Preview + save plan
  $ terraform apply plan.tfplan       # Execute saved plan

  ⚠ SKIPPING PLAN = PRODUCTION OUTAGE RISK
  ✅ ALWAYS: plan → review → apply
Q2

What command initializes a Terraform working directory?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform init

📖 Explanation

Init is the FIRST command in any Terraform project. It downloads required providers, configures the backend (local or remote), and creates .terraform.lock.hcl. You must run init again if you change provider versions, module sources, or backend configuration.

Q3

How do you format all Terraform files in a directory?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform fmt -recursive

📖 Explanation

terraform fmt formats .tf files to the canonical HCL style. -recursive formats all subdirectories too. -check only checks formatting without changing files (used in CI pipelines as a gate). Best practice: run fmt before every commit.

Q4

What does terraform validate check?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Syntax validity and internal consistency of .tf files (does NOT check cloud API access).

📖 Explanation

Validate checks: valid HCL syntax, correct resource type names, valid variable references, consistent attribute types. It does NOT check if AWS credentials work or if resource names conflict — that happens during plan/apply. Always validate before plan — it's fast and catches basic errors.

Q5

What is the purpose of the .terraform.lock.hcl file?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

It locks provider versions to ensure reproducible builds across all team members and CI/CD pipelines.

📖 Explanation

The lock file records the exact version and checksum of every provider used. It should be committed to Git. Without it, different team members might get different provider versions, leading to inconsistent behavior. The lock file is auto-generated — never edit it manually.

Q6

What 4 required fields does every resource block need?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

resource type (e.g., "aws_s3_bucket"), resource name (e.g., "assets"), plus at least one argument appropriate to the resource type.

📖 Explanation

Syntax: resource "TYPE" "NAME" { argument = value }. The TYPE identifies which provider resource to create. The NAME is your local identifier for referencing. Arguments vary by resource type — check terraform docs or the registry. Some resources have required arguments (e.g., S3 bucket needs a name).

Q7

How do you save a plan to apply later without re-prompting?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan then terraform apply plan.tfplan

📖 Explanation

Saving a plan file lets you review it, get approval, and apply exactly what was planned — even if the .tf files changed in between. The saved plan is a binary file. Applying a saved plan skips the interactive confirmation prompt. This is the standard pattern for CI/CD pipelines and production deployments.

  SAVED PLAN WORKFLOW:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CI/CD PIPELINE PATTERN                               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │                                                      │
  │  PR OPENED:                                          │
  │  $ terraform plan -out=pr-42.tfplan                  │
  │  # → Plan saved to pr-42.tfplan (binary)            │
  │  # → Post plan output as PR comment                  │
  │  # → Reviewer sees: "Plan: 3 to add, 0 to destroy"  │
  │                                                      │
  │  PR MERGED:                                          │
  │  $ terraform apply pr-42.tfplan                      │
  │  # → Executes EXACTLY what was planned               │
  │  # → NO interactive prompt (plan already approved)   │
  │  # → Even if main.tf changed, applies original plan  │
  │                                                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠ WARNING: If .tf files changed after plan, apply will
     differ from current code. Best practice: re-plan.

  $ terraform show plan.tfplan    # Read binary plan file
  $ terraform show -json plan.tfplan  # JSON format
Q8

Why should terraform.tfvars be in .gitignore?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Because it may contain sensitive values (passwords, API keys). Even if it doesn't, it contains environment-specific values that shouldn't be in shared Git history.

📖 Explanation

If terraform.tfvars contains db_password = "supersecret" and you commit it, that password is now permanently in Git history. Even if you delete it later, anyone can find it in old commits. Use .auto.tfvars for non-sensitive defaults you DO want to commit, and terraform.tfvars for sensitive/environment-specific values.

Q9

What is the difference between main.tf and terraform.tfvars?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

main.tf defines WHAT to create (resource declarations). terraform.tfvars assigns VALUES to variables.

📖 Explanation

Think of main.tf as the blueprint (I need a VPC with CIDR var.vpc_cidr) and terraform.tfvars as the specifications (vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"). The separation lets you reuse the same main.tf across environments while changing only the .tfvars file.

Q10

How does Terraform achieve idempotency?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

By comparing desired state (.tf) with actual state (state file) — if they match, nothing changes. Running the same terraform apply multiple times produces the same result.

📖 Explanation

Idempotency means "run once or run 100 times, same result." After the first terraform apply, the state file records all created resources. Subsequent applies see that desired = actual and output "No changes." This is critical for CI/CD — you can safely re-run apply without creating duplicate resources.

  IDEMPOTENCY DEMONSTRATED:

  RUN 1: terraform apply
  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐
  │ .tf says │────▶│ COMPARE  │────▶│ CREATE   │
  │ "VPC-10" │     │ desired  │     │ VPC      │
  └──────────┘     │ vs actual│     └──────────┘
                   │ (no VPC) │
                   └──────────┘
  Result: 1 added → state updated → vpc-abc123 created

  RUN 2: terraform apply (same .tf, no changes)
  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐
  │ .tf says │────▶│ COMPARE  │
  │ "VPC-10" │     │ desired  │──▶ "No changes. Your infrastructure
  └──────────┘     │ vs actual│     matches the configuration."
                   │ VPC exists│
                   │ ✅ MATCH │
                   └──────────┘
  Result: 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed

  🎯 SAME .tf + SAME state = SAME result — every time
  🎯 This is why Terraform is SAFE in CI/CD loops
