Chapter 4: The Terraform Configuration Language (HCL Basics)

Now that you understand the "why," let's dive into the "how." HCL is Terraform's domain-specific language — designed to be both human-readable and machine-friendly. We'll cover blocks, variables, outputs, locals, and data sources with anihpj examples.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours📝 HCL🎯 Core Skill

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ All 10 HCL block types and when to use each one
  • ✅ Variables: 9 types, assignment methods, precedence rules
  • ✅ Outputs: exposing infrastructure information after apply
  • ✅ Locals: DRY principle inside a module
  • ✅ Data Sources: reading external information from AWS
🎓 Exam Relevance
Domain 2: Dynamic ConfigVariables & Outputs

4.1 HCL Syntax — Blocks, Arguments, and Expressions

HCL files consist of blocks that contain arguments in key = value format. Every resource, variable, and output is defined as a block.

HCL Syntax Anatomy — Resource Block Breakdown
  resource "aws_instance" "jobpost_server" {
  ↑        ↑            ↑
  Block    Provider     Resource Name (your label)
  Type     Type

    ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"
    ↑             ↑
    Argument      Value

    instance_type = var.instance_size
                    ↑
                    Expression (variable reference)
  }
  Comments: # single-line, // single-line, /* multi-line */
All 10 HCL Block Types
  BLOCK TYPE    PURPOSE                        EXAMPLE
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  terraform     Meta-config (versions, backend)  terraform { required_version = ">= 1.5" }
  provider      Cloud API connection              provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }
  resource      WHAT to create (main block!)      resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" { ... }
  data          READ existing cloud info          data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" { ... }
  variable      DECLARE inputs                    variable "env" { type = string }
  output        EXPOSE values after apply         output "eks_endpoint" { value = ... }
  locals        DRY reusable expressions          locals { common_tags = { ... } }
  module        CALL a child module               module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" }
  moved         REFACTOR without destroying       moved { from = old; to = new }
  import        BRING existing resources in       import { to = resource; id = "..." }
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 EXAM: resource, data, variable, output, module — these 5 are in EVERY config

4.2 Variables — Making Configurations Reusable

Variables let you parameterize your Terraform configuration — same .tf files, different values for dev/staging/prod.

Variable Types

TypeExampleAssignment
string"anihpj"TF_VAR_name
number3TF_VAR_count
booltrue-var='enabled=true'
list(string)["us-east-1a","us-east-1b"]*.tfvars lists
map(string){dev="t3.small", prod="t3.large"}*.tfvars maps
set(string)toset(["http","https"])unique values
object({...}){name=string, cidr=string}*.tfvars objects
tuple([...])[string, number, bool]positional
anyaccepts any typeflexible

Variable Assignment Priority

When a variable is set in multiple ways, Terraform uses this priority (highest first):

  1. CLI -var or -var-file (overrides EVERYTHING)
  2. *.auto.tfvars (automatically loaded)
  3. terraform.tfvars (loaded by default)
  4. TF_VAR_name environment variables
  5. default value in variable declaration

Anihpj Variable Example

variables.tf
variable "environment" {
  type    = string
  default = "dev"
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev","staging","prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "Must be dev, staging, or prod"
  }
}
variable "instance_types" {
  type = map(string)
  default = { dev = "t3.small", staging = "t3.medium", prod = "t3.large" }
}
# Usage: instance_type = var.instance_types[var.environment]

4.3 Outputs — Getting Information Back

Outputs expose values after terraform apply completes. They're how you get the EKS endpoint, RDS hostname, or ALB DNS name after infrastructure is created.

outputs.tf
output "eks_endpoint" { value = aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.endpoint; description = "EKS API endpoint" }
output "rds_hostname" { value = aws_db_instance.jobpost.address; sensitive = true }
output "alb_dns"      { value = aws_lb.main.dns_name }

4.4 Locals — DRY Inside a Module

Locals define reusable expressions within a module. Unlike variables, locals can't be overridden from outside.

locals block
locals {
  common_tags = { Project = "anihpj"; ManagedBy = "terraform" }
  name_prefix = "${var.environment}-anihpj"
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" { tags = merge(local.common_tags, { Name = local.name_prefix }) }
💡 Locals vs Variables — When to Use Which

Variables = inputs from the outside (can be overridden by callers). Locals = internal computations (can't be overridden). Use variables for things that CHANGE per environment (var.instance_size). Use locals for things you COMPUTE from other values (local.name_prefix = "${var.env}-${var.app}") or for constants shared across resources (local.common_tags). If you find yourself repeating the same expression, make it a local.

4.5 Data Sources — Reading External Information

Data sources READ existing cloud resources without creating or modifying them. They execute during plan and apply.

Data SourceWhat It ReadsAnihpj Use Case
aws_amiLatest Ubuntu AMIEC2 instance launch
aws_caller_identityAWS Account IDIAM policies
aws_eks_cluster_authEKS auth tokenKubernetes provider
aws_secretsmanager_secret_versionDB passwordK8s secrets
aws_availability_zonesAvailable AZsSubnet planning

4.6 Why HCL? — The Design Philosophy Behind Terraform's Language

HCL wasn't created by accident. HashiCorp designed it to solve specific problems that plague infrastructure management. Understanding the "why" behind HCL makes you a better Terraform practitioner — and helps on the exam.

HCL Design Goals — What Makes It Different
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ GOAL 1: HUMAN-READABLE (unlike JSON/YAML for complex infra)       │
  │ HCL: resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" }   │
  │ JSON: {"resource":{"aws_vpc":{"main":{"cidr_block":"10..."}}}}   │
  │ → HCL eliminates noise: no quotes on keys, no commas, no braces  │
  │   for every level. Your eyes focus on WHAT matters, not syntax.  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ GOAL 2: DECLARATIVE (you say WHAT, not HOW)                       │
  │ HCL: "I want a VPC with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16"                        │
  │ Terraform figures out: check if exists → create if not → order   │
  │ → You don't write: "Step 1: create, Step 2: check, Step 3: retry"│
  │   Terraform handles ALL the procedural complexity for you.       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ GOAL 3: EXPRESSIVE (variables, functions, references)             │
  │ HCL: instance_type = var.env == "prod" ? "t3.large" : "t3.small" │
  │ → Conditional logic, for-loops, functions, and type constraints  │
  │   let you express complex infrastructure logic cleanly.          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ GOAL 4: IDEMPOTENT BY DEFAULT                                     │
  │ HCL + State: Running the same .tf twice = SAME result, no dupes. │
  │ → Terraform compares desired vs actual. If they match = no-op.   │
  │   This is why terraform is SAFE in CI/CD loops.                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝
HCL vs YAML: The Infrastructure Language War

YAML (used by CloudFormation, Ansible, Kubernetes) is great for flat key-value configs but becomes painful with deep nesting. A 200-line CloudFormation template can be 50 lines of HCL. HCL eliminates YAML's indentation sensitivity, confusing array syntax (- vs []), and multi-line string escaping. For infrastructure where resources reference each other heavily, HCL is dramatically more readable.

🔗
References: The Secret Sauce

HCL's killer feature is cross-resource references: subnet_id = aws_subnet.public.id. This SINGLE line tells Terraform: (1) the subnet must exist before the EC2 instance, (2) use the subnet's ID as the value, (3) if the subnet changes, the EC2 instance may need updating. In YAML, you'd need !Ref, !GetAtt, DependsOn, and external scripts to achieve the same result. HCL's reference system is what makes Terraform so powerful.

Chapter 5: Planning and Applying — The Heart of Terraform

The plan→apply cycle is where Terraform's power truly shines. Understanding plan output symbols and lifecycle meta-arguments is critical for both the exam and real-world production use.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours⚡ Core Workflow🎯 High-Yield Exam

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Interpret every plan output symbol (+ - ~ -/+ <=)
  • ✅ Master apply modes: saved plan, auto-approve, parallelism
  • ✅ Use destroy safely with targeting and lifecycle protections
  • ✅ Apply 6 lifecycle meta-arguments for production safety
🎓 Exam Relevance
Domain 1: Resource LifecycleDomain 2: Dynamic ConfigHIGH YIELD
🧪 Exam Traps in Plan/Apply Questions
  • Trap 1: You see -/+ and ignore it — that RDS database WILL be destroyed! Always read plan output carefully.
  • Trap 2: Using -auto-approve in production without saving the plan first. Always plan -out=FILE → review → apply FILE.
  • Trap 3: Confusing prevent_destroy (blocks deletion) with create_before_destroy (controls replacement order).
  • Trap 4: Using -target regularly instead of removing resources from config. -target is for emergencies only.

5.1 terraform plan — Preview Before You Leap

SymbolMeaningImpact
+CREATE (doesn't exist yet)New resource
-DESTROY (removed from config)Resource gone
~UPDATE IN-PLACE (modify attribute)Safe, no downtime
-/+REPLACE (destroy then create)⚠️ DOWNTIME!
<=READ (data source, no change)Info only
No changesMATCHES (desired = actual)✅ All good
🔑 -/+ Means DESTROY AND RECREATE

If you see -/+ next to aws_db_instance, that RDS database will be destroyed and recreated — all data lost! Always investigate -/+ before approving. Common causes: changing engine, storage_type, or identifier on RDS.

5.2 terraform apply — Make It Real

Terminal
# Standard: show plan, ask confirmation, apply
terraform apply

# Save plan for review, apply later (no re-prompt)
terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
terraform apply plan.tfplan

# CI/CD: skip confirmation
terraform apply -auto-approve

# Increase parallelism (default 10)
terraform apply -parallelism=20

5.3 terraform destroy — Clean Up Everything

⚠️ DESTROY IS IRREVERSIBLE

terraform destroy removes ALL resources in the current state. Use -target=resource for selective destruction. Always run terraform plan -destroy first to preview what will be removed.

5.4 Resource Lifecycle — Meta-Arguments

Meta-ArgumentWhat It DoesAnihpj Use Case
create_before_destroyCreate new BEFORE destroying oldZero-downtime EKS node upgrade
prevent_destroyBlock terraform destroyRDS database, S3 with user data
ignore_changesDon't update specific attributesTags added by external automation
replace_triggered_byReplace when referenced value changesEC2 replace on AMI change
preconditionValidate BEFORE creationRDS port must be 5432

5.5 Understanding What Happens During Plan and Apply — Deep Dive

The plan→apply cycle is more than just two commands. Understanding the internal mechanics helps you debug issues, predict behavior, and answer exam questions correctly. Here's what actually happens:

🔍

Plan Phase — What Runs Under the Hood

$ terraform plan
1
Configuration Parsing

Terraform reads ALL .tf and .tfvars files. Validates HCL syntax — catches typos, missing brackets, bad refs. If PARSING fails → error immediately, no API calls made.

2
State Refresh(unless -refresh=false)

Queries cloud APIs: "What resources do I already manage?" Compares cloud reality against the state file. Detects DRIFT: "State says port 80, but AWS shows port 443!" This is why plans get slower with more resources.

3
Diff Computation

Compares desired state (.tf files) vs actual state (after refresh). Determines: + CREATE, - DESTROY, ~ UPDATE, -/+ REPLACE. Builds the dependency graph to order operations correctly.

4
Plan Output

Shows you exactly what WOULD change. NOTHING has changed yet. This is Terraform's superpower — preview BEFORE execution. READ ONLY ✅

🚀

Apply Phase — Making Changes Real

$ terraform apply
1
Re-Run Plan(unless applying saved plan file)

Same as terraform plan — refreshes state, computes diff. Shows plan output AGAIN for final review. Apply time ≈ 2× plan time (unless using -out=FILE saved plan).

2
User Confirmation(unless -auto-approve or saved plan)

Terraform pauses: "Do you want to perform these actions?" Type yes to proceed. This is your LAST chance to abort. With -auto-approve, this step is skipped — use ONLY in CI/CD pipelines.

3
Resource Creation / Modification

Calls cloud APIs in dependency order. Independent resources are created IN PARALLEL (up to -parallelism=N, default 10). Each resource: CREATE → READ → UPDATE STATE. If one resource fails: Terraform stops, marks partial state.

4
State Update

Writes new state file with all resource IDs and attributes. The state file is the BRIDGE between your .tf code and cloud reality. Without this step, Terraform would "forget" what it created. INFRA UPDATED ✅

🔮

Plan = Preview Only

0 API changes. 100% safe.

⏱️

Apply = 2× Plan Time

Plan re-runs before apply.

💾

Save Plan to Skip

-out=tfplan skips re-plan.

🔮
Why Plan First?

Plan is FREE — it makes zero changes to your infrastructure. It's like a "dry run" that tells you exactly what will happen. Running apply without plan is like deploying code without code review. Always plan first. The exam tests this: "What command do you run to preview changes?" — answer is always terraform plan.

💾
Saved Plans: The CI/CD Pattern

terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan captures the EXACT diff at that moment. Later, terraform apply plan.tfplan executes precisely what was planned — even if .tf files changed in between. This is how CI/CD pipelines work: plan in the PR, apply after merge. The saved plan is a binary file (not human-readable — use terraform show plan.tfplan to inspect it).

Chapter 6: Working with Multiple Resources

Terraform shines when managing many resources. Learn how to create multiple copies with count, iterate over maps with for_each, and use dynamic blocks to reduce repetition.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔁 Iteration🎯 Exam Essential

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Implicit vs explicit resource dependencies
  • ✅ count for creating identical resource copies
  • ✅ for_each for map/set-based iteration (MORE stable)
  • ✅ Dynamic blocks to reduce nested repetition
  • ✅ When to use count vs for_each (exam favorite!)

6.1 Resource Dependencies — Implicit vs Explicit

Implicit: Terraform figures it out from references. Explicit: You use depends_on. Prefer implicit — it's cleaner and safer.

✅ IMPLICIT (Preferred)
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  subnet_id = aws_subnet.public.id  # ← Creates dependency
}

Terraform sees the reference and knows: subnet must be created FIRST. No extra code needed. 95% of dependencies should be implicit.

⚠️ EXPLICIT (Use Sparingly)
resource "null_resource" "cleanup" {
  depends_on = [aws_instance.web]  # ← Manual dependency
}

Use ONLY when Terraform can't infer the link (scripts after resource creation). Overusing depends_on creates unnecessary bottlenecks.

6.2 Count — Creating Multiple Copies

main.tf
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  count         = 3
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  tags          = { Name = "web-${count.index}" }  # web-0, web-1, web-2
}
# ⚠️ Removing index[1] may re-create ALL instances — count is positional!

6.3 for_each — Iterate Over Maps and Sets

main.tf — Anihpj Subnets
variable "subnets" { type = map(object({ cidr = string; az = string })) }
resource "aws_subnet" "env" {
  for_each   = var.subnets
  vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block = each.value.cidr
  tags       = { Name = "subnet-${each.key}" }  # subnet-dev, subnet-prod
}
# ✅ Removing "dev" from map = only dev subnet destroyed — stable!
Count vs for_each — Side-by-Side
  ❌ COUNT (positional — fragile)              ✅ FOR_EACH (key-based — stable)
  ─────────────────────────────────           ─────────────────────────────────
  resource "aws_subnet" "env" {                resource "aws_subnet" "env" {
    count = 3                                    for_each = var.environments
    cidr  = "10.0.${count.index}.0/24"          cidr    = each.value.cidr
    tags  = { Name = "subnet-${count.index}" }  tags    = { Env = each.key }
  }                                            }
  Result: env[0], env[1], env[2]               Result: env["dev"], env["staging"],
                                                       env["prod"]
  Removing [1] shifts all indexes:             Removing "staging" key:
  env[1] and env[2] DESTROYED & recreated 💀    only staging destroyed ✅
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  🔑 for_each = STABLE (key-based). count = SEQUENTIAL (index-based).
     Use for_each when resources are named/different.
     Use count only for identical, interchangeable clones.
🔑 Count vs for_each — Exam Favorite

count = sequential (index 0,1,2). Removing index 1 may cause all to recreate. for_each = key-based. Removing a key only affects that one resource. Rule: use count for identical clones, for_each for named/different resources.

6.4 Dynamic Blocks — Generate Nested Blocks

Dynamic blocks eliminate repetition when you have many similar nested blocks — like security group rules or IAM policy statements.

Dynamic Block Example — Security Group
variable "ingress_ports" { type = list(number); default = [80, 443, 8080] }

resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  name = "anihpj-web-sg"
  
  dynamic "ingress" {
    for_each = var.ingress_ports
    content {
      from_port   = ingress.value
      to_port     = ingress.value
      protocol    = "tcp"
      cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
    }
  }
}
# Generates 3 ingress rules (ports 80, 443, 8080) from 5 lines
# Without dynamic: 30+ lines of repeated ingress blocks

6.5 The Splat Expression (*) and For Expressions

Transform lists and maps into new shapes. Essential for extracting information from multiple resources.

For Expression Examples
# Splat: get all public IPs from count-created instances
aws_instance.web[*].public_ip  →  ["54.1.2.3", "54.4.5.6", "54.7.8.9"]

# For expression: transform list
[for s in var.subnets : s.cidr_block]  →  ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]

# Filter with condition
[for s in var.subnets : s.id if s.public == true]  →  only public subnet IDs

# Map from list (key = element property)
{ for s in var.subnets : s.name => s.cidr_block }  →  {"dev"="10.0.1.0/24", ...}
Q1

What are the 4 required fields in every Terraform resource block?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Block type (resource), provider type ("aws_s3_bucket"), resource name ("assets"), and at least one argument.

📖 Explanation

Syntax: resource "TYPE" "NAME" { ARGUMENT = VALUE }. The TYPE tells Terraform which provider resource to create. The NAME is your local identifier. Arguments vary by resource — check the registry or terraform docs for required arguments per resource type.

Q2

What is the highest priority way to assign a variable value?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

CLI flags: -var or -var-file override EVERYTHING else.

📖 Explanation

Priority order (highest→lowest): 1) CLI -var/-var-file, 2) *.auto.tfvars, 3) terraform.tfvars, 4) TF_VAR_name env vars, 5) default in variable declaration. The exam may test: "What overrides a default variable value?" — CLI always wins.

# variables.tf
variable "instance_type" {
  type    = string
  default = "t3.micro"         # Priority 5 (lowest)
}

# Priority 4: Environment variable
$ export TF_VAR_instance_type="t3.small"

# Priority 3: terraform.tfvars
instance_type = "t3.medium"

# Priority 2: *.auto.tfvars (automatically loaded)
instance_type = "t3.large"

# Priority 1: CLI flag (WINS over everything)
$ terraform plan -var="instance_type=t3.xlarge"
# → t3.xlarge is used, ignoring ALL other sources

# Priority 1 (alt): Variable file
$ terraform plan -var-file="prod.tfvars"
# → Values in prod.tfvars override terraform.tfvars

# Any value set via -var or -var-file CANNOT be overridden
Q3

When do data sources execute during the Terraform lifecycle?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

At plan time and apply time (they read at both stages).

📖 Explanation

Data sources execute during plan (to build the plan) and again during apply (to get current values). This means data sources can depend on resources NOT YET created if those resources are being created in the same apply. If a data source depends on a resource being created, use depends_on.

# Data source reads EXISTING AWS resources
data "aws_vpc" "existing" {
  id = "vpc-abc123"  # Must already exist!
}

data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" {
  most_recent = true
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd/ubuntu-jammy-22.04-*"]
  }
  owners = ["099720109477"]  # Canonical
}

# Data source depending on a resource BEING CREATED
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id  # Reads at plan time AND apply time
}

# ⚠ If data source reads something not yet created:
# data "aws_instance" "just_created" {
#   instance_id = aws_instance.web.id  # ERROR at plan time!
#   depends_on  = [aws_instance.web]   # ← MUST use depends_on
# }
Q4

What is the difference between locals and variables in Terraform?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Variables are external inputs (can be overridden from CLI, tfvars, env vars). Locals are internal computed values (cannot be overridden from outside).

📖 Explanation

Use variables for things that DIFFER per environment (var.instance_count). Use locals for COMPUTED values (local.name_prefix = "${var.env}-${var.app}") and for shared constants (local.common_tags). Locals are like private functions — they help DRY up your code within a module but aren't part of the module's public API.

  VARIABLES vs LOCALS — DECISION MATRIX:

  ┌──────────────────┬─────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │ Feature          │ variable {}     │ locals {}        │
  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ Overridable?     │ ✅ YES (6 ways) │ ❌ NO            │
  │ Has default?     │ ✅ YES          │ N/A (always set) │
  │ Type validation? │ ✅ YES          │ ❌ NO (inferred) │
  │ Sensitive?       │ ✅ YES          │ ❌ NO            │
  │ Part of API?     │ ✅ YES (inputs) │ ❌ NO (internal) │
  └──────────────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────┘

  variable "instance_type" {       locals {
    type    = string                name_prefix = "${var.env}-${var.app}"
    default = "t3.medium"           common_tags = {
  }                                   Project   = "anihpj"
                                       ManagedBy = "terraform"
  # Called from outside:             }
  $ terraform apply -var="..."     }

  # Usage:                          # Usage:
  var.instance_type                 local.name_prefix

  RULE: If it changes per env → variable
        If it's computed/shared  → local
Q5

How do you make an output value sensitive (hidden from console output)?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Add sensitive = true to the output block. The value is still stored in state but hidden from terraform output and plan/apply display.

📖 Explanation
output "db_password" {
  value     = aws_db_instance.main.password
  sensitive = true  # Hidden in output, still in state!
}

Sensitive outputs are masked in the terminal but the actual value IS still stored in the state file. For truly sensitive data, combine with sensitive = true on the variable and use a secrets manager for the actual value retrieval.

Q6

What is the purpose of the terraform {} block?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

It configures Terraform itself — required version, required providers, backend configuration, and cloud integration.

📖 Explanation
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.7.0"           # Terraform binary version
  required_providers {                   # Provider requirements
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws"; version = "~> 5.0" }
  }
  backend "s3" { ... }                  # Where state is stored
}

The terraform block is always at the top of the configuration. It's the only block that controls Terraform's own behavior rather than infrastructure resources.

Q7

What is the moved block used for?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

To refactor resources without destroying and recreating them. If you rename a resource or move it into a module, moved tells Terraform "this is the same resource at a new address."

📖 Explanation
# Before: resource at root level
# resource "aws_instance" "web" { ... }

# After: move into module
moved {
  from = aws_instance.web
  to   = module.compute.aws_instance.web
}

Without moved, Terraform would plan to destroy aws_instance.web and create module.compute.aws_instance.web. With moved, it simply updates the state file with zero downtime. This is a critical exam topic for Domain 4 (Modules).

Q8

How do you read the current AWS account ID in Terraform?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Use the aws_caller_identity data source: data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {}. Then reference data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id.

📖 Explanation

This data source requires no arguments and returns the current AWS account ID, user ID, and ARN. It's commonly used for building ARNs dynamically: "arn:aws:iam::${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}:role/my-role". The exam may test that you DON'T hardcode account IDs — use this data source instead.

# NEVER hardcode account IDs:
# ❌ resource "aws_iam_role" "bad" {
#   assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
#     Statement = [{
#       Principal = { AWS = "arn:aws:iam::123456789:root" }
#     }]
#   })
# }

# ✅ Use aws_caller_identity instead:
data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {}

resource "aws_iam_role" "good" {
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Statement = [{
      Principal = {
        AWS = "arn:aws:iam::${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}:root"
      }
    }]
  })
}

# Also useful for S3 bucket policies:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_policy" "state" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.state.id
  policy = jsonencode({
    Statement = [{
      Principal = {
        AWS = "arn:aws:iam::${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}:role/terraform"
      }
    }]
  })
}
Q9

What happens if you don't specify a default value for a required variable?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Terraform will prompt you interactively during plan/apply, OR you must provide the value via -var, .tfvars, or TF_VAR_ env var. Without any of these, the command fails.

📖 Explanation

Variables without defaults are "required" — Terraform can't proceed without them. During interactive use, Terraform prompts: var.instance_count: Enter a value:. In CI/CD, interactive prompts fail, so you MUST provide values non-interactively. Best practice: provide sensible defaults for optional vars, leave required vars without defaults so they're explicitly set.

# variables.tf
variable "environment" {
  type    = string
  # NO default → REQUIRED variable
}

variable "instance_count" {
  type    = number
  default = 1  # Optional — has default
}

# Interactive mode (your terminal):
$ terraform plan
# var.environment
#   Enter a value: prod   ← MUST type something

# CI/CD (non-interactive) — will FAIL without providing value:
$ terraform plan
# Error: No value for required variable

# CI/CD fix — provide via ANY method:
$ terraform plan -var="environment=prod"              # CLI flag
$ TF_VAR_environment=prod terraform plan               # Env var
# Or use a .tfvars file:
# prod.tfvars:
#   environment = "prod"
$ terraform plan -var-file="prod.tfvars"
Q10

How do you define a variable that accepts a complex object with specific attributes?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Use the object({...}) type constraint with named attributes and their types.

📖 Explanation
variable "node_config" {
  type = object({
    instance_type = string
    min_size      = number
    max_size      = number
    labels        = optional(map(string), {})
  })
  default = {
    instance_type = "t3.medium"
    min_size      = 2
    max_size      = 8
  }
}

Object types enforce structure — if you pass {instance_type = "t3.large"} without min_size, Terraform errors. Use optional() (v1.3+) for attributes that can be omitted. This is tested in Domain 2 (Dynamic Configuration).

Q1

What does the -/+ symbol mean in terraform plan output?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

The resource will be DESTROYED and RECREATED — this means DOWNTIME and potential data loss.

📖 Explanation

-/+ appears when a change forces resource replacement (e.g., changing an RDS engine, EC2 AMI, or S3 bucket name). Terraform will destroy the existing resource first, then create a new one. For databases, this means ALL DATA IS LOST unless you have backups. Always investigate -/+ before approving.

Q2

How do you apply Terraform changes without the interactive confirmation prompt?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Option A: terraform apply -auto-approve. Option B: Save plan with -out=plan.tfplan, then terraform apply plan.tfplan.

📖 Explanation

Option A is common in CI/CD pipelines. Option B is safer — you can review the saved plan before applying. Saved plans are binary files. Applying a saved plan skips the confirmation prompt because you already approved the plan output.

Q3

What lifecycle meta-argument protects a resource from accidental deletion?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

prevent_destroy = true

📖 Explanation

When set, terraform destroy will ERROR on that resource. Use this on RDS databases, S3 buckets with user data, and any production-critical resource. To actually delete, you must first remove prevent_destroy from the config, run apply, then destroy.

# Protect your production database from accidental deletion
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  identifier     = "anihpj-prod-db"
  engine         = "postgres"
  engine_version = "16.3"
  instance_class = "db.t3.medium"
  allocated_storage = 100

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true  # terraform destroy will ERROR here
  }
}

# $ terraform destroy
# Error: Instance cannot be destroyed
# Resource aws_db_instance.jobpost has lifecycle.prevent_destroy
# set to true. Remove it to allow destruction.

# To ACTUALLY delete:
# 1. Remove prevent_destroy from .tf
# 2. terraform apply    (updates state, removes protection)
# 3. terraform destroy  (now it works)
Q4

How do you save a plan to apply later without an interactive prompt?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan then terraform apply plan.tfplan. The saved plan applies exactly what was reviewed — no re-prompt.

📖 Explanation

Saving a plan creates a binary file capturing the exact diff at that moment. Applying a saved plan skips the confirmation prompt and applies exactly what was in the plan — even if .tf files changed. This is the standard CI/CD pattern: plan in PR, apply after merge. The plan file is binary and not human-readable.

Q5

What does the create_before_destroy lifecycle argument do?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

It creates the replacement resource FIRST, then destroys the old one — achieving zero-downtime replacements.

📖 Explanation

Default behavior: destroy old → create new (downtime). With create_before_destroy = true: create new → destroy old (zero downtime). Use this for web servers, load balancers, and any resource that can't tolerate downtime during replacement. However, it may cause naming conflicts if the resource name must be unique.

# WITHOUT create_before_destroy (DEFAULT):
# Plan: -/+ destroy aws_instance.web, then create new
# Result: 30-60 seconds of DOWNTIME

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type = "t3.medium"
  # Default: destroy first → create second (downtime)
}

# WITH create_before_destroy (ZERO DOWNTIME):
# Plan: + create new aws_instance.web FIRST
#       - destroy old aws_instance.web SECOND
# Result: Both exist briefly, then old is removed

resource "aws_launch_template" "web" {
  name_prefix = "anihpj-web-"  # Name must allow duplicates
  image_id    = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id

  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true  # New before old = no downtime
  }
}

# ⚠ GOTCHA: If resource name must be UNIQUE (like S3 bucket name),
# create_before_destroy FAILS because new can't be created
# while old with same name still exists.
Q6

How do you destroy only a specific resource without affecting others?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform destroy -target=RESOURCE_ADDRESS. Example: terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.dev_server.

📖 Explanation

-target destroys the specified resource AND its dependencies. Use with caution — targeting bypasses Terraform's normal dependency tracking. It's a surgical tool for emergencies, not a daily workflow. For routine cleanup, remove the resource from .tf files and run normal apply — Terraform will plan the destroy as part of the full configuration.

Q7

What does the ignore_changes lifecycle argument do?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

It tells Terraform to ignore changes to specific attributes — even if they differ from the desired configuration.

📖 Explanation
lifecycle {
  ignore_changes = [
    tags["LastModified"],  # Changed by external process
    desired_capacity,        # Changed by autoscaling
  ]
}

Common use: ASG desired_capacity changes when autoscaling triggers. Without ignore_changes, the next plan would show it reverting. Also used for tags modified by external systems. Use sparingly — it masks drift.

Q8

What's the difference between terraform plan and terraform plan -refresh-only?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Normal plan: detects drift AND proposes config changes. -refresh-only: ONLY detects drift (changes outside Terraform) without proposing config changes.

📖 Explanation

terraform plan -refresh-only is a diagnostic tool — it shows you what changed outside Terraform but doesn't try to fix it. Output shows ~ for drifted resources with a note. After reviewing, you can decide whether to update .tf files or run normal apply to revert drift.

Q9

What happens when you run terraform apply -parallelism=1?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Resources are created one at a time, sequentially — no parallel operations. Useful for debugging or when cloud API rate limits are being hit.

📖 Explanation

Default parallelism is 10 — Terraform creates up to 10 independent resources simultaneously. Reducing to 1 makes everything serial, which is slower but easier to debug (errors are clearly associated with the current resource). Resources that depend on each other are always created sequentially regardless of parallelism.

Q10

What does the replace_triggered_by lifecycle argument do?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

It forces a resource to be replaced when a referenced attribute changes, even if that attribute isn't directly used by the resource.

📖 Explanation
resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  ami = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  lifecycle {
    replace_triggered_by = [
      data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id  # Replace when AMI changes
    ]
  }
}

This is useful when a resource should be replaced based on an external change that Terraform can't automatically detect as a dependency. Example: replace all EC2 instances when the AMI updates, even if the AMI ID is referenced through a data source.

Q1

When should you use for_each instead of count?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

When resources are named/different (e.g., dev/staging/prod subnets). count is for identical clones.

📖 Explanation

count uses indexes 0,1,2 — removing index 1 may cause recreation of ALL resources. for_each uses keys — removing a key only affects that one resource. The exam loves this comparison. Rule of thumb: if resources have meaningful names, use for_each.

# ❌ COUNT — index-based (fragile):
variable "subnet_cidrs" {
  type    = list(string)
  default = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24", "10.0.3.0/24"]
}
resource "aws_subnet" "by_count" {
  count      = length(var.subnet_cidrs)
  cidr_block = var.subnet_cidrs[count.index]
  # Address: aws_subnet.by_count[0], [1], [2]
  # Remove index 1 → ALL resources after shift! [2] becomes [1]
}

# ✅ FOR_EACH — key-based (stable):
variable "subnets" {
  type = map(object({ cidr = string, az = string }))
  default = {
    "public-a"  = { cidr = "10.0.1.0/24", az = "us-east-1a" }
    "public-b"  = { cidr = "10.0.2.0/24", az = "us-east-1b" }
    "private-a" = { cidr = "10.0.3.0/24", az = "us-east-1a" }
  }
}
resource "aws_subnet" "by_key" {
  for_each          = var.subnets
  cidr_block        = each.value.cidr
  availability_zone = each.value.az
  # Address: aws_subnet.by_key["public-a"], ["public-b"], ["private-a"]
  # Remove "public-a" → ONLY that one is destroyed. Others UNCHANGED.
}
Q2

What is the difference between implicit and explicit dependencies?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Implicit: Terraform infers from references. Explicit: You use depends_on. Prefer implicit.

📖 Explanation

Implicit: subnet_id = aws_subnet.public.id — Terraform knows the subnet must exist first. Explicit: depends_on = [aws_instance.web] — used when Terraform can't infer (e.g., a null_resource running a script after EC2 creation). Best practice: let Terraform figure it out.

Q3

What does dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.ports ... } do?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Generates multiple nested ingress blocks from a variable — eliminating repetitive code.

📖 Explanation

Without dynamic blocks, you'd write each ingress rule manually. With dynamic blocks, one for_each loop generates all rules. Common uses: security group rules, IAM policy statements, ALB listener rules. The content block defines the template — use ingress.value (or your iterator name) to access each element.

# WITHOUT dynamic blocks — repetitive:
resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  ingress {
    from_port   = 80
    to_port     = 80
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }
  ingress {
    from_port   = 443
    to_port     = 443
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }
  ingress {
    from_port   = 22
    to_port     = 22
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["10.0.0.0/16"]
  }
  # ... 10 more rules = 50+ lines!
}

# WITH dynamic blocks — clean & scalable:
variable "ingress_rules" {
  default = [
    { port = 80,  cidr = "0.0.0.0/0",   proto = "tcp" },
    { port = 443, cidr = "0.0.0.0/0",   proto = "tcp" },
    { port = 22,  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16", proto = "tcp" },
  ]
}
resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  dynamic "ingress" {
    for_each = var.ingress_rules
    content {
      from_port   = ingress.value.port
      to_port     = ingress.value.port
      protocol    = ingress.value.proto
      cidr_blocks = [ingress.value.cidr]
    }
  }
}
# Add 100 more rules = just add to the variable list!
Q4

How do you create resources in multiple AWS regions from one config?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Use provider aliases. Define multiple provider blocks with alias, then reference provider = aws.alias_name in the resource.

📖 Explanation
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }              # default
provider "aws" { region = "us-west-2"; alias = "west" }  # aliased

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "east" { ... }                 # uses default
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "west" { provider = aws.west } # uses alias

The first provider block (no alias) is the default. Additional blocks with alias are referenced explicitly. This is tested in Domain 5 (Providers).

Q5

What does count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 accomplish?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Conditional resource creation. If var.enabled is true, 1 resource is created. If false, 0 resources are created (the resource is skipped entirely).

📖 Explanation

Since you can't use if statements in Terraform, count with a ternary is the standard pattern for conditional resources. When count = 0, the resource is completely absent — no API calls, no state entry. Alternative: for modules, you can't use count directly on a module call (use for_each instead, or wrap in count outside).

Q6

What is a pre-condition and when does it execute?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

A validation check that runs BEFORE a resource is created or updated. If the condition fails, Terraform stops with an error before making any changes.

📖 Explanation
lifecycle {
  precondition {
    condition     = data.aws_region.current.name == "us-east-1"
    error_message = "Only us-east-1 is supported."
  }
}

Pre-conditions run during the plan phase. They validate that the environment is correct before any changes are applied. Use them to enforce organizational policies like region restrictions, instance type requirements, or encryption settings.

Q7

How do you handle sensitive variables in Terraform?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

Mark them sensitive = true in the variable declaration. This hides the value from plan/apply output. For maximum security, retrieve values from AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault instead of tfvars.

📖 Explanation

Sensitive variables are masked in CLI output but the value IS still stored in the state file. The security hierarchy: (1) Best: Retrieve at runtime from Secrets Manager/Vault, (2) Good: Pass via TF_VAR_ env var with sensitive = true, (3) Risky: Store in .tfvars (even if gitignored, the value sits on disk). Never hardcode secrets in .tf files.

# variables.tf
variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true  # Hidden in plan/apply/output
}

# ❌ NEVER do this:
# variable "db_password" {
#   default = "SuperSecret123!"  # Visible in git, plan output
# }

# ✅ Option 1: Environment variable (CI/CD friendly)
# $ export TF_VAR_db_password="SuperSecret123!"

# ✅ Option 2: AWS Secrets Manager (most secure)
data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" {
  secret_id = "anihpj/prod/database"
}
locals {
  db_password = jsondecode(
    data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db.secret_string
  ).password
}

# ✅ Option 3: HashiCorp Vault
data "vault_generic_secret" "db" {
  path = "secret/anihpj/database"
}
locals {
  db_password = data.vault_generic_secret.db.data["password"]
}

# ⚠ STATE FILE still contains the password (encrypted at rest)
# ⚠ terraform output db_password → (sensitive value)
Q8

What is a post-condition and when does it execute?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

A validation check that runs AFTER a resource is created or updated. It verifies the resource was created correctly — if the condition fails, Terraform errors but the resource already exists.

📖 Explanation
lifecycle {
  postcondition {
    condition     = self.arn != ""
    error_message = "Resource ARN must not be empty after creation."
  }
}

Post-conditions validate the RESULTS of resource creation. Use self to reference the current resource's attributes. Common checks: verifying ARN is populated, ensuring tags are applied, confirming endpoint is reachable. Post-conditions prevent silently broken infrastructure.

Q9

What is the .terraform.lock.hcl file and should it be committed to Git?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

It locks exact provider versions and checksums for reproducible builds. YES, commit it to Git — it ensures all team members and CI/CD use identical provider versions.

📖 Explanation

The lock file records the exact version and cryptographic checksum of every provider. Without it, different team members might download different provider versions, causing inconsistent behavior. The file is auto-generated by terraform init and should NEVER be edited manually. Use terraform init -upgrade to update it when changing provider version constraints.

Q10

What's the difference between terraform taint and terraform apply -replace?

Show Answer & Explanation
✅ Answer

terraform taint marks a resource for recreation on the NEXT apply (two-step). terraform apply -replace=ADDR does it immediately (one-step). taint is deprecated — use -replace instead.

📖 Explanation

terraform taint aws_instance.web only marks the resource — nothing happens until the next apply. terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web immediately plans and applies the replacement. HashiCorp recommends using -replace because it's explicit and atomic. The exam may still reference taint for backward compatibility, but the correct modern answer is -replace.

📝HCL Syntax10 block types, argument format, comments
🔧Variables9 types, 5 assignment methods, validation
📤Outputs & LocalsExpose values, DRY expressions
📖Data SourcesRead existing cloud resources
🔮Plan Symbols+ - ~ -/+ <= — 6 symbols mastered
🚀Apply ModesInteractive, saved plan, auto-approve
🛡️Lifecycle6 meta-arguments for production safety
🔁Count & for_eachMultiple resources, map/set iteration

🟡 Part 3: HCL Deep DiveChapters 7-9

Chapter 7: Functions and Expressions

Terraform provides 100+ built-in functions for string manipulation, collection handling, encoding, filesystem operations, and more. The exam heavily tests your ability to pick the right function for the right scenario. templatefile(), lookup(), merge(), jsonencode(), and can()/try() are the most critical for the certification.

🔑 Key Exam Insight

You WILL be tested on functions. The exam expects you to know: (1) which function to use for a given task, (2) the exact syntax and argument order, and (3) common gotchas like lookup() needing a default vs direct map access crashing on missing keys.

7.1 String Functions — Name Generation & Formatting

String functions transform text for naming conventions, resource tagging, and output formatting. In the anihpj project, you'll use them constantly — generating unique resource names, building tags, and formatting output.

FunctionPurposeExampleResult
format()printf-style formattingformat("anihpj-%s-%s", "prod", "web")"anihpj-prod-web"
join()Join list with separatorjoin(",", ["a","b","c"])"a,b,c"
split()Split string into listsplit("-", "anihpj-prod-web")["anihpj","prod","web"]
replace()Search and replacereplace("hello-world", "-", "_")"hello_world"
trimspace()Remove leading/trailing whitespacetrimspace(" hello ")"hello"
lower()Convert to lowercaselower("AnihPJ")"anihpj"
upper()Convert to uppercaseupper("anihpj")"ANIHPJ"
title()Title casetitle("hello world")"Hello World"
substr()Extract substringsubstr("anihpj", 0, 4)"anih"
length()String lengthlength("anihpj")6
Anihpj Name Generation with String Functions
locals {
  # Consistent naming across ALL anihpj resources
  name_prefix = format("anihpj-%s", var.environment)        # "anihpj-production"
  full_name   = join("-", [local.name_prefix, var.component]) # "anihpj-production-jobpost"

  # Transform tags for different uses
  tag_string  = join(",", [for k, v in local.common_tags : "${k}=${v}"]) # "Project=anihpj,ManagedBy=terraform"

  # Clean user input
  clean_env   = lower(replace(var.environment, " ", "-"))   # "dev" not "Dev "

  # Extract parts of a resource ARN
  # arn:aws:eks:us-east-1:123456789:cluster/anihpj-cluster
  account_id  = split(":", aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.arn)[4]  # "123456789"
  region      = split(":", aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.arn)[3]  # "us-east-1"
}
💡 Naming Convention Best Practice

Always use format() for predictable, consistent naming. Avoid hand-rolling strings with "${var.env}-${var.app}" — format() gives you control over padding (%03d), hex (%x), and more. For the anihpj project: format("%s-%s-%03d", local.name_prefix, "task", count.index) gives names like anihpj-prod-task-001.

7.2 Collection Functions — Lists, Maps & Sets

Collection functions operate on lists, maps, and sets — the backbone of dynamic Terraform configurations. You use them to look up values, merge configurations, flatten nested structures, and safely access data.

FunctionInputOutputAnihpj Use Case
length(list)List/Map/SetNumberCount subnets in each AZ
element(list, idx)List + IndexSingle elementPick first AZ for a resource
lookup(map, key, default)Map + Key + DefaultValueInstance type per environment
contains(list, val)List + ValueboolValidate env is in allowed list
keys(map)MapList of keysGet all environment names
values(map)MapList of valuesGet all instance types
merge(map1, map2, ...)Multiple MapsSingle merged mapCombine default + custom tags
flatten(nested_lists)List of ListsFlat listFlatten AZ subnet configs
chunklist(list, n)List + SizeList of chunksDistribute pods across subnets
setproduct(l1, l2)Two ListsCartesian productEnv × AZ combinations
Collection Functions in Anihpj
variable "instance_types" {
  type = map(string)
  default = { dev = "t3.small"; staging = "t3.medium"; prod = "t3.large" }
}

variable "allowed_envs" {
  type    = list(string)
  default = ["dev", "staging", "prod"]
}

locals {
  # SAFE map access — returns default if key missing
  instance_type = lookup(var.instance_types, var.environment, "t3.medium")

  # Validation — won't crash if environment is wrong
  is_valid_env = contains(var.allowed_envs, var.environment)

  # Merge tags — custom tags OVERRIDE common tags
  final_tags = merge(
    { Project = "anihpj"; ManagedBy = "terraform"; Environment = var.environment },
    var.custom_tags  # custom_tags override if same key exists
  )

  # Flatten nested subnet configurations
  all_subnet_cidrs = flatten([
    for env_key, env_config in var.environments : [
      for subnet in env_config.subnets : {
        env  = env_key
        name = subnet.name
        cidr = subnet.cidr_block
      }
    ]
  ])

  # Cartesian product: all envs × all AZs
  env_az_combos = setproduct(keys(var.environments), ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"])
}
⚠️ Exam Gotcha: lookup() vs Direct Map Access

var.my_map["missing_key"] CRASHES at plan time if the key doesn't exist. lookup(var.my_map, "missing_key", "default") gracefully returns "default". The exam will test this — always use lookup() when you're not 100% sure the key exists!

🔍 lookup()

Safe map access with fallback. Essential when reading from variables with optional keys.

lookup(map, key, default)
🔄 merge()

Combine multiple maps. Later maps override earlier ones. Perfect for tag layering.

merge(base, override)
📐 flatten()

Un-nest list of lists into single list. Critical for processing nested for expressions.

flatten([[a,b],[c]]) → [a,b,c]

7.3 Numeric, Boolean & Error-Handling Functions

These functions handle math operations, boolean logic, and — critically for the exam — safe expression evaluation with can() and try().

🔢 Numeric Functions
min(a,b,...)Smallest value
max(a,b,...)Largest value
ceil(3.14)→ 4 (round up)
floor(3.14)→ 3 (round down)
abs(-5)→ 5 (absolute)
signum(-5)→ -1 (sign)
🛡️ Error Handling (EXAM CRITICAL)
can(expr)Returns true/false if expr works
try(expr, fallback)Returns expr or fallback if error
try(expr1, expr2, fallback)Tries each, returns first that works
Anihpj: can() vs try() — When to Use Each
# can() — TEST if an expression works (returns bool)
can(regex("^t[23]\\.", var.instance_type))  # true if t2/t3 instance
can(cidrnetmask(var.vpc_cidr))              # true if valid CIDR
can(var.optional_field.nested.value)         # true if path exists

# try() — TRY expressions, return first that works (returns value)
instance_type = try(var.custom_type, var.env_type, "t3.medium")
# Try custom_type → if null/error, try env_type → if null/error, use "t3.medium"

# REAL anihpj example: Database port with safe defaults
db_port = try(
  var.rds_config.port,     # Try explicit port
  lookup({ postgres = 5432; mysql = 3306 }, var.db_engine, 5432), # Try engine default
  5432                      # Absolute fallback
)

# Size constraints using min/max
actual_replicas = max(1, min(var.desired_replicas, var.max_replicas))
# Ensures replicas stays between 1 and max_replicas
⚠️ Critical: can() vs try() — Don't Mix Them Up!

can() returns true/false — use it in conditionals and validations. try() returns the actual value or fallback — use it when you need the result. The exam WILL have questions distinguishing these two. Remember: can() = "CAN this work?" (boolean), try() = "TRY these, give me the value" (returns value).

7.4 Type Conversion Functions

Terraform is strongly typed. You often need to convert between types when working with outputs, data sources, or module interfaces. The type() function is your debugging friend — it reveals what type Terraform thinks a value is.

FunctionConverts ToExample
tostring(42)String"42"
tonumber("42")Number42
tobool("true")Booleantrue
tolist({a,b,c})List["a","b","c"]
toset([1,1,2])Set (unique)[1, 2]
tomap({key="val"})Map{"key"="val"}
type(expr)Type string"string", "list", etc.
Type Conversion in Anihpj
# Data sources often return numbers as strings
# aws_db_instance.jobpost.port returns "5432" (string), not 5432 (number)
db_port_number = tonumber(aws_db_instance.jobpost.port)  # "5432" → 5432

# Boolean from module output (string "true" → bool true)
enable_monitoring = tobool(var.monitoring_enabled)  # "true" → true

# Convert tuple to list for count
subnet_ids = tolist(data.aws_subnets.private.ids)  # Ensure it's a list
count      = length(local.subnet_ids)

# DEBUGGING: What type is this value?
# Run in terraform console:
# > type(var.instance_types)
# "map(string)"
# > type(aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.certificate_authority)
# list(object({ data = string }))
💡 Exam Tip: type() in terraform console

When you're unsure what type a variable or resource attribute is, use terraform console and run type(some_expression). This is especially useful for complex nested structures from data sources — it tells you exactly what you're working with.

7.5 Filesystem and Encoding Functions

These functions bridge Terraform with the outside world — reading files, rendering templates, and encoding data for APIs. templatefile() is the single most important function for any Terraform + Kubernetes workflow.

7.5a file() & templatefile() — Reading and Rendering

📄 file(path)

Reads a file as a string. Path is relative to the .tf file (use path.module).

user_data = file("${path.module}/init.sh")

⚠️ File must exist before plan time!

📝 templatefile(path, vars)

Reads a template file, substitutes ${var} placeholders with actual values.

yaml_body = templatefile("${path.module}/deploy.yaml.tpl", { replicas = 3 })

🔑 THE most important function for K8s manifests!

templatefile() — Anihpj K8s Deployment Generator
# STEP 1: Create the template file (jobpost.yaml.tpl)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# apiVersion: apps/v1
# kind: Deployment
# metadata:
#   name: ${app_name}
#   namespace: ${namespace}
#   labels:
#     app: ${app_name}
#     env: ${environment}
# spec:
#   replicas: ${replicas}
#   selector:
#     matchLabels: { app: ${app_name} }
#   template:
#     metadata:
#       labels:
#         app: ${app_name}
#         env: ${environment}
#     spec:
#       containers:
#       - name: ${app_name}
#         image: ${image}:${tag}
#         ports:
#         - containerPort: ${container_port}
#         env:
#         - name: DATABASE_URL
#           value: "${db_host}:${db_port}"
#         resources:
#           limits:    { cpu: "${cpu_limit}", memory: "${mem_limit}" }
#           requests:  { cpu: "${cpu_request}", memory: "${mem_request}" }

# STEP 2: Call templatefile() in Terraform
# ────────────────────────────────────────
resource "kubernetes_manifest" "jobpost_deployment" {
  manifest = yamldecode(templatefile("${path.module}/jobpost.yaml.tpl", {
    app_name       = "jobpost"
    namespace      = var.environment
    environment    = var.environment
    replicas       = var.environment == "prod" ? 3 : 1
    image          = "ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost"
    tag            = var.image_tag
    container_port = 8000
    db_host        = aws_db_instance.jobpost.address
    db_port        = 5432
    cpu_limit      = "500m"
    mem_limit      = "512Mi"
    cpu_request    = "250m"
    mem_request    = "256Mi"
  }))
}
templatefile() Data Flow
┌─────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────┐
│  jobpost.yaml.tpl   │     │  Terraform Variables   │
│  (TEMPLATE)         │     │  (VALUES)              │
│                     │     │                        │
│  name: ${app_name}  │     │  app_name = "jobpost"  │
│  replicas: ${reps}  │     │  reps = 3              │
│  image: ${img}:${t} │     │  img = "ghcr.io/..."   │
│                     │     │  t = "v2.4.1"          │
└─────────┬───────────┘     └───────────┬────────────┘
          │                             │
          └──────────┬──────────────────┘
                     ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │  templatefile()     │
          │  Combines template  │
          │  with values        │
          └─────────┬───────────┘
                    ▼
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  RENDERED YAML (string)                 │
          │  apiVersion: apps/v1                    │
          │  kind: Deployment                       │
          │  metadata:                              │
          │    name: jobpost                        │
          │  spec:                                  │
          │    replicas: 3                          │
          │    template:                            │
          │      spec:                              │
          │        containers:                      │
          │        - name: jobpost                  │
          │          image: ghcr.io/anihpj/         │
          │                 jobpost:v2.4.1           │
          └────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                               ▼
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │  yamldecode() → Kubernetes Manifest     │
          │  Applied to EKS cluster                 │
          └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

7.5b jsonencode() & yamlencode() — Structuring API Data

These functions convert Terraform data structures (maps, lists, objects) into the JSON or YAML strings that cloud APIs expect.

jsonencode() & yamlencode() in Anihpj
# jsonencode() — IAM policies, ECS task definitions, API Gateway
resource "aws_iam_policy" "jobpost_s3" {
  name   = "anihpj-jobpost-s3-access"
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [
      {
        Effect   = "Allow"
        Action   = ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"]
        Resource = ["${aws_s3_bucket.assets.arn}/*"]
      }
    ]
  })
}
# Result (auto-generated JSON):
# {
#   "Version": "2012-10-17",
#   "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"], ... }]
# }

# yamlencode() — K8s manifests, Helm values, ConfigMaps
locals {
  jobpost_config = yamlencode({
    database = {
      host     = aws_db_instance.jobpost.address
      port     = 5432
      name     = "jobpost"
      ssl_mode = "require"
    }
    redis = {
      host = aws_elasticache_cluster.anihpj.cache_nodes[0].address
      port = 6379
    }
  })
}

resource "kubernetes_config_map" "jobpost_config" {
  metadata { name = "jobpost-config"; namespace = var.environment }
  data = { "app.yaml" = local.jobpost_config }
}

7.5c filebase64() — Binary Files

filebase64() — Lambda Zip, SSL Certs
# Lambda deployment package
resource "aws_lambda_function" "jobpost_processor" {
  filename         = "${path.module}/jobpost_lambda.zip"
  source_code_hash = filebase64sha256("${path.module}/jobpost_lambda.zip")
}

# SSL certificate upload
resource "aws_acm_certificate" "anihpj" {
  private_key      = file("${path.module}/certs/private.key")
  certificate_body = file("${path.module}/certs/cert.pem")
  # certificate_chain is the intermediate CA cert
  certificate_chain = file("${path.module}/certs/chain.pem")
}
