7.6 Additional Critical Functions — Date, Crypto & IP/CIDR

Beyond the core categories above, the exam also tests date/time manipulation, cryptographic hashing, and IP subnet calculations. These are especially important for resource uniqueness, checksums, and network planning.

📅 Date/Time Functions
timestamp()→ "2026-06-09T12:34:56Z" (current UTC)
formatdate("YYYY-MM-DD", ts)→ "2026-06-09"
timeadd(ts, "24h")Adds duration to timestamp

Anihpj Use: Tag resources with deployment time, generate time-based unique names.

🔐 Crypto/Hash Functions
sha256("hello")SHA-256 hash (64 hex chars)
md5("data")MD5 hash (32 hex chars)
base64sha256("data")Base64-encoded SHA-256
uuid()Random UUID v4

Anihpj Use: S3 bucket names (must be globally unique), Lambda source code hash triggers.

🌐 IP/CIDR Functions
cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 0)→ "10.0.0.0/24"
cidrhost("10.0.1.0/24", 5)→ "10.0.1.5"
cidrnetmask("10.0.0.0/16")→ "255.255.0.0"

Anihpj Use: Subnet calculations for VPC, EKS pod networking, security group CIDR rules.

Anihpj: Date, Crypto & CIDR in Practice
# DATE/TIME: Tag all resources with deployment timestamp
locals {
  deployment_time = formatdate("YYYY-MM-DD-hhmm", timestamp())
  # → "2026-06-09-1430"
}

# CRYPTO: Globally unique S3 bucket name
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-${var.environment}-${substr(sha256(var.environment), 0, 8)}"
  # → "anihpj-prod-a3f2b8c1"  ← 8-char hash suffix ensures GLOBAL uniqueness
}

# CRYPTO: Lambda source code hash — triggers update only when code changes
resource "aws_lambda_function" "processor" {
  source_code_hash = filebase64sha256("${path.module}/jobpost_lambda.zip")
  # Hash changes → Lambda updates. Hash unchanged → no-op.
}

# IP/CIDR: Calculate subnet ranges for EKS VPC
locals {
  vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"
  # Split into /20 subnets: 10.0.0.0/20, 10.0.16.0/20, 10.0.32.0/20, ...
  public_subnets = [for i in range(0, 3) : cidrsubnet(local.vpc_cidr, 4, i)]
  # → ["10.0.0.0/20", "10.0.16.0/20", "10.0.32.0/20"]

  private_subnets = [for i in range(3, 6) : cidrsubnet(local.vpc_cidr, 4, i)]
  # → ["10.0.48.0/20", "10.0.64.0/20", "10.0.80.0/20"]

  # CIDR host: Get specific IP within a subnet
  nat_gateway_ip = cidrhost(local.public_subnets[0], 10)
  # → "10.0.0.10" (useful for fixed private IPs)
}

# Validate CIDR in variable block
variable "vpc_cidr" {
  type        = string
  default     = "10.0.0.0/16"
  validation {
    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.vpc_cidr))
    error_message = "Invalid CIDR block: ${var.vpc_cidr}"
  }
}
🏗️ Anihpj Real-World: Functions in Daily Work

Here's how functions combine in a single real deployment scenario — deploying the jobpost app to EKS:

One Deploy, 10 Functions — The Full Picture
# SCENARIO: Deploy jobpost Django app to EKS with RDS, S3, and CloudFront
# This single deployment uses: format, join, merge, lookup, templatefile,
#   jsonencode, yamlencode, can, try, cidrsubnet, flatten, file, sha256

locals {
  # STRING: Consistent naming
  name_prefix = format("anihpj-%s", var.environment)              # format()

  # COLLECTION: Safe defaults + tag merging
  db_class     = lookup(var.db_sizes, var.environment, "db.t3.medium") # lookup()
  all_tags     = merge({ Project="anihpj"; Env=var.environment },  # merge()
                       var.custom_tags)

  # FOR + FLATTEN: Subnet configurations across environments
  subnets = flatten([for env_key, env in var.environments :       # flatten()
    [for subnet in env.subnets : { env=env_key; cidr=subnet.cidr; # for expr
      az=subnet.az; public=can(regex("pub", subnet.name)) }]])    # can()

  # IP/CIDR: Calculate VPC subnets
  vpc_cidr    = "10.0.0.0/16"
  pub_cidrs   = [for i in range(0, 3) : cidrsubnet(local.vpc_cidr, 4, i)]

  # YAMLENCODE: K8s ConfigMap for Django settings
  django_config = yamlencode({                                     # yamlencode()
    DATABASE_URL  = "postgres://${aws_db_instance.jobpost.address}:5432/jobpost"
    ALLOWED_HOSTS = join(",", [for s in var.allowed_hosts : s])    # join() + for
    MEDIA_BUCKET  = aws_s3_bucket.assets.bucket
  })

  # TEMPLATEFILE: K8s deployment manifest
  k8s_manifest = templatefile("${path.module}/deploy.yaml.tpl", {  # templatefile()
    app_name  = "jobpost"
    image_tag = var.image_tag
    replicas  = try(var.manual_replicas, var.env_replicas["${var.environment}"], 1) # try()
  })

  # JSONENCODE: IAM policy for S3 access
  s3_policy = jsonencode({                                         # jsonencode()
    Version = "2012-10-17";
    Statement = [{ Effect = "Allow"; Action = ["s3:*"];
      Resource = "${aws_s3_bucket.assets.arn}/*" }]
  })

  # CRYPTO: Globally unique bucket name
  bucket_name = "anihpj-${var.environment}-${substr(sha256(var.environment), 0, 8)}"
}

# RESULT: All 10+ function categories work TOGETHER in one deployment!

🔑 Key insight: No function works in isolation. Real Terraform code combines 5-10 functions in a single locals block. The exam tests your ability to chain them correctly.

Chapter 7 — Practice Questions

Q1
Which function would you use to safely access a map value that might not exist?
Show Answer
Answer

lookup(map, key, default). Direct map access (var.map["key"]) crashes at plan time if the key is missing. lookup() returns the default value instead.

Explanation

The syntax is lookup(map, key, default) — always provide all three arguments for clarity. If the key exists in the map, lookup returns its value. If the key doesn't exist, it returns the default.

variable "instance_types" {
  type = map(string)
  default = {
    dev     = "t3.small"
    staging = "t3.medium"
    prod    = "t3.large"
  }
}

# ❌ DANGEROUS — crashes if env not in map
instance_type = var.instance_types[var.environment]

# ✅ SAFE — returns "t3.micro" if env key is missing
instance_type = lookup(var.instance_types, var.environment, "t3.micro")
# If var.environment = "uat" (not in map) → "t3.micro"
# If var.environment = "prod" → "t3.large"

# ✅ Also works with data sources that may return null
subnet_id = lookup(data.aws_subnet.selected, "id", null)

# 🎯 EXAM GOTCHA: lookup() is THE correct answer for safe map access
Q2
How do you generate a Kubernetes Deployment YAML dynamically with different replica counts per environment?
Show Answer
Answer

Use templatefile() with a .tpl template and pass variables including replicas.

templatefile("${path.module}/deploy.yaml.tpl", {
  replicas = var.environment == "prod" ? 3 : 1
})
Explanation

templatefile() reads a template file with ${variable} placeholders and substitutes them with values from the second argument. This is THE standard way to generate K8s manifests dynamically. The template file uses ${key} syntax (NOT ${var.key}) — the keys come from the map you pass as the second argument.

Q3
What's the difference between can() and try()?
Show Answer
Answer

can(expr) returns true/false (boolean) — use in conditionals. try(expr, fallback) returns the expression value or fallback — use when you need the result.

# can() — for validation
validation { condition = can(regex("^t[23]", var.type)) }
# try() — for value assignment
instance_type = try(var.custom, var.default, "t3.medium")
Explanation

Think of can() as a safety check: "Can this expression evaluate without error?" Think of try() as a fallback chain: "Try this, then this, then this." can() is perfect for variable validation blocks. try() is perfect for optional data sources and graceful degradation.

Q4
You need to merge default tags with user-provided tags where user tags override defaults. Write the expression.
Show Answer
Answer

merge(local.default_tags, var.custom_tags)

Explanation

merge() combines maps left to right. Later maps override earlier ones for duplicate keys. So merge({a=1,b=2},{b=99}) gives {a=1,b=99} — custom_tags override default_tags.

# locals.tf
locals {
  default_tags = {
    Project   = "anihpj"
    ManagedBy = "terraform"
    CostCenter = "engineering"
  }
}

# variables.tf
variable "custom_tags" {
  type    = map(string)
  default = {}
}

# main.tf — usage in resources
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
  tags = merge(local.default_tags, var.custom_tags)
}

# User provides: custom_tags = { CostCenter = "ml-team", Env = "prod" }
# Result: { Project="anihpj", ManagedBy="terraform",
#           CostCenter="ml-team", Env="prod" }
#                        ↑ overrides default

# If defaults should ALWAYS win (user can't override):
# tags = merge(var.custom_tags, local.default_tags)
Q5
You have a list of lists of subnet configs that needs to be a single flat list. Which function?
Show Answer
Answer

flatten(). flatten([[a,b],[c,d]]) returns [a,b,c,d].

Explanation

This is especially common when you have nested for expressions generating nested lists — you flatten at the end. Example: flatten([for az in var.azs : [for subnet in var.subnets : "${az}-${subnet}"]]) produces a flat list of all AZ-subnet combinations. Without flatten(), you'd get a list of lists.

Q6
How do you create an IAM policy document in Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

Use jsonencode() with a Terraform map/object structure.

policy = jsonencode({
  Version = "2012-10-17"
  Statement = [{ Effect = "Allow"; Action = ["s3:*"]; Resource = "*" }]
})
Explanation

jsonencode() converts HCL data structures into valid JSON strings. This is preferred over raw JSON strings because you get Terraform syntax checking, can use variables inside, and avoid escaping issues. The exam may test whether you use jsonencode() or write raw JSON — jsonencode() is the correct answer.

Q7
How do you format a resource name as "anihpj-production-jobpost-001" using string functions?
Show Answer
Answer

format("anihpj-%s-%s-%03d", var.environment, "jobpost", count.index + 1)

Explanation

format() uses printf-style formatting. %s for strings, %03d for zero-padded numbers (001, 002, etc.).

# format() — printf-style string formatting
# %s = string, %d = decimal, %03d = zero-padded to 3 digits
# %f = float, %t = boolean, %% = literal percent

resource "aws_instance" "jobpost" {
  count = 3
  # Results: "anihpj-prod-jobpost-001", "...-002", "...-003"
  tags = {
    Name = format("anihpj-%s-%s-%03d", var.environment, "jobpost", count.index + 1)
  }
}

# More format examples:
format("%-20s", "left")          # "left                " (left-align)
format("%s-v%s", "app", "2.1")   # "app-v2.1"
format("port=%d", 5432)           # "port=5432"
format("80%%")                    # "80%" (%% = literal %)

# Alternative: string interpolation (simpler for basic cases)
"anihpj-${var.environment}-jobpost-${count.index + 1}"
# → "anihpj-prod-jobpost-1" (no zero-padding)
Q8
You need to convert a string port "5432" from a data source to a number. How?
Show Answer
Answer

tonumber("5432") returns 5432.

Explanation

AWS data sources often return numbers as strings. Use tonumber() to convert. Related conversion functions: tostring(42) → "42", tobool("true") → true, tolist() / toset() for collection conversions. Knowing when you need explicit conversion vs when Terraform auto-converts is an exam nuance.

Q9
How do you validate that a variable contains a valid CIDR block?
Show Answer
Answer

can(cidrnetmask(var.vpc_cidr)) used in a validation {} block.

Explanation

cidrnetmask() crashes if given invalid CIDR input. Wrapping it in can() returns false instead of crashing. The same pattern works for any function that might error.

variable "vpc_cidr" {
  type        = string
  description = "CIDR block for the VPC"

  validation {
    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.vpc_cidr))
    error_message = "Invalid CIDR: ${var.vpc_cidr}. Must be like 10.0.0.0/16."
  }
}

# The can() wrapper pattern works for ANY error-prone function:
validation { condition = can(regex("^t[23]\\.", var.type)) }       # regex
validation { condition = can(jsondecode(var.policy)) }              # json
validation { condition = can(tostring(var.value)) }                 # typecast
validation { condition = can(cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 8, 0)) }         # CIDR math

# Test in console first:
# $ terraform console
# > can(cidrnetmask("10.0.0.0/16"))   → true
# > can(cidrnetmask("not-a-cidr"))     → false
Q10
How do you read a shell script file into an EC2 user_data attribute?
Show Answer
Answer

user_data = file("${path.module}/init.sh")

Explanation

file() reads the contents of a file as a string. Always use path.module to reference files relative to the .tf file. The file must exist at plan time — Terraform reads it immediately, not at apply time.

# modules/compute/init.sh (shell script)
#!/bin/bash
apt-get update && apt-get install -y docker.io
systemctl start docker
echo "Hello from ${environment}" > /etc/motd

# modules/compute/main.tf
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type = "t3.medium"
  user_data     = file("${path.module}/init.sh")
  # file() reads init.sh at PLAN TIME — must exist on disk
}

# For BASE64-encoded content (required by some services):
# user_data = filebase64("${path.module}/init.sh")

# For TEMPLATED scripts (with variables):
# user_data = templatefile("${path.module}/init.tftpl", {
#   environment = var.environment
#   docker_tag  = var.docker_tag
# })

# ⚠ file() reads at PLAN time — script must exist before terraform plan
# ⚠ Use path.module (NOT hardcoded paths) for portability

Chapter 8: Advanced HCL Techniques

Beyond basic expressions, Terraform offers conditional logic, sophisticated for expressions, an interactive console for debugging, and built-in sensitive data protection. These techniques separate junior from senior practitioners — and the exam tests all of them.

🔑 Exam Focus

Conditional expressions (? :), for expressions (list and map forms), terraform console for debugging, and sensitive data handling are all Domain 2 exam topics. Know the gotcha: both branches of a conditional are evaluated, so use try() to protect against errors in unused branches.

8.1 Conditional Expressions — Making Decisions

Conditional expressions use the ternary operator condition ? true_value : false_value. They're essential for environment-specific configurations, feature toggles, and safe defaults.

PatternCodeAnihpj Use Case
Env-based sizingsize = var.env == "prod" ? "large" : "small"EC2 instance type per environment
Default valuesname = var.name != "" ? var.name : "default"Optional resource naming
Count togglecount = var.enable_monitoring ? 1 : 0Conditional resource creation
Nested conditionstype = env=="prod" ? "large" : (env=="staging" ? "medium" : "small")Multi-environment sizing
Null/empty checkvalue = var.optional != null ? var.optional : "fallback"Handling optional variables
Anihpj Conditional Patterns
# Pattern 1: Environment-specific resource sizing
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  instance_class = var.environment == "prod" ? "db.t3.large" : "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage = var.environment == "prod" ? 100 : 20
  # prod gets 100GB, dev/staging get 20GB
}

# Pattern 2: Conditional resource creation (count toggle)
resource "aws_cloudwatch_dashboard" "anihpj" {
  count          = var.environment == "prod" ? 1 : 0  # Only in prod
  dashboard_name = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
  dashboard_body = jsonencode(local.dashboard_config)
}

# Pattern 3: Nested conditions for multi-env
locals {
  instance_size = var.environment == "prod" ? "t3.large" : (
    var.environment == "staging" ? "t3.medium" : "t3.small"
  )
  # prod → large, staging → medium, dev → small
}

# Pattern 4: Safe optional values
locals {
  domain_name = var.custom_domain != "" ? var.custom_domain : "${var.environment}.anihpj.local"
}

# Pattern 5: Feature flag (bool variable)
locals {
  backup_retention = var.enable_long_backup ? 35 : 7  # days
}
⚠️ CRITICAL GOTCHA: Both Branches Are Evaluated!

Unlike most programming languages, Terraform evaluates BOTH the true and false branches of a conditional. If either branch references a nonexistent value, the plan FAILS even if that branch wouldn't be selected.

# THIS WILL FAIL if var.custom doesn't exist:
result = var.use_custom ? var.custom.name : var.default_name
# Even if var.use_custom is false, var.custom.name is still evaluated!

# FIX: Use try() to protect the unsafe branch:
result = var.use_custom ? try(var.custom.name, var.default_name) : var.default_name
🔴 Nested Ternary (Anti-Pattern for 3+ envs)
size = var.env == "prod" ? "large" : (
  var.env == "staging" ? "medium" : (
    var.env == "qa" ? "small" : "micro"
  )
)

Problems: Hard to read, hard to maintain, adding a 5th environment means deeper nesting.

🟢 lookup() Map (Clean Pattern for multi-env)
locals {
  env_sizes = {
    prod    = "t3.large"
    staging = "t3.medium"
    qa      = "t3.small"
    dev     = "t3.micro"
  }
}
size = lookup(local.env_sizes, var.env, "t3.micro")

Benefits: One line, easy to read, adding environments is trivial, consistent fallback.

8.2 Advanced For Expressions — Transforming Data

For expressions transform lists and maps into new collections. The syntax: [for item in collection : result] for lists, {for key, value in map : key => value} for maps. These are some of the most powerful — and most tested — HCL features.

8.2a List Transformation

Transform every element of a list into something new: [for item in list : expression]

List Transformation Examples
# Extract CIDR blocks from subnet objects
[for s in var.subnets : s.cidr_block]
# Input: [{name="pub", cidr="10.0.1.0/24"}, {name="priv", cidr="10.0.2.0/24"}]
# Output: ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]

# Uppercase all environment names
[for env in var.environments : upper(env)]
# Input: ["dev", "staging", "prod"]
# Output: ["DEV", "STAGING", "PROD"]

# Generate AZ-qualified names
[for az in ["a","b","c"] : format("us-east-1%s", az)]
# Output: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]

8.2b List Filtering

Filter and transform simultaneously: [for item in list : result if condition]

List Filtering Examples
# Get only public subnet IDs
[for s in var.subnets : s.id if s.public == true]
# Filters out private subnets, returns only public subnet IDs

# Get only enabled instance names
[for i in var.instances : i.name if i.enabled]
# Skips disabled instances

# Get CIDR blocks larger than /24
[for s in var.subnets : s.cidr_block if tonumber(split("/", s.cidr_block)[1]) < 24]

8.2c Map from List — Building Lookup Tables

Convert lists to maps using {for item in list : key => value}

Map from List Examples
# Build a subnet lookup: name → CIDR
{for s in var.subnets : s.name => s.cidr_block}
# { "dev-pub" = "10.0.1.0/24", "dev-priv" = "10.0.2.0/24", ... }

# Build an instance type map: environment → type
{for i in var.env_configs : i.env => i.instance_type}
# { "dev" = "t3.small", "prod" = "t3.large" }

# Build tag map: key → formatted value
{for k, v in var.tags : k => upper(v)}
# { "env" = "PROD", "app" = "ANIHPJ" }

# Group: index → name (useful for count iteration)
{for idx, subnet in var.subnets : idx => subnet.name}
# { "0" = "dev-pub", "1" = "dev-priv" }

8.2d Nested Structures — Flattening & Combining

Process nested data by combining for expressions with flatten()

Nested For Expression Patterns
# Flatten: environments × subnets → flat list of objects
locals {
  all_subnet_configs = flatten([
    for env_key, env in var.environments : [
      for subnet in env.subnets : {
        env_name   = env_key
        subnet_cidr = subnet.cidr_block
        az         = subnet.availability_zone
        is_public  = subnet.public
      }
    ]
  ])
}

# Result: [ {env="dev", cidr="10.0.1.0/24", az="us-east-1a", public=true},
#           {env="dev", cidr="10.0.2.0/24", az="us-east-1b", public=false},
#           {env="prod", cidr="10.0.11.0/24", az="us-east-1a", public=true}, ... ]

# Use with for_each for dynamic resource creation
resource "aws_subnet" "all" {
  for_each = { for s in local.all_subnet_configs : "${s.env_name}-${s.subnet_cidr}" => s }
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block        = each.value.subnet_cidr
  availability_zone = each.value.az
  tags              = { Name = each.key; Environment = each.value.env_name }
}
🧪 For Expression Quick Reference — 6 Essential Patterns
#PatternSyntaxReturns
1Transform list[for x in list : f(x)]list
2Filter list[for x in list : f(x) if cond]list
3List → Map{for x in list : x.key => x.val}map
4Map → Map{for k,v in map : k => f(v)}map
5Nested flattenflatten([for...:[for...]])list
6Filter+Transform[for x in list : f(x) if g(x)]list
🏗️ For Expressions in Anihpj Daily Operations

Here are 5 real scenarios where for expressions solve problems you'll encounter daily:

🔹 Subnet filtering[for s in data.aws_subnets.all.ids : s if length(s) > 5] — Get only valid subnet IDs
🔹 Tag cleanup{for k, v in var.tags : k => v if v != null} — Remove null tags before applying
🔹 Env × AZ matrix{for pair in setproduct(["dev","prod"], ["1a","1b"]) : "${pair[0]}-${pair[1]}" => pair} — Generate all env-AZ combos
🔹 IAM → minimal[for s in var.statements : s if try(s.actions, []) != [] ] — Skip statements with no actions
🔹 Port mapping{for p in var.ports : p.name => { from = p.from; to = p.to }} — Build SG rules from port list

8.3 The Terraform Console — Your Interactive Debugger

terraform console opens an interactive REPL where you can test expressions, inspect variables, and debug templates in real-time — without running plan or apply. This is arguably the most important tool for exam success and daily development.

terraform console — Live Debugging Session
$ terraform console
# Opens interactive shell with access to ALL variables, locals, and resources

> var.environment
"production"

> max(1, 3, 2)
3

> cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 4, 5)
"10.0.80.0/20"

> can(regex("^t[23]\\.", "t3.large"))
true

> can(regex("^t[23]\\.", "m5.large"))
false

> lookup({a=1, b=2}, "c", "not found")
"not found"

> type(var.instance_types)
"map(string)"

> templatefile("${path.module}/jobpost.yaml.tpl", {
    app_name = "jobpost",
    env      = "prod",
    replicas = 3,
    image    = "ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost",
    tag      = "v2.4.1"
  })
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jobpost
  ...

> [for s in ["dev","staging","prod"] : upper(s)]
["DEV", "STAGING", "PROD"]

> exit    # or Ctrl+D to leave
💡 Console Workflow for Anihpj

Before adding a complex expression to main.tf, test it in terraform console first: (1) Test function behavior, (2) Verify type conversions, (3) Debug templatefile output, (4) Inspect resource attributes. This saves countless plan/apply cycles. The exam expects you to know how to debug expressions using the console.

8.4 Sensitive Data Handling 🎯

Terraform provides built-in mechanisms to protect sensitive data like passwords, API keys, and database credentials. The sensitive = true flag prevents values from appearing in plan/apply output and CLI displays.

🔒 Marking Variables Sensitive
variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true  # Hidden from output
}

Prevents the value from appearing in: plan output, apply output, terraform console, and logs.

🔒 Marking Outputs Sensitive
output "rds_password" {
  value     = aws_db_instance.jobpost.password
  sensitive = true  # Hidden from CLI
}

Value is still in state file (encrypted in remote backends). Use terraform output -json to access programmatically.

Anihpj Sensitive Data Patterns
# Variable secrets — use sensitive = true
variable "rds_master_password" {
  description = "RDS master password for jobpost database"
  type        = string
  sensitive   = true
}

# ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES (most secure for CI/CD)
# export TF_VAR_rds_master_password="super-secret-value"
# Terraform auto-reads TF_VAR_* environment variables

# Retrieving from AWS Secrets Manager (best practice for production)
data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db_password" {
  secret_id = "anihpj/${var.environment}/rds-password"
}
locals {
  db_password = jsondecode(data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db_password.secret_string)["password"]
}

# The nonsensitive() escape hatch — USE WITH CAUTION!
# Sometimes you need to use a sensitive value in a place that
# requires a non-sensitive type. nonsensitive() removes the flag.
# ONLY use when you're 100% sure the derived value is safe.
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  password = var.rds_master_password  # Terraform handles sensitive automatically
  # RDS tags should NOT contain the password:
  tags = merge(local.common_tags, {
    # DO NOT: Password = var.rds_master_password  ← BAD!
    Name = "jobpost-${var.environment}"
  })
}
⚠️ Secrets Best Practices for Anihpj

NEVER hardcode secrets in .tf files. Hierarchy of best practices: (1) AWS Secrets Manager — retrieve at plan time via data source, (2) Environment variables — TF_VAR_rds_password, (3) terraform.tfvars — but .gitignore this file!, (4) Remote state encryption — S3 backend with KMS SSE. Remember: the state file CONTAINS all sensitive values — protect it like a password database.

Chapter 8 — Practice Questions

Q1
Write a conditional expression that sets instance_type to "t3.large" for prod and "t3.small" otherwise.
Show Answer
Answer

instance_type = var.environment == "prod" ? "t3.large" : "t3.small"

Explanation

The ternary operator syntax is condition ? if_true : if_false. Always consider readability — for 3+ conditions, prefer lookup() with a map over nested ternaries. Example: lookup({dev="t3.small", staging="t3.medium", prod="t3.large"}, var.env, "t3.small").

Q2
What happens if you write var.flag ? var.optional.field : "default" and var.flag is false but var.optional is null?
Show Answer
Answer

It FAILS. Both branches are evaluated regardless of the condition. Fix: var.flag ? try(var.optional.field, "default") : "default"

Explanation

Terraform evaluates BOTH branches at plan time. Even though var.flag is false, Terraform still tries to access var.optional.field and crashes. This is a critical exam gotcha — always wrap unsafe branches in try().

Q3
How do you extract only the public subnet IDs from a list of subnet objects?
Show Answer
Answer

[for s in var.subnets : s.id if s.public == true]

Explanation

The if clause after the colon filters the list. Only elements where the condition is true are included.

variable "subnets" {
  type = list(object({
    name   = string
    id     = string
    public = bool
    cidr   = string
  }))
  default = [
    { name="web-a",  id="subnet-aaa", public=true,  cidr="10.0.1.0/24" },
    { name="web-b",  id="subnet-bbb", public=true,  cidr="10.0.2.0/24" },
    { name="db-a",   id="subnet-ccc", public=false, cidr="10.0.3.0/24" },
  ]
}

# Extract ONLY public subnet IDs
locals {
  public_subnet_ids = [for s in var.subnets : s.id if s.public]
  # Result: ["subnet-aaa", "subnet-bbb"] — db-a is filtered out

  # With transformation + filtering:
  public_subnet_names = [for s in var.subnets : upper(s.name) if s.public]
  # Result: ["WEB-A", "WEB-B"]
}

# Usage in ALB (needs at least 2 public subnets)
resource "aws_lb" "main" {
  subnets = local.public_subnet_ids
}
Q4
Convert a list of subnet objects into a map of name → cidr_block.
Show Answer
Answer

{for s in var.subnets : s.name => s.cidr_block}

Explanation

The curly brace form {for...in...: key => value} returns a map. The key expression (before =>) must be unique — duplicates will cause errors. This is the standard pattern for building lookup tables from lists of objects.

Q5
How do you test a CIDR block validation before putting it in a variable block?
Show Answer
Answer

Use terraform console: > can(cidrnetmask("10.0.0.0/16")) → true

Explanation

The console lets you instantly test any function or expression. Test your validation logic there before adding it to variables.tf.

$ terraform console

# Test function behavior before coding:
> can(cidrnetmask("10.0.0.0/16"))
true
> can(cidrnetmask("not-a-cidr"))
false

# Test regex patterns:
> can(regex("^t[23]\\.", "t3.large"))
true
> can(regex("^t[23]\\.", "m5.large"))
false

# Test type conversions:
> tonumber("5432")
5432
> tostring(42)
"42"

# Test CIDR math:
> cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 0)
"10.0.0.0/24"
> cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 255)
"10.0.255.0/24"

# Inspect variables and locals from your config:
> var.environment
"production"
> local.common_tags
{ "Project" = "anihpj", "ManagedBy" = "terraform" }

# Test JSON encoding:
> jsonencode({env="prod", count=3})
"{\"count\":3,\"env\":\"prod\"}"

> exit
Q6
How do you mark a variable as sensitive so its value never appears in plan output?
Show Answer
Answer

Add sensitive = true to the variable declaration.

variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
Explanation

Sensitive variables are redacted in plan/apply output, console, and logs. The value still exists in state — ensure your remote state backend encrypts it. Use terraform output -json to access sensitive outputs programmatically. Combine with AWS Secrets Manager or Vault for maximum security.

Q7
You need to conditionally create a CloudWatch dashboard only in production. Write the resource block.
Show Answer
Answer
resource "aws_cloudwatch_dashboard" "main" {
  count          = var.environment == "prod" ? 1 : 0
  dashboard_name = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
  dashboard_body = jsonencode({...})
}
Explanation

count = condition ? 1 : 0 is the standard pattern for conditional resource creation. When count is 0, no resource is created — no API calls, no state entry. When 1, exactly one is created. This is how you implement feature flags and environment-specific resources in Terraform.

Q8
What does [for s in var.subnets : s.cidr_block] return?
Show Answer
Answer

A list of strings containing only the cidr_block values from each subnet object.

Explanation

Square bracket [...] for-expressions always return lists. Curly brace {...} returns maps.

variable "subnets" {
  default = [
    { name="web",  cidr_block="10.0.1.0/24", az="us-east-1a" },
    { name="app",  cidr_block="10.0.2.0/24", az="us-east-1b" },
    { name="db",   cidr_block="10.0.3.0/24", az="us-east-1a" },
  ]
}

# [...] → LIST
[for s in var.subnets : s.cidr_block]
# → ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24", "10.0.3.0/24"]

# {...} → MAP
{for s in var.subnets : s.name => s.cidr_block}
# → {"web"="10.0.1.0/24", "app"="10.0.2.0/24", "db"="10.0.3.0/24"}

# With grouping (group by AZ):
{for s in var.subnets : s.az => s.cidr_block...}
# → {"us-east-1a"=["10.0.1.0/24","10.0.3.0/24"], "us-east-1b"=["10.0.2.0/24"]}
# Note: ... (ellipsis) enables GROUPING mode
Q9
How do you flatten a nested list-of-lists into a single flat list?
Show Answer
Answer

flatten([[a,b],[c,d,e]]) returns [a,b,c,d,e]

Explanation

flatten() takes a list of lists and returns a single flat list. This is commonly used after nested for-expressions. Example: flatten([for env in var.envs : [for subnet in env.subnets : subnet.id]]). Without flatten, you'd get [["subnet-1","subnet-2"],["subnet-3"]].

Q10
You want to create a map where keys are environment names and values are their instance types. Write the for expression.
Show Answer
Answer

{for config in var.env_configs : config.name => config.instance_type}

Explanation

This converts a list of objects into a lookup map. You can then use lookup() for safe access.

variable "env_configs" {
  type = list(object({
    name          = string
    instance_type = string
    min_nodes     = number
  }))
  default = [
    { name="dev",     instance_type="t3.small",  min_nodes=1 },
    { name="staging", instance_type="t3.medium", min_nodes=2 },
    { name="prod",    instance_type="t3.large",  min_nodes=3 },
  ]
}

locals {
  # Convert list → map for easy lookup
  instance_types = {for c in var.env_configs : c.name => c.instance_type}
  # → {"dev"="t3.small", "staging"="t3.medium", "prod"="t3.large"}

  node_counts    = {for c in var.env_configs : c.name => c.min_nodes}
  # → {"dev"=1, "staging"=2, "prod"=3}
}

# Safe access with lookup:
resource "aws_eks_node_group" "main" {
  cluster_name = aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.name
  instance_types = [
    lookup(local.instance_types, var.environment, "t3.medium")
  ]
  scaling_config {
    desired_size = lookup(local.node_counts, var.environment, 2)
    max_size     = lookup(local.node_counts, var.environment, 2) * 2
    min_size     = 1
  }
}

Chapter 9: Type Constraints and Validation

Terraform's type system catches errors before they reach your cloud. Complex type constraints let you define exactly what shape your variables must have, while validation rules catch invalid values with clear error messages. Preconditions and postconditions (TF 1.2+) add resource-level guardrails.

🔑 Exam Focus

The exam tests: (1) writing object({...}) type constraints, (2) using optional() (TF 1.3+), (3) creating validation {} blocks with can() and regex, and (4) knowing when to use variable validation vs lifecycle preconditions.

9.1 Complex Type Constraints

Beyond simple types like string and number, Terraform supports list(type), set(type), map(type), and object({...}). The optional() modifier (TF 1.3+) makes specific object attributes optional with defaults.

Type ConstraintExample ValueWhen to Use
list(string)["us-east-1a","us-east-1b"]Ordered list of same-type items
set(string)["us-east-1a","us-east-1b"]Unique, unordered items
map(string){dev="t3.small"; prod="t3.large"}Key-value with same value type
object({name=string, cidr=string}){name="web"; cidr="10.0.1.0/24"}Fixed-schema objects
list(object({...}))List of structured objectsMultiple items with same schema
anyAny typeWhen type truly varies (rare)
Anihpj Complex Types — Subnet, Environment & Scaling Configs
# TYPE 1: list(object({...})) — Multiple subnets with the same schema
variable "subnet_config" {
  description = "Subnet configuration for anihpj VPC"
  type = list(object({
    name       = string               # REQUIRED: subnet identifier
    cidr_block = string               # REQUIRED: IP range
    az         = string               # REQUIRED: availability zone
    public     = optional(bool, true) # OPTIONAL: defaults to true
    tags       = optional(map(string), {}) # OPTIONAL: extra tags
  }))
  default = [
    { name = "dev-pub-1a";   cidr_block = "10.0.1.0/24"; az = "us-east-1a"; public = true },
    { name = "dev-priv-1a";  cidr_block = "10.0.2.0/24"; az = "us-east-1a"; public = false;
      tags = { Tier = "private" } },
    { name = "dev-pub-1b";   cidr_block = "10.0.3.0/24"; az = "us-east-1b" },  # public defaults to true
  ]
}

# TYPE 2: map(object({...})) — Environment-specific configurations
variable "environments" {
  type = map(object({
    instance_type  = string
    min_size       = number
    max_size       = number
    desired_count  = number
    enable_backups = optional(bool, false)
  }))
  default = {
    dev = { instance_type = "t3.small";  min_size = 1; max_size = 2; desired_count = 1 }
    prod = { instance_type = "t3.large"; min_size = 2; max_size = 6; desired_count = 3;
      enable_backups = true }
  }
}

# TYPE 3: list(string) — Simple ordered list
variable "availability_zones" {
  type    = list(string)
  default = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]
}

# TYPE 4: object({...}) with nested structures
variable "scaling_config" {
  type = object({
    cpu_threshold    = number
    memory_threshold = number
    cooldown         = number
    metric_config = object({
      statistic   = string
      period      = number
      eval_periods = number
    })
  })
  default = {
    cpu_threshold    = 70
    memory_threshold = 80
    cooldown         = 300
    metric_config = {
      statistic    = "Average"
      period       = 60
      eval_periods = 3
    }
  }
}
Type Constraint Anatomy — Nested Object Breakdown
variable "subnet_config" {
  type = list(          ← OUTER TYPE: ordered collection
    object({            ← INNER TYPE: fixed-schema object
      name       = string              ← REQUIRED (no optional wrapper)
      cidr_block = string              ← REQUIRED
      az         = string              ← REQUIRED
      public     = optional(bool, true) ← OPTIONAL → defaults to true
      tags       = optional(map(string), {}) ← OPTIONAL → defaults to {}
    })
  )
}

🔑 optional() was added in Terraform 1.3.
   Before TF 1.3, ALL object attributes were REQUIRED.
   This is a COMMON exam distinction.

9.2 Custom Validation Rules 🎯

Validation blocks catch bad input early — at plan time — with clear, actionable error messages. Every variable with constraints should have validation rules.

5 Exam-Ready Validation Patterns for Anihpj
variable "environment" {
  type    = string
  default = "dev"

  # PATTERN 1: Allowed values check (most common)
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "Environment must be one of: dev, staging, prod. Got: ${var.environment}"
  }
}

variable "vpc_cidr" {
  type    = string

  # PATTERN 2: Format validation with regex/can()
  validation {
    condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.vpc_cidr))
    error_message = "Invalid CIDR format: ${var.vpc_cidr}. Must be like 10.0.0.0/16."
  }
}

variable "instance_type" {
  type    = string

  # PATTERN 3: Regex pattern matching
  validation {
    condition     = can(regex("^t[23]\\.", var.instance_type))
    error_message = "Only t2/t3 instance families allowed. Got: ${var.instance_type}"
  }
}

variable "app_port" {
  type    = number

  # PATTERN 4: Numeric range check
  validation {
    condition     = var.app_port >= 1024 && var.app_port <= 65535
    error_message = "Port must be between 1024-65535. Got: ${var.app_port}"
  }
}

variable "cluster_name" {
  type    = string

  # PATTERN 5: String length check
  validation {
    condition     = length(var.cluster_name) >= 1 && length(var.cluster_name) <= 32
    error_message = "Cluster name must be 1-32 characters. Got: ${length(var.cluster_name)} chars."
  }
}

# PATTERN 6: Multiple validations on one variable
variable "db_engine" {
  type    = string
  default = "postgres"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["postgres", "mysql", "mariadb"], var.db_engine)
    error_message = "Supported engines: postgres, mysql, mariadb."
  }
  validation {
    condition     = var.db_engine == "postgres" || var.db_engine == "mysql"
    error_message = "Anihpj only supports PostgreSQL and MySQL."
  }
}
💡 Validation Best Practices

1) Always include the actual value in error_message using ${var.name} — it saves hours of debugging. 2) Use can() to wrap functions that might error on bad input (like can(regex(...))). 3) One validation block per concern — combine related checks only if logically related. 4) Validation runs at plan time — before any resources are touched.

9.3 Preconditions and Postconditions (TF 1.2+)

Lifecycle conditions validate resource-level logic — preconditions check inputs before resource creation, postconditions verify outputs after creation. Unlike variable validation (which checks a single input), these can cross-reference multiple values.

TypeWhen It RunsWhat It Can AccessAnihpj Example
preconditionBEFORE resource create/updateInput variables, data sources, other resource attrsVerify RDS engine is PostgreSQL
postconditionAFTER resource create/updateself (the resource's own attributes)Verify EKS cluster is ACTIVE
validation (variable)Plan time (on variable input)Only the variable's own valueVerify env is in allowed list
Anihpj: Pre & Postconditions in Action
# PRECONDITION: Check BEFORE creating the RDS instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  engine         = var.db_engine
  engine_version = var.db_version
  instance_class = var.db_instance_class

  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = var.db_engine == "postgres"
      error_message = "Anihpj jobpost requires PostgreSQL. Got: ${var.db_engine}"
    }
    precondition {
      condition     = var.db_instance_class != "db.t2.micro"
      error_message = "t2.micro is too small for production. Use t3.small or larger."
    }
  }
}

# POSTCONDITION: Check AFTER the EKS cluster is created
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" {
  name     = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.eks_cluster.arn
  version  = var.kubernetes_version
  vpc_config {
    subnet_ids = aws_subnet.private[*].id
  }

  lifecycle {
    postcondition {
      condition     = self.status == "ACTIVE"
      error_message = "EKS cluster is not ACTIVE. Status: ${self.status}"
    }
    postcondition {
      condition     = self.version == var.kubernetes_version
      error_message = "EKS version mismatch: expected ${var.kubernetes_version}, got ${self.version}"
    }
  }
}

# POSTCONDITION: Verify S3 bucket encryption is enabled
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-${var.environment}-assets"

  lifecycle {
    postcondition {
      condition     = can(self.server_side_encryption_configuration[0].rule[0].apply_server_side_encryption_by_default[0].sse_algorithm)
      error_message = "S3 bucket ${self.bucket} must have SSE enabled!"
    }
  }
}
🔵 Variable Validation

Checks: Single variable value

When: Plan time

Use for: "Is this input valid?"

validation { condition = ... }
🟡 Precondition

Checks: Multiple inputs/resources

When: Before resource create

Use for: "Should we even create this?"

lifecycle { precondition { ... }}
🟢 Postcondition

Checks: Resource's own outputs

When: After resource create

Use for: "Did it deploy correctly?"

lifecycle { postcondition { ... }}
Validation Decision Flow — Which to Use When?
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                    │  "I need to validate something"  │
                    └───────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                    │
                    ┌───────────────▼─────────────────┐
                    │  Is it checking a SINGLE         │
                    │  variable input value?           │
                    └───────┬───────────────┬─────────┘
                            │ YES           │ NO (cross-referencing)
                            ▼               ▼
            ┌───────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐
            │ variable "x" {        │  │ "Should we even create    │
            │   validation {        │  │  this resource?"          │
            │     condition = ...   │  │                           │
            │   }                   │  └───────────┬───────────────┘
            │ }                     │              │
            └───────────────────────┘  ┌───────────▼───────────────┐
            ✅ VARIABLE VALIDATION      │                           │
            Examples:                  │ lifecycle {               │
            • allowed env list         │   precondition {          │
            • CIDR format              │     condition = ...       │
            • port range               │   }                       │
            • string length            │ }                         │
                                       └───────────────────────────┘
                                       ✅ PRECONDITION
                                       Examples:
                                       • "RDS must be PostgreSQL"
                                       • "EKS version >= 1.27"
                                       • "Prod needs t3.large+"

                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │  "Did it deploy correctly?"                   │
                    │  Checking the resource AFTER creation         │
                    └───────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                                        │
                         ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
                         │ lifecycle {                             │
                         │   postcondition {                       │
                         │     condition = self.attribute == ...   │
                         │   }                                     │
                         │ }                                       │
                         └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         ✅ POSTCONDITION
                         Examples:
                         • self.status == "ACTIVE"
                         • self.version == var.kubernetes_version
                         • Bucket has SSE enabled

9.5 Check Blocks — Post-Apply Validation (TF 1.5+) 🆕

The check block (introduced in Terraform 1.5) validates infrastructure AFTER apply — unlike precondition/postcondition which run during plan/apply. Check blocks are ideal for verifying that your infrastructure is healthy and operational after deployment.

Check Block — Post-Deployment Health Verification
check "s3_versioning_check" {
  data "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
    bucket = aws_s3_bucket.assets.id
  }

  assert {
    condition     = data.aws_s3_bucket.assets.versioning[0].enabled
    error_message = "S3 bucket ${aws_s3_bucket.assets.id} does NOT have versioning enabled!"
  }

  assert {
    condition     = data.aws_s3_bucket.assets.server_side_encryption_configuration[0].rule[0].apply_server_side_encryption_by_default[0].sse_algorithm == "aws:kms"
    error_message = "S3 bucket must use KMS encryption!"
  }
}

# Check blocks for anihpj EKS health:
check "eks_health" {
  data "http" "cluster_health" {
    url = "${aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.endpoint}/healthz"
  }
  assert {
    condition     = data.http.cluster_health.status_code == 200
    error_message = "EKS cluster health check FAILED!"
  }
}
📖 Check vs Precondition vs Postcondition
BlockWhen It RunsEffect on FailureUse Case
preconditionBEFORE resource create/updateBLOCKS the operation"Don't create RDS if port != 5432"
postconditionAFTER resource create/updateERRORS but resource exists"Verify ARN is not empty after creation"
check (1.5+)AFTER entire apply completesWARNINGS only (doesn't block)"Verify versioning is on, endpoint is healthy"

Key difference: Check blocks run after ALL resources are applied and report warnings — they never block infrastructure changes. They're designed for ongoing compliance monitoring, not gating.

Chapter 9 — Practice Questions

Q1
Write a variable type constraint for a list of objects, each with name (string), cidr (string), and optional public (bool, default true).
Show Answer
Answer
type = list(object({
  name   = string
  cidr   = string
  public = optional(bool, true)
}))
Explanation

optional() was added in Terraform 1.3. For earlier versions, all attributes in object({...}) were required. The second argument to optional() is the default value when not specified. This is a commonly tested version-specific feature — if the exam asks about optional fields, optional() is the answer.

Q2
Write a validation that ensures a variable named environment is one of "dev", "staging", or "prod".
Show Answer
Answer
validation {
  condition     = contains(["dev","staging","prod"], var.environment)
  error_message = "Environment must be dev, staging, or prod."
}
Explanation

contains(list, value) checks if a value exists in a list — much cleaner than chaining || operators. The error_message is shown to the user when validation fails. Always include the actual value in the error message using ${var.name}.

Q3
When would you use a precondition instead of a variable validation?
Show Answer
Answer

When you need to validate using multiple values or cross-reference other resources and data sources. Variable validation can only check the variable's own value in isolation.

Explanation

Preconditions can check: other variables, data sources, resource attributes, and complex multi-value logic like "if env is prod, then instance type must be at least medium." They run during the plan phase, before any resources are modified, so they prevent bad applies just like variable validation.

Q4
Write a postcondition that verifies an S3 bucket has versioning enabled after creation.
Show Answer
Answer
lifecycle {
  postcondition {
    condition     = self.versioning[0].enabled
    error_message = "S3 bucket ${self.bucket} must have versioning enabled!"
  }
}
Explanation

self refers to the resource being created/updated — the resource that owns the lifecycle block. Postconditions run after the resource exists, so you can access all its attributes including computed ones. This is critical for verifying resources were created correctly.

Q5
What version of Terraform introduced the optional() type modifier?
Show Answer
Answer

Terraform 1.3. Before this, all attributes in object({...}) types were required.

Explanation

The optional(type, default) modifier allows callers to omit specific fields — they get the default value instead. This is a commonly tested version-specific feature. If the exam shows a config with optional(), you know it requires TF ≥ 1.3.

Q6
Write a validation that ensures a CIDR block is valid.
Show Answer
Answer
validation {
  condition     = can(cidrnetmask(var.vpc_cidr))
  error_message = "Invalid CIDR: ${var.vpc_cidr}"
}
Explanation

cidrnetmask() throws an error on invalid CIDR input. can() catches this and returns false instead of crashing. This can(function_that_might_error()) pattern is the standard approach for all validation that involves functions that can throw errors.

Q7
How do you validate that a number is between 1 and 65535?
Show Answer
Answer
validation {
  condition     = var.port >= 1 && var.port <= 65535
  error_message = "Port must be 1-65535. Got: ${var.port}"
}
Explanation

Number range validation is straightforward — use && to chain comparisons. Always include the actual invalid value in the error message so the user knows what they provided. This pattern applies to any numeric range check (min/max size, storage GB, etc.).

Q8
Can a variable have multiple validation blocks?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. A single variable can have multiple independent validation blocks. ALL must pass for the plan to proceed.

Explanation

Each validation block runs independently. This lets you separate concerns: one validation checks format (regex), another checks allowed values, another checks length/range. If any validation fails, the plan stops with that specific error message — helping users fix issues one at a time.

Q9
What does self refer to in a postcondition block?
Show Answer
Answer

self refers to the resource being created/updated — the resource that owns the lifecycle block.

Explanation

In a postcondition on aws_eks_cluster.anihpj, self.status is equivalent to aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.status. This is how you check the resource's own computed attributes after creation. self is only available inside postcondition blocks — not in precondition blocks (where the resource doesn't exist yet).

Q10
Write a precondition that ensures an RDS instance is not db.t2.micro for production.
Show Answer
Answer
lifecycle {
  precondition {
    condition     = var.environment != "prod" || var.db_instance_class != "db.t2.micro"
    error_message = "db.t2.micro is not allowed in production!"
  }
}
Explanation

The logic: "If env is NOT prod, allow anything (skip check). If env IS prod, then instance_class must NOT be t2.micro." This is a cross-reference precondition — it checks two variables together, which variable validation alone can't do. This pattern is essential for environment-specific guardrails.
