🟡 Part 4: State Management — The Source of TruthChapters 10-12

Chapter 10: Understanding Terraform State

State is Terraform's brain — a JSON file that maps your HCL code to real cloud resources. Without state, Terraform can't know what it created, what changed, or what to destroy. State is the single source of truth for your infrastructure, and protecting it is the most critical operational concern.

🎓 Exam Relevance
Domain 1: Resource LifecycleDomain 3: Collaborative WorkflowsHANDS-ON LABS
🧪 State Manipulation on the Exam
  • You WILL be asked to: import an existing resource, move a resource between modules, or fix a corrupted state.
  • Key commands: terraform state list, state show, state mv, state rm, import.
  • Deadly trap: state rm removes from state but KEEPS the real resource. destroy deletes the real resource.
  • Import needs BOTH: the command AND a matching .tf resource block.
🔑 Key Exam Insight

The exam tests: (1) understanding what state tracks and why, (2) state locking mechanics, (3) state CLI commands (list, show, mv, rm, import), and (4) refresh operations. Know that state contains ALL resource attributes including secrets — it's not config, it's a database of your infrastructure.

10.1 What is State? — The Brain of Terraform

State is stored in terraform.tfstate — a JSON file mapping every resource in your .tf files to its real-world cloud counterpart. It tracks resource IDs, attributes, dependencies, and metadata.

📄 What State Tracks
Resource IDsi-0abcd1234 (AWS EC2 instance ID)
Resource AttributesAll computed values: public_ip, arn, endpoint
DependenciesWhich resources depend on which
MetadataProvider info, Terraform version
🔐 State is PRIVATE
Contains SecretsPasswords, keys, tokens — all in plain JSON!
NOT Config.tf files = desired; state = actual
Must Be ProtectedEncrypt at rest, never commit to git
Team SharedRemote backends for collaboration
State File Anatomy — An Anihpj EC2 Instance in State
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  RESOURCE IN STATE: aws_instance.jobpost_server                   │
│                                                                  │
│  "id":            "i-0abcd1234efgh5678"   ← AWS-assigned ID      │
│  "arn":           "arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:..."                     │
│  "public_ip":     "54.123.45.67"          ← RUNTIME value         │
│  "private_ip":    "10.0.1.45"             ← RUNTIME value         │
│  "ami":           "ami-0c55b159cb..."     ← FROM .tf config       │
│  "instance_type": "t3.medium"             ← FROM .tf config       │
│  "subnet_id":     "subnet-0xyz..."        ← FROM .tf config       │
│  "tags":          { Name = "anihpj-jobpost-prod" }                │
│  "password":      "SuperSecret123!"       ← ⚠️ SECRET EXPOSED!    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
How State Powers Terraform Operations
┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────┐
│  .tf files   │          │  STATE FILE  │
│  (DESIRED)   │          │  (ACTUAL)    │
│              │          │              │
│  resource    │          │  id: i-abc   │
│  "aws_inst"  │          │  type: t3.m  │
│  "web" {     │          │  ami: ami-.. │
│    type=t3.l │          │              │
│  }           │          └──────┬───────┘
└──────┬───────┘                 │
       │                         │
       └────────┬────────────────┘
                ▼
       ┌────────────────┐
       │  terraform     │
       │  plan          │
       │                │
       │  DIFF: type    │
       │  t3.m → t3.l   │
       │  ~ modify      │
       └───────┬────────┘
               │
               ▼
       ┌────────────────┐
       │  terraform     │
       │  apply         │
       │                │
       │  1. Call AWS   │
       │     API        │
       │  2. Change     │
       │     instance   │
       │  3. Update     │
       │     state      │
       └────────────────┘
⚠️ State is NOT Optional — Why You Can't Skip It

Without state, Terraform is blind. It can't know what exists, what changed, or what to destroy. If you lose your state file, Terraform can't manage your infrastructure — it would try to recreate everything from scratch, causing massive outages. This is why remote state with backups and versioning is non-negotiable for production.

10.2 The State Lock — Preventing Race Conditions 🎯

When two people run terraform apply at the same time, they could both write to the state file simultaneously — corrupting it. State locking prevents this by ensuring only one process can modify state at a time.

State Locking — Alice vs Bob Timeline
TIME   ALICE (terraform apply)              BOB (terraform apply)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T+0s   Acquires state lock 🔒               Attempts acquire lock...
       │                                     WAITING ⏳
T+5s   Reads state from S3                  "Lock held by Alice"
       │                                     (terraform waits)
T+30s  Builds dependency graph              Still waiting...
       │
T+1m   Shows plan, Alice confirms           Waiting...
       "yes" (approves 15 changes)
T+3m   Applies changes to AWS               Waiting...
       Creates VPC, EKS, RDS
T+5m   Writes new state to S3              Waiting...
       Releases lock 🔓                     │
                                            "Lock acquired!" 🔒
T+6m   Done ✅                              Reads latest state from S3
                                            (includes Alice's new resources!)
                                            Builds graph, shows plan...

WITHOUT LOCKING: Both write simultaneously → state corruption → 💀
🔒 How Locking Works

Before any state-modifying operation (apply, destroy), Terraform acquires a lock. The backend stores this lock (DynamoDB for S3, object lock for GCS, lease blob for Azure).

⏱️ Lock Duration

The lock is held for the entire apply. If the process crashes, the lock stays — you need terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID to release it manually.

✅ Locking Backends

S3+DynamoDB, GCS, Azure, Terraform Cloud, Consul, pg all support locking. local and http backends do NOT — avoid them for team use.

⚠️ force-unlock — The Nuclear Option

terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID removes a lock. ONLY use this if you're 100% sure no one is running apply. If someone IS running terraform and you force-unlock, two applies will run simultaneously — corrupting the state. Always check with your team first!

10.3 State Commands — Manual State Operations 🎯

Terraform provides subcommands for inspecting and manipulating state directly. These are critical for debugging, refactoring, and importing existing resources.

10.3a terraform state list — What's in My State?

terraform state list
$ terraform state list
aws_vpc.main
aws_subnet.public[0]
aws_subnet.public[1]
aws_subnet.private[0]
aws_eks_cluster.anihpj
aws_db_instance.jobpost
aws_s3_bucket.assets
aws_iam_role.eks_cluster
aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.eks_cluster_AmazonEKSClusterPolicy
# ... 45 resources total for anihpj production

# Useful variations:
$ terraform state list | grep eks        # Find EKS-related resources
$ terraform state list | wc -l           # Count total resources: 45
$ terraform state list module.vpc        # Resources in the vpc module

10.3b terraform state show — Inspect One Resource

terraform state show
$ terraform state show aws_db_instance.jobpost
# aws_db_instance.jobpost:
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
    address               = "anihpj-prod-db.xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com"
    allocated_storage     = 100
    arn                   = "arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:123456789:db:anihpj-prod-db"
    db_name               = "jobpost"
    endpoint              = "anihpj-prod-db.xyz...:5432"
    engine                = "postgres"
    engine_version        = "15.4"
    id                    = "anihpj-prod-db"
    instance_class        = "db.t3.large"
    password              = "SuperSecret123!"  # ⚠️ SENSITIVE!
    port                  = 5432
    storage_encrypted     = true
    username              = "jobpost_admin"
}

10.3c terraform state mv — Rename/Refactor Resources

terraform state mv — Rename Without Destroy
# SCENARIO: You renamed aws_s3_bucket.assets to aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets
# Without state mv, Terraform would DESTROY the old bucket and CREATE a new one!

$ terraform state mv aws_s3_bucket.assets aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets
Move "aws_s3_bucket.assets" to "aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets"
Successfully moved 1 resource.

# SCENARIO: Moving a resource into a module (refactoring)
$ terraform state mv aws_instance.jobpost module.compute.aws_instance.jobpost

# SCENARIO: Moving WITHIN count/for_each
$ terraform state mv 'aws_subnet.public[0]' 'aws_subnet.public["us-east-1a"]'

10.3d terraform state rm — Detach Without Destroying

terraform state rm
# SCENARIO: Stop managing a resource with Terraform
# but keep the actual cloud resource running

$ terraform state rm aws_security_group.manually_managed
Removed aws_security_group.manually_managed from state.
# The security group STILL EXISTS in AWS, but Terraform no longer manages it

# DANGER: terraform destroy will NOT destroy this resource
# because Terraform doesn't know about it anymore!

# BATCH REMOVAL:
$ terraform state list | grep "module.old_vpc" | xargs terraform state rm

10.3e terraform import — Bring Existing Resources Under Management

terraform import — Adopt an existing S3 bucket
# STEP 1: Write the resource block (can be empty)
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "anihpj_assets" {
  # Leave empty for now
}

# STEP 2: Import the existing bucket into state
$ terraform import aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets anihpj-assets-prod
aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets: Importing from ID "anihpj-assets-prod"...
Import successful!

# STEP 3: Run plan to see the diff
$ terraform plan  # Shows ALL differences — .tf is still empty!

# STEP 4: Fill in the .tf to match the imported state
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "anihpj_assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-assets-prod"
  tags   = { Name = "anihpj-assets"; Environment = "prod" }
}

# STEP 5: Plan again — should show NO changes
$ terraform plan
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

10.4 Refreshing State — Syncing with Reality

What happens when someone changes a resource manually in the AWS console? Terraform doesn't know — until you refresh. Refresh reads the current state of all resources from the cloud and updates the state file.

State Refresh Operations
# Modern approach (TF ≥ 0.15.4):
$ terraform apply -refresh-only
# Shows what changed OUTSIDE of Terraform:
# Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform
#     ~ resource "aws_security_group" "allow_ssh" {
#         ~ ingress = [
#             + {  # Someone added this rule manually!
#                 from_port   = 8080
#                 to_port     = 8080
#                 protocol    = "tcp"
#                 cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
#               }
#           ]
#       }

# Plan auto-refreshes:
$ terraform plan
# Automatically does a refresh before showing the plan
# (unless you use -refresh=false)
💡 Anihpj Drift Scenario

Someone manually resized the RDS instance from db.t3.large to db.t3.xlarge via AWS console. After terraform apply -refresh-only, the state shows the new size. Then terraform plan shows Terraform wants to change it BACK to db.t3.large (because that's what's in .tf). This is how you detect drift!

Chapter 10 — Practice Questions

Q1
What does the Terraform state file contain and why is it considered the "single source of truth"?
Show Answer
Answer

A JSON file mapping every resource in .tf files to its real-world cloud counterpart. It contains resource IDs, computed attributes, dependencies, and metadata — including all secrets (passwords, keys in plain text). It's the single source of truth because .tf files define desired state while state tracks actual state. The plan operation computes the diff between them.

Explanation

Without state, Terraform is blind — it can't know what it created, what exists, or what to destroy. State bridges your HCL code and the cloud API. Key exam points: (1) state contains secrets, (2) state is NOT configuration, (3) remote state is required for teams, (4) losing state = losing your infrastructure map.

  STATE FILE — THE BRIDGE BETWEEN CODE AND CLOUD:

  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
  │   .tf FILES  │────────▶│ STATE FILE   │────────▶│  CLOUD API   │
  │  (desired)   │         │ (terraform.  │         │  (actual)    │
  │              │         │  tfstate)    │         │              │
  │ resource     │         │              │         │ aws_vpc      │
  │ "aws_vpc"    │   MAPS  │ ".tf name"  │  MAPS   │ vpc-abc123   │
  │ "main" {    │────────▶│ → "vpc-abc" │────────▶│ 10.0.0.0/16  │
  │   cidr=...   │         │              │         │              │
  │ }            │         │ {            │         │              │
  └──────────────┘         │   "resources":│        └──────────────┘
                            │   [{          │
                            │     "type":   │
                            │     "aws_vpc",│
                            │     "name":   │
                            │     "main",   │
                            │     "id":     │
                            │     "vpc-abc"│
                            │   }]          │
                            │ }             │
                            └──────────────┘

  ⚠ STATE CONTAINS SECRETS — encrypt at rest (S3 SSE, GCS CMEK)
  ⚠ Losing state = losing the map between code and cloud
Q2
What happens if two team members run terraform apply simultaneously without state locking?
Show Answer
Answer

State file corruption. Both processes write to the state file at the same time, creating an inconsistent state that doesn't match reality. One person's changes are lost, and the infrastructure drifts from what Terraform believes exists.

WITHOUT LOCKING:
Alice writes state ───┐
                      ├── STATE CORRUPTED 💀
Bob writes state ─────┘

WITH LOCKING:
Alice acquires lock → writes state → releases lock
Bob waits → acquires lock → reads updated state → writes state
Explanation

State locking prevents race conditions. Before any state-modifying operation, Terraform acquires a lock via the backend (DynamoDB for S3, object lock for GCS, lease blob for Azure). If the process crashes, the lock may get stuck — use terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID only after verifying no one is actually running apply.

Q3
You renamed aws_s3_bucket.assets to aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets in your .tf files. Running terraform plan shows it wants to destroy the old bucket and create a new one. How do you prevent this?
Show Answer
Answer

Use terraform state mv to update the resource address in state without touching the cloud resource:

terraform state mv aws_s3_bucket.assets aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets
Explanation

When you rename a resource in .tf files, Terraform sees it as "old resource deleted, new resource needed." state mv tells Terraform "the old name and new name refer to the same real resource" — it updates the address in state without destroying anything. Also works for moving resources into modules: terraform state mv aws_vpc.main module.networking.aws_vpc.main.

Q4
What is the difference between terraform state rm and terraform destroy?
Show Answer
Answer

state rm: Removes the resource from state only — the actual cloud resource continues running. Terraform "forgets" about it.
destroy: Deletes the actual cloud resource AND removes it from state.

Explanation

Use state rm when you want to stop managing a resource with Terraform but keep it running (e.g., migrating it to another tool). Use destroy when you want to permanently delete the resource. Warning: after state rm, terraform destroy will NOT destroy that resource — Terraform no longer knows about it.

Q5
You have an S3 bucket created manually via AWS Console. How do you bring it under Terraform management?
Show Answer
Answer

The 5-step import workflow:

# STEP 1: Write empty resource block
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {}

# STEP 2: Import into state
terraform import aws_s3_bucket.assets my-existing-bucket

# STEP 3: See the diff
terraform plan  # Shows ALL differences — .tf is still empty

# STEP 4: Update .tf to match
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "my-existing-bucket"
  tags   = { Name = "my-bucket" }
}

# STEP 5: Verify
terraform plan  # "No changes" ✅
Explanation

Import writes to state only, not to .tf files. You MUST manually write the matching configuration. Use terraform state show after import to see what attributes the resource has. TF 1.5+ introduced declarative import blocks that can be checked into git.

Q6
Someone manually changed an EC2 security group via AWS Console. How do you detect this drift?
Show Answer
Answer

Run terraform apply -refresh-only (TF ≥ 0.15.4) or the legacy terraform refresh. This updates the state file to match what actually exists in AWS, showing any differences detected.

Explanation

After refresh-only, the state reflects the manual change. Running terraform plan will then show Terraform wants to change it BACK to what's in .tf — this is how you discover unauthorized changes. Regular terraform plan also auto-refreshes before showing the plan.

Q7
What AWS services does the S3 backend use for state storage and locking, and why is the locking component necessary?
Show Answer
Answer

S3 stores the state file (with SSE encryption + versioning). DynamoDB provides distributed locking (table with LockID as primary key). S3 itself has no native locking mechanism — DynamoDB fills this gap.

Explanation

The DynamoDB table uses LockID as the hash key with PAY_PER_REQUEST billing. When Terraform starts an operation, it writes a lock entry; if another process holds the lock, it waits. The lock is released after state is written. Always enable S3 versioning on state buckets — it's your lifeline for recovery.

Q8
When should you use terraform force-unlock and what is the risk?
Show Answer
Answer

ONLY when you are 100% certain no one is running terraform apply and the lock is stuck from a crashed process. The risk: force-unlocking while another apply is active causes two simultaneous state writes → state corruption.

Explanation

Always verify with your team before force-unlocking. Check CI/CD pipelines — a stuck pipeline job may still hold the lock. If the original process is truly dead (killed mid-apply, network timeout), then force-unlock is safe. It's called the "nuclear option" for a reason.

Q9
Where should you NEVER store your Terraform state file, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Never in Git — state files contain plaintext secrets (passwords, API keys, tokens). Committing them exposes all your infrastructure credentials. Also never store only on a single local laptop (no team access, no backup, single point of failure).

Explanation

State files are JSON blobs that include every resource attribute — including password, access_key, secret_key fields. Even if you mark variables as sensitive = true, the values are still in the state file. Always use remote backends with encryption (S3+SSE, GCS+managed keys) and restrict access via IAM.

Q10
How do you list all resources currently managed in state, and how do you inspect a single resource's details?
Show Answer
Answer
# List all resources
terraform state list

# Filter by type or module
terraform state list | grep eks
terraform state list module.vpc

# Inspect one resource in detail
terraform state show aws_db_instance.jobpost
Explanation

state list shows every resource Terraform tracks — ordered alphabetically with indices for counted resources (aws_subnet.public[0]). state show prints all attributes including sensitive ones. These commands read from state only — they don't contact the cloud API.

Chapter 11: Remote State Backends

Local state works for a solo developer. For teams, you need remote state — stored in a shared, encrypted, lockable location. Remote backends enable collaboration, protect secrets, and provide disaster recovery through versioning.

🔑 Exam Focus

The exam tests: (1) why remote state is essential for teams, (2) S3 + DynamoDB backend configuration, (3) backend configuration options (inline vs external), and (4) knowing which backends support locking.

11.1 Why Remote State? — Team Collaboration 🎯

🏠 Local State (Single Developer)
  • State lives on your laptop
  • Only YOU can run terraform
  • Laptop dies → state lost → 💀
  • No locking — two terminals can corrupt
  • Can't share with teammates
  • No versioning/backup
☁️ Remote State (Team)
  • State stored in S3/GCS/Azure
  • Whole team can run terraform
  • Durable storage — 99.999999999% durability
  • DynamoDB locking prevents conflicts
  • IAM policies control access
  • Versioning = instant rollback

11.2 S3 Backend (AWS) — The Most Common Backend 🎯

For AWS shops, the S3 backend with DynamoDB locking is the gold standard. S3 stores the state file with server-side encryption; DynamoDB provides the distributed lock.

S3 Backend Architecture — Anihpj Production
┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐
│  Terraform  │────▶│  DynamoDB Table  │     │  S3 Bucket       │
│   apply     │     │  (LOCKING)       │     │  (STATE STORAGE) │
│             │     │                  │     │                  │
│  1. Acquire │     │  LockID = "prod/ │     │  prod/           │
│     lock    │     │  terraform.      │     │  terraform.      │
│             │     │  tfstate-md5"    │     │  tfstate         │
└──────┬──────┘     └──────────────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘
       │                                               │
       │  2. Read state ──────────────────────────────▶│
       │  3. Plan changes                              │
       │  4. Apply changes to AWS                      │
       │  5. Write new state ─────────────────────────▶│ (versioned!)
       │  6. Release lock                              │
       ▼
   Done ✅
Anihpj S3 Backend — Complete Configuration
# File: backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "anihpj-tfstate-prod"     # S3 bucket for state
    key            = "prod/terraform.tfstate"  # State file path within bucket
    region         = "us-east-1"               # Bucket region
    encrypt        = true                      # SSE-S3 encryption at rest
    dynamodb_table = "anihpj-tfstate-locks"    # DynamoDB for locking
    kms_key_id     = "alias/tfstate-key"       # Optional: KMS CMK
  }
}

# ┌─────────────────── SETUP STEPS ───────────────────────┐
# │ 1. aws s3 mb s3://anihpj-tfstate-prod                 │
# │ 2. aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket ...       │
# │ 3. aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket ...       │
# │ 4. aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket ...     │
# │ 5. aws dynamodb create-table \                        │
# │      --table-name anihpj-tfstate-locks \              │
# │      --attribute-definitions AttributeName=LockID,... │
# │      --key-schema AttributeName=LockID,KeyType=HASH \ │
# │      --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST                   │
# │ 6. terraform init  (migrates local→remote state)      │
# └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

# PER-ENVIRONMENT STATE ORGANIZATION:
# s3://anihpj-tfstate-prod/dev/terraform.tfstate
# s3://anihpj-tfstate-prod/staging/terraform.tfstate
# s3://anihpj-tfstate-prod/prod/terraform.tfstate
⚠️ CRITICAL: Enable S3 Versioning!

If state gets corrupted, S3 versioning lets you restore a previous version in seconds. Without versioning, a bad terraform apply that corrupts state means you've lost your infrastructure map. Always enable versioning on state buckets.

11.3 Other Backends

11.3a GCS (Google Cloud Storage)

GCS Backend
terraform {
  backend "gcs" {
    bucket = "anihpj-tfstate-prod"
    prefix = "prod"  # State stored at prod/default.tfstate
  }
}

11.3b azurerm (Azure Storage)

Azure Backend
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "anihpj-tfstate-rg"
    storage_account_name = "anihpjtfstate"
    container_name       = "tfstate"
    key                  = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
  }
}

11.3c Terraform Cloud

Terraform Cloud Backend
terraform {
  backend "remote" {
    hostname     = "app.terraform.io"
    organization = "anihpj"

    workspaces {
      name = "anihpj-production"
    }
  }
}

11.3d pg (PostgreSQL)

PostgreSQL Backend
terraform {
  backend "pg" {
    conn_str = "postgres://user:pass@db.anihpj.com/tfstate?sslmode=require"
  }
}

11.3f kubernetes (K8s Secret Backend)

Store state as a Kubernetes Secret — useful when your entire workflow runs inside K8s.

Kubernetes Backend
terraform {
  backend "kubernetes" {
    secret_suffix = "tfstate"     # Secret name: tfstate-default
    namespace     = "terraform"   # K8s namespace
    in_cluster_config = true      # Use in-cluster ServiceAccount
  }
}
# State stored as: kubectl get secret tfstate-default -n terraform

11.3e Backend Comparison Matrix

BackendLockingTeam SharingEncryptionBest For
S3+DynamoDB✅ DynDB✅ IAM✅ SSE-S3AWS shops
GCS✅ Object lock✅ GCS IAM✅ Managed keysGCP shops
azurerm✅ Lease blobs✅ Azure RBAC✅ Storage encryptionAzure shops
Terraform Cloud✅ Auto✅ Teams✅ Built-inTFC users
pg✅ Table lock✅ DB users✅ pgcryptoCustom setups
http❌ None❌ URL❌ ManualLegacy/niche

🔑 Rule: Always use a backend that supports locking. Without locking, team usage leads to state corruption.

11.4 Backend Configuration

Backend configuration can't use variables (it's processed before variables are resolved). Use external configuration for dynamic values:

Backend Configuration Options
# OPTION 1: Inline (hardcoded)
# backend.tf:
terraform { backend "s3" { bucket="my-bucket"; key="prod/state"; region="us-east-1" } }

# OPTION 2: External file (recommended for CI/CD)
$ terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl
# backend.hcl:
bucket  = "anihpj-tfstate-prod"
key     = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
region  = "us-east-1"
encrypt = true
dynamodb_table = "anihpj-tfstate-locks"

# OPTION 3: CLI overrides (partial)
$ terraform init -backend-config="key=${ENV}/terraform.tfstate"
# Allows dynamic key per environment from CI/CD variable

# OPTION 4: Migrate from local to remote
$ terraform init -migrate-state
# Terraform asks: "Do you want to copy existing state to the new backend?"
# Answer "yes" to migrate!

Chapter 11 — Practice Questions

Q1
Why can't teams use local state for production Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

Local state lives on one person's laptop — no team access, no locking, no backup, no encryption. If that laptop dies, all infrastructure state is lost and must be rebuilt from scratch (or manually). Remote state solves all of these: shared access via IAM, DynamoDB locking, S3 durability (99.999999999%), SSE encryption, and versioning for instant rollback.

Explanation

The exam expects you to understand the progression: solo dev → local state is fine; team → remote state is required. Remote backends provide three things local can't: shared access, locking, and durability. Without all three, production Terraform is unsafe.

Q2
What AWS services does the S3 backend use, and what is each component's role?
Show Answer
Answer

S3: Stores the state file (JSON). Must have versioning enabled, SSE-S3 or KMS encryption, and public access blocked.
DynamoDB: Provides distributed locking. Table has LockID as the hash key, PAY_PER_REQUEST billing. Terraform writes a lock entry before any state-modifying operation.

Explanation

S3 has no native locking — it's an object store. DynamoDB provides the mutual exclusion. Together they form the most common backend for AWS shops. Setup requires creating both resources BEFORE terraform init (they can't be managed by the same Terraform config — chicken-and-egg problem).

Q3
Write the complete S3 backend configuration for anihpj production, including DynamoDB locking and KMS encryption.
Show Answer
Answer
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "anihpj-tfstate-prod"
    key            = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    encrypt        = true
    dynamodb_table = "anihpj-tfstate-locks"
    kms_key_id     = "alias/tfstate-key"
  }
}
Explanation

Key fields: encrypt = true enables SSE-S3 by default; use kms_key_id for custom KMS keys. dynamodb_table enables locking. The key field determines the state file path within the bucket — use per-environment keys like dev/terraform.tfstate, prod/terraform.tfstate.

Q4
Why can't you use variables or locals in a backend block?
Show Answer
Answer

The backend block is processed during terraform init — BEFORE Terraform resolves any variables, locals, or data sources. At init time, the provider hasn't been downloaded yet, and variables haven't been read. Use -backend-config=file.hcl or -backend-config="key=value" CLI flags for dynamic configuration.

Explanation

This is a critical exam point. The backend config must be known before anything else because it determines where state is stored — and state is needed for everything else. It's a bootstrap problem: you need state to know where state is stored. Use external .hcl files for environment-specific backend configs.

Q5
You've been using local state. How do you migrate to an S3 remote backend without losing your state?
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Add backend block to backend.tf
# 2. Run init with migrate flag
terraform init -migrate-state

# Terraform prompts:
# "Do you want to copy existing state to the new backend?"
# Answer: yes

# 3. Terraform copies local state → S3
# 4. Local state file is now empty (state is in S3)
Explanation

-migrate-state is the key flag. Without it, Terraform would initialize a new empty backend and you'd lose all your existing state. The migration copies all resources, their IDs, and all metadata. After migration, the local terraform.tfstate file is emptied — all state now lives in S3.

Q6
Which Terraform backends support state locking, and which do NOT?
Show Answer
Answer

Support locking: S3+DynamoDB, GCS, azurerm, Terraform Cloud, Consul, pg, kubernetes
Do NOT support locking: local, http

Explanation

This is a common exam question. Always use a backend with locking for team environments. The local backend has no locking at all — two terminals on the same machine can corrupt state. The http backend is a legacy option for niche use cases. If a question asks about team collaboration and locking isn't mentioned, that's a red flag.

Q7
Your team discovers the state file is corrupted after a failed apply. S3 versioning is enabled. What's the recovery procedure?
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. List versions to find the last good one
aws s3api list-object-versions \
  --bucket anihpj-tfstate-prod \
  --prefix prod/terraform.tfstate

# 2. Download the good version (before corruption)
aws s3api get-object \
  --bucket anihpj-tfstate-prod \
  --key prod/terraform.tfstate \
  --version-id "good-version-id" \
  ./restored.tfstate

# 3. Verify
terraform plan  # Should show NO unexpected changes
Explanation

S3 versioning is your lifeline. Every state write creates a new version. Without versioning enabled, corrupted state = lost infrastructure map. Always enable versioning AND test the restore procedure regularly. Also set up lifecycle rules to expire old versions after 30-90 days to control costs.

Q8
How do you organize state files for dev, staging, and prod environments in the S3 backend?
Show Answer
Answer

Use different key values within the same bucket (or separate buckets for stronger isolation):

# Same bucket, different keys:
s3://anihpj-tfstate/dev/terraform.tfstate
s3://anihpj-tfstate/staging/terraform.tfstate
s3://anihpj-tfstate/prod/terraform.tfstate

# Or separate buckets for stronger isolation:
s3://anihpj-tfstate-dev/terraform.tfstate
s3://anihpj-tfstate-prod/terraform.tfstate
Explanation

The key prefix pattern (dev/, prod/) keeps all states in one bucket for simplicity. Separate buckets provide stronger isolation (different IAM policies per environment) but more management overhead. The exam may test both patterns.

Q9
What does terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl do and why is it preferred over inline configuration?
Show Answer
Answer

It reads backend configuration from an external file instead of hardcoding it in the terraform {} block. This is preferred because: (1) you can .gitignore environment-specific configs, (2) CI/CD can dynamically provide backend values, (3) different environments can use different backends without changing code.

Explanation

Example: CI/CD pipeline sets $ terraform init -backend-config="key=${ENV}/terraform.tfstate". This dynamically sets the key per environment. You can also use partial configuration: the backend block declares the backend type, and -backend-config provides the specific values.

Q10
Can you switch from one backend type to another (e.g., S3 to Terraform Cloud)? If so, how?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. Change the backend block to the new type and run:

terraform init -migrate-state

Terraform detects the backend change, prompts for confirmation, then copies state from the old backend to the new one.

Explanation

The -migrate-state flag works for any backend-to-backend migration (local→S3, S3→TFC, GCS→Azure, etc.). Terraform reads state from the old backend and writes it to the new one. After migration, verify with terraform plan that everything is intact.

Chapter 12: State Operations & Troubleshooting

Production Terraform requires knowing how to manage multiple environments, import existing resources, restructure state during refactoring, and recover from failures. These operational skills are the difference between confidence and panic.

🔑 Exam Focus

The exam tests workspaces (create, select, list), the import workflow, state mv for refactoring, and troubleshooting common state errors. Know when to use workspaces vs directory-per-environment.

12.1 Workspaces — Multiple Environments, One Config 🎯

Workspaces let you use the same .tf files for multiple environments, with each workspace having its own isolated state file.

12.1a terraform workspace list

Workspace Commands
$ terraform workspace list
  default
* dev
  staging
  prod

$ terraform workspace show
dev  # Current workspace

12.1b terraform workspace new

Create & Delete Workspaces
$ terraform workspace new staging
Created and switched to workspace "staging"!

$ terraform workspace delete dev
Workspace "dev" is not empty. Use -force to delete.
$ terraform workspace delete -force dev
Deleted workspace "dev"!

12.1c terraform workspace select

Switch Workspaces & Use in Config
$ terraform workspace select prod
Switched to workspace "prod".

# Use terraform.workspace in your .tf files:
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-assets-${terraform.workspace}"  # anihpj-assets-prod
}

# Conditional logic per workspace:
locals {
  instance_size = terraform.workspace == "prod" ? "t3.large" : "t3.small"
  backup_retention = terraform.workspace == "prod" ? 35 : 7
}

# Workspace-specific variables (terraform.tfvars doesn't auto-switch):
# Use: terraform apply -var-file="${terraform.workspace}.tfvars"

12.1d Workspaces vs Directory-per-Environment

FactorWorkspacesDirectories (env/dev, env/prod)
State StorageSame backend, different keysSeparate backends or paths
Code Reuse✅ Same .tf files❌ Copy-paste between dirs
Isolation🟡 Moderate (shared config)✅ Strong (completely separate)
Complexity🟢 Simple🔴 More complex CI/CD
Config DifferencesLimited (same modules)✅ Full flexibility
Best For2-3 similar envsStrict isolation, 4+ envs

Anihpj Choice: Directories. Different configs (instance sizes, replica counts, CIDR ranges per env) make directory-per-environment the better fit. Each env gets its own env/dev/, env/staging/, env/prod/ with shared modules.

12.2 Importing Existing Infrastructure 🎯

The import workflow brings manually-created resources under Terraform management. Remember: import only writes to state, not to .tf files.

The 5-Step Import Workflow
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 1: Write EMPTY resource block in .tf                       │
│  resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {}                            │
│                                                                  │
│  STEP 2: terraform import aws_s3_bucket.assets my-bucket         │
│  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  Terraform reads the live resource → writes to STATE             │
│  State now has: id, arn, bucket, region, acl, tags...           │
│                                                                  │
│  STEP 3: terraform plan                                          │
│  Shows DIFF between empty .tf and state → lots of changes!       │
│                                                                  │
│  STEP 4: UPDATE .tf TO MATCH STATE                               │
│  resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {                             │
│    bucket = "my-bucket"; acl = "private";                       │
│    tags = { Name = "my-bucket" }                                 │
│  }                                                               │
│                                                                  │
│  STEP 5: terraform plan → "No changes" ✅                        │
│  Resource is now fully managed by Terraform!                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA: import writes STATE, not .tf!

After terraform import, your .tf file is still empty/incomplete. You MUST manually write the matching configuration. Use terraform state show to see what attributes the resource has, then copy them into your .tf.

🆕 TF 1.5+: Declarative import Blocks

Terraform 1.5 introduced import blocks — you can now declare imports directly in .tf files instead of running CLI commands:

# File: imports.tf
import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.anihpj_assets    # Resource address in state
  id = "anihpj-assets-prod"           # Real-world resource ID
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "anihpj_assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-assets-prod"       # Must match what exists
  tags   = { Name = "anihpj-assets" }
}

# Now just run: terraform plan
# Terraform reads the import block, finds the bucket,
# checks if .tf matches, and imports automatically!

This is much cleaner than the CLI workflow — everything is declarative and version-controlled. The exam may test TF 1.5+ features.

12.3 Moving Resources in State — Refactoring

When you restructure your code (rename resources, move into modules), use terraform state mv to update state without destroying anything. TF 1.1+ also supports declarative moved blocks.

Refactoring Anihpj: Flat → Modular
# BEFORE: Flat structure in root module
# main.tf has: aws_vpc.main, aws_subnet.public[0], aws_subnet.private[0]...

# AFTER: We want to move networking into module "networking"
# New structure: module.networking.aws_vpc.main, module.networking.aws_subnet.public[0]...

# Use state mv to migrate WITHOUT destroying:
$ terraform state mv aws_vpc.main module.networking.aws_vpc.main
$ terraform state mv 'aws_subnet.public[0]' 'module.networking.aws_subnet.public[0]'
$ terraform state mv 'aws_subnet.public[1]' 'module.networking.aws_subnet.public[1]'
# ... repeat for all resources

# MODERN APPROACH (TF 1.1+): moved block (declarative, with history)
moved {
  from = aws_vpc.main
  to   = module.networking.aws_vpc.main
}
# This is checked into git — everyone sees the refactoring history!
🔴 state mv (Imperative, TF all versions)

Must be run manually by every team member on their local machine. If someone forgets, their plan shows destroy+create.

$ terraform state mv \
  aws_vpc.main \
  module.networking.aws_vpc.main

❌ Not version-controlled
❌ Easy to forget
❌ No audit trail

🟢 moved block (Declarative, TF 1.1+)

Checked into git — Terraform automatically follows the move history. No manual commands needed.

moved {
  from = aws_vpc.main
  to   = module.networking.aws_vpc.main
}

✅ Version-controlled in git
✅ Automatic for all teammates
✅ Full audit trail of refactoring

12.4 State Recovery — When Things Go Wrong

State problems are scary but recoverable if you've planned ahead. Here's how to handle the 5 most common state emergencies:

ErrorCauseFix
"Failed to acquire state lock"Someone else is running applyWait, or terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID (if stuck)
"Resource already exists but not in state"Resource created outside Terraformterraform import
"State snapshot was created by newer version"Version mismatchRestore from backup, or upgrade Terraform
"Backend configuration changed"Backend block modifiedterraform init -migrate-state
"Error refreshing state"Cloud API issue (auth/network)terraform apply -refresh-only
State Recovery from S3 — Lifesaving Procedure
# EMERGENCY: State file is corrupted. Restore from S3 version history!

# 1. List all versions of the state file
$ aws s3api list-object-versions \
    --bucket anihpj-tfstate-prod \
    --prefix prod/terraform.tfstate

# 2. Find the last good version ID (before corruption timestamp)
# VersionId: "abc123..." (from 10 minutes ago — before the bad apply)

# 3. Download the good version
$ aws s3api get-object \
    --bucket anihpj-tfstate-prod \
    --key prod/terraform.tfstate \
    --version-id "abc123..." \
    ./restored.tfstate

# 4. Replace corrupted state
$ cp ./restored.tfstate ./terraform.tfstate

# 5. Verify — should show NO unexpected changes
$ terraform plan
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration. ✅

# PREVENTION: Enable S3 versioning + lifecycle rules
# Keep versions for 30 days minimum!
🛡️ State Protection Checklist for Anihpj Production
  • ✅ S3 bucket with versioning enabled (instant rollback)
  • ✅ DynamoDB locking table (prevents corruption)
  • ✅ SSE-S3 or KMS encryption (protects secrets in state)
  • ✅ Block public access on S3 bucket
  • ✅ IAM policy: only specific roles can read/write state
  • ✅ Separate state per environment (dev/, staging/, prod/)
  • ✅ CloudWatch alarm on force-unlock events
  • ✅ Regular backup testing: restore a version and run plan

Chapter 12 — Practice Questions

Q1
How do you create and switch to a new Terraform workspace for the staging environment?
Show Answer
Answer
# Creates AND switches in one command:
terraform workspace new staging

# Or two separate commands:
terraform workspace new staging
terraform workspace select staging

# Verify:
terraform workspace show   # "staging"
terraform workspace list   # default, *staging
Explanation

workspace new creates and auto-switches. The default workspace always exists. Each workspace has its own isolated state file even though they share the same .tf files. Deleting a workspace (with -force if it has resources) removes its state.

Q2
What expression gives you the current workspace name in HCL, and how would you use it to create environment-specific resource names?
Show Answer
Answer

terraform.workspace returns the current workspace name. Use it in resource naming, tags, and conditionals:

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-assets-${terraform.workspace}"  # anihpj-assets-prod
}

locals {
  instance_size = terraform.workspace == "prod" ? "t3.large" : "t3.small"
  backup_days   = terraform.workspace == "prod" ? 35 : 7
}
Explanation

terraform.workspace is a built-in interpolation value — not a variable, not a function. It's always available and cannot be overridden. Default workspace returns "default". Use it to make the same code behave differently based on which workspace is active.

Q3
When should you use Terraform workspaces vs separate directories per environment?
Show Answer
Answer

Workspaces: 2-3 similar environments, same backend, same .tf files. Simple, but limited configuration differences.
Directories: 4+ environments, different configurations per env, strict isolation, separate backends. More complex CI/CD.

Explanation

Workspaces work when environments are nearly identical (just different sizes/names). Directories are needed when environments differ significantly — different VPC CIDRs, different module versions, different providers. Anihpj uses directories because dev, staging, and prod have fundamentally different configurations.

  WORKSPACES vs DIRECTORIES — DECISION GUIDE:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WORKSPACES (terraform workspace)                         │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ anihpj/terraform/                                       │
  │   ├── main.tf           ← SAME .tf for all envs         │
  │   └── terraform.tfstate.d/                              │
  │       ├── dev/terraform.tfstate     ← Isolated state    │
  │       ├── staging/terraform.tfstate                     │
  │       └── prod/terraform.tfstate                        │
  │                                                          │
  │ ✅ Simple structure, easy to manage                      │
  │ ✅ terraform.workspace for conditional logic             │
  │ ❌ Same backend, same credentials, same providers       │
  │ ❌ Hard to make envs truly different                    │
  │ ❌ terraform destroy in wrong workspace = DISASTER      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ DIRECTORIES (per-environment folders)                    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ anihpj/terraform/                                       │
  │   ├── envs/                                             │
  │   │   ├── dev/                                          │
  │   │   │   ├── main.tf       ← DIFFERENT per env         │
  │   │   │   └── terraform.tfvars                          │
  │   │   ├── staging/                                      │
  │   │   │   ├── main.tf       ← Different node counts     │
  │   │   │   └── terraform.tfvars                          │
  │   │   └── prod/                                         │
  │   │       ├── main.tf       ← Different VPC CIDRs       │
  │   │       └── terraform.tfvars                          │
  │   └── modules/              ← SHARED module code        │
  │                                                          │
  │ ✅ Complete isolation (different backends, credentials) │
  │ ✅ Fully different configurations per env               │
  │ ✅ Separate AWS accounts possible                       │
  │ ❌ More files, more complex CI/CD                       │
  │ ❌ Must sync module versions across envs                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ANIHPJ CHOICE: Directories — dev/staging/prod are different
Q4
You need to import an existing RDS database into Terraform. Walk through the complete 5-step workflow.
Show Answer
Answer
# STEP 1: Write empty resource block
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {}

# STEP 2: Import
terraform import aws_db_instance.jobpost anihpj-prod-db

# STEP 3: See diff
terraform plan
# Shows ~ update, -/+ replace — .tf is still empty!

# STEP 4: Update .tf to match state
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  identifier     = "anihpj-prod-db"
  engine         = "postgres"
  engine_version = "15.4"
  instance_class = "db.t3.large"
  # ... copy ALL attributes from state show
}

# STEP 5: Verify
terraform plan
# "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration."
Explanation

Import only writes to state, not to .tf. Use terraform state show aws_db_instance.jobpost after import to see all attributes you need to copy. The exam tests this workflow — missing step 4 (updating .tf) means your next plan will try to destroy the imported resource!

Q5
After running terraform import, is your .tf file automatically updated? What command helps you see what to write?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Import writes to state only. Use terraform state show RESOURCE to see all attributes:

terraform state show aws_db_instance.jobpost
# Prints ALL attributes including computed ones
# Copy the relevant ones into your .tf file
Explanation

This is the #1 gotcha with import. Many people think import magically generates .tf — it doesn't. You must manually write the matching configuration. If you run terraform plan with an empty resource block after import, Terraform will try to destroy the resource because the .tf says "nothing" but state says "something exists."

Q6
You're refactoring the anihpj codebase — moving all networking resources into a separate module. How do you migrate resources without destroying them?
Show Answer
Answer
# Move each resource from root to module
terraform state mv aws_vpc.main module.networking.aws_vpc.main
terraform state mv 'aws_subnet.public[0]' 'module.networking.aws_subnet.public[0]'
terraform state mv 'aws_subnet.public[1]' 'module.networking.aws_subnet.public[1]'

# OR use moved blocks (TF 1.1+) — declarative, version-controlled:
moved {
  from = aws_vpc.main
  to   = module.networking.aws_vpc.main
}
Explanation

state mv must be run by every team member on their local machine. moved blocks (TF 1.1+) are declarative — checked into git, automatically followed by Terraform. Both achieve the same result: updating the resource address in state without touching the cloud resource.

Q7
What is the difference between terraform state mv and moved blocks? Which is preferred and why?
Show Answer
Answer

state mv (TF all versions): Imperative CLI command. Must be run manually by every developer. Not version-controlled. Easy to forget.
moved block (TF 1.1+): Declarative, checked into git. Terraform follows the move history automatically. All teammates benefit without running any command.

Explanation

Prefer moved blocks for refactoring that affects the whole team. They document the refactoring history in git. state mv is still useful for one-off operations or when using older Terraform versions. The exam may test both — know when to use each.

Q8
Your state file is corrupted after a failed apply. S3 versioning is enabled on your state bucket. Walk through the recovery procedure step by step.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Find good version
aws s3api list-object-versions \
  --bucket anihpj-tfstate-prod \
  --prefix prod/terraform.tfstate

# 2. Download the last known good version
aws s3api get-object \
  --bucket anihpj-tfstate-prod \
  --key prod/terraform.tfstate \
  --version-id "good-version-id" \
  ./restored.tfstate

# 3. Replace corrupted state
cp ./restored.tfstate ./terraform.tfstate

# 4. Verify
terraform plan
# Should show "No changes" — or minimal expected drift
Explanation

Versioning is the ONLY reliable recovery mechanism. Without it, you'd need to manually reconstruct state or re-import every resource. Always enable versioning AND test this procedure before you need it in an emergency. Set up lifecycle rules to manage version retention.

Q9
When exactly should you use terraform force-unlock, and what safety checks must you perform first?
Show Answer
Answer

Only when a lock is stuck from a crashed/dead process — never when someone might still be running apply. Safety checks: (1) Ask your team if anyone is running terraform, (2) Check CI/CD pipeline status, (3) Verify no active terraform processes on any machine. Then: terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID

Explanation

Force-unlock during an active apply = two simultaneous state writes = state corruption. This is unrecoverable without S3 versioning. The lock ID is shown in the error message when you try to run operations while locked. Consider setting up CloudWatch alarms on force-unlock events for audit trails.

Q10
What are the three most critical things to configure on your S3 state bucket for production use?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Versioning — enables recovery from corruption (most important!)
2. Encryption — SSE-S3 or KMS to protect secrets in state
3. Block Public Access — prevent accidental exposure of state (contains passwords!)

Explanation

Versioning = recovery, encryption = security, block public access = safety. Additional good practices: enable DynamoDB locking, use IAM policies to restrict access, set up lifecycle rules for old versions, and monitor with CloudTrail. These form the foundation of production-grade state management.
