🟡 Part 5: Modules — Building Blocks of InfrastructureChapters 13-15

Chapter 13: Understanding Modules

Modules are the LEGO blocks of Terraform — reusable containers that group related resources together. Every Terraform configuration is already a module (the root module). Domain 4 (Modules) is 20% of the exam and tests creating, using, and refactoring modules with hands-on labs.

🎓 Exam Relevance
Domain 4: ModulesDomain 2: Dynamic Config20% OF EXAM
🧪 Module Exam Patterns — What You'll Actually Do
  • Create a module: Given a flat config, extract resources into a module with proper variables.tf and outputs.tf.
  • Use a module: Call modules from the Registry (VPC, EKS) with correct source and version.
  • Refactor with moved: moved { from = aws_instance.web; to = module.app.aws_instance.web } — zero downtime refactoring.
  • Module outputs syntax: module.NAME.OUTPUT — the #1 most tested module pattern.
🔑 Key Exam Insight

The exam tests: (1) module structure and sources, (2) passing inputs and accessing outputs, (3) module composition (layering), and (4) understanding the root vs child module relationship. Know that module.NAME.OUTPUT is the syntax for accessing module outputs.

13.1 What is a Module? — The LEGO of Terraform 🎯

A module is a container for multiple resources used together. Instead of writing 20 resources for a VPC every time, you call one module that encapsulates them all. Every terraform working directory is a root module, and modules it calls are child modules.

Module Hierarchy — Anihpj Root → Child Modules → Resources
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ROOT MODULE (anihpj/terraform/)                                  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" }                  │  │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │  aws_vpc.main          aws_subnet.public[0][1][2]    │  │  │
│  │  │  aws_subnet.private[0][1][2]                         │  │  │
│  │  │  aws_nat_gateway.main  aws_route_table.public/private│  │  │
│  │  │  aws_internet_gateway.main                           │  │  │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  module "eks" { source = "./modules/eks" }                  │  │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │  aws_eks_cluster.anihpj    aws_eks_node_group.main   │  │  │
│  │  │  aws_iam_role.cluster      aws_iam_role.node_group   │  │  │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  module "rds" { source = "./modules/rds" }                  │  │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │  aws_db_instance.jobpost   aws_db_subnet_group.main  │  │  │
│  │  │  aws_db_parameter_group.postgres15                    │  │  │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧱 Root Module

Every terraform init directory. Calls child modules and defines top-level resources. Has its own state.

📦 Child Module

Called by root or other modules via module "name" {}. Self-contained with variables, outputs, and resources.

🔗 Published Module

Shared via Registry, GitHub, or S3. Versioned with semver. Battle-tested by the community.

💡 The Module Mindset

Think: "What infrastructure pattern do I repeat?" That's a module waiting to be created. Anihpj examples: VPC (repeated per environment), EKS cluster (repeated for dev/staging/prod), RDS database (same config, different sizes). Modules eliminate copy-paste and make infrastructure consistent.

Anihpj Module Pattern — Complete VPC Module (All Files)
# ─── modules/vpc/main.tf ───
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = var.vpc_cidr
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  tags = merge(var.tags, { Name = "${var.name}-vpc" })
}
resource "aws_subnet" "public" {
  for_each                = var.public_subnets
  vpc_id                  = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block              = each.value.cidr
  availability_zone       = each.value.az
  map_public_ip_on_launch = true
  tags = merge(var.tags, { Name = "public-${each.key}" })
}

# ─── modules/vpc/variables.tf ───
variable "vpc_cidr"       { type = string }
variable "name"            { type = string }
variable "public_subnets"  { type = map(object({ cidr = string; az = string })) }
variable "tags"            { type = map(string); default = {} }

# ─── modules/vpc/outputs.tf ───
output "vpc_id"            { value = aws_vpc.main.id }
output "public_subnet_ids" { value = [for s in aws_subnet.public : s.id] }

# ─── ROOT main.tf (USAGE) ───
module "vpc" {
  source   = "./modules/vpc"
  name     = "anihpj"
  vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"
  public_subnets = {
    "us-east-1a" = { cidr = "10.0.1.0/24"; az = "us-east-1a" }
    "us-east-1b" = { cidr = "10.0.2.0/24"; az = "us-east-1b" }
  }
  tags = local.common_tags
}

# REFERENCING MODULE OUTPUTS:
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" {
  vpc_id     = module.vpc.vpc_id               # ← single output
  subnet_ids = module.vpc.public_subnet_ids     # ← list output
}

# 🔑 MODULE RULES:
# • Each module = separate directory (main.tf + variables.tf + outputs.tf)
# • Inputs go in via variables.tf → Outputs come out via outputs.tf
# • Root references: module.NAME.OUTPUT_NAME

13.2 Module Sources — Where Modules Come From 🎯

The source argument tells Terraform where to find the module code. Terraform supports local paths, registries, GitHub, S3, and more.

Source TypeSyntaxWhen to Use
Local pathsource = "./modules/vpc"Your own modules in the same repo
Public Registrysource = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"Community modules (2,000+ available)
Private Registrysource = "app.terraform.io/anihpj/vpc/aws"Organization-internal modules
GitHubsource = "github.com/anihpj/terraform-aws-vpc"Git-hosted modules (public or private)
S3source = "s3::https://s3.amazonaws.com/bucket/vpc.zip"Archived module packages
Generic Gitsource = "git::https://gitlab.com/team/vpc.git?ref=v1.0"Any Git provider with ref/tag support
Anihpj Module Sources in Practice
# Local: Your own custom modules (fastest iteration)
module "vpc" {
  source = "./modules/vpc"
  name   = "anihpj"
}

# Registry: Battle-tested community modules (with version pinning!)
module "security_group" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/security-group/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"  # Accept 5.x, reject 6.x (breaking changes)
}

# GitHub: Your org's shared modules (version via git tags)
module "eks" {
  source = "github.com/anihpj/terraform-aws-eks?ref=v2.1.0"
}

# Private registry: Enterprise-grade internal modules
module "monitoring" {
  source  = "app.terraform.io/anihpj/monitoring/aws"
  version = ">= 1.0, < 2.0"
}

13.3 Module Inputs and Outputs 🎯

Modules communicate through input variables (configuration going IN) and output values (information coming OUT). This is the fundamental module contract.

Module Data Flow — Inputs → Module → Outputs
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                  │
│   INPUTS (variables)           OUTPUTS (values)                  │
│   ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐              │
│   │ vpc_cidr          │        │ vpc_id            │              │
│   │ name              │───▶ ┌──┴──┐ ───▶│ public_subnet_ids │              │
│   │ public_subnets    │    │ MOD  │     │ private_subnet_ids│              │
│   │ private_subnets   │    │ ULE  │     │ nat_gateway_ip    │              │
│   │ tags              │───▶ │      │ ───▶│ vpc_arn           │              │
│   └──────────────────┘    └─────┘     └──────────────────┘              │
│                                                                  │
│   ROOT CALL:                                                     │
│   module "vpc" {                                                 │
│     source    = "./modules/vpc"                                  │
│     name      = "anihpj-prod"         ← INPUT                    │
│     vpc_cidr  = "10.0.0.0/16"        ← INPUT                    │
│   }                                                              │
│                                                                  │
│   ROOT USAGE:                                                    │
│   resource "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {                            │
│     vpc_id     = module.vpc.vpc_id              ← OUTPUT         │
│     subnet_ids = module.vpc.public_subnet_ids   ← OUTPUT (list)  │
│   }                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Module I/O — Complete VPC Module Example
# ─── MODULE: modules/vpc/variables.tf (INPUTS) ───
variable "name"      { type = string }
variable "vpc_cidr"  { type = string; default = "10.0.0.0/16" }
variable "azs"       { type = list(string); default = ["us-east-1a","us-east-1b"] }
variable "tags"      { type = map(string); default = {} }

# ─── MODULE: modules/vpc/outputs.tf (OUTPUTS) ───
output "vpc_id" {
  value       = aws_vpc.main.id
  description = "The ID of the VPC"
}
output "public_subnet_ids" {
  value       = [for s in aws_subnet.public : s.id]
  description = "List of public subnet IDs"
}
output "private_subnet_ids" {
  value       = [for s in aws_subnet.private : s.id]
  description = "List of private subnet IDs"
}

# ─── ROOT: main.tf (USING THE MODULE) ───
module "vpc" {
  source = "./modules/vpc"
  name   = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
}

# Access outputs: module.NAME.OUTPUT
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  vpc_id     = module.vpc.vpc_id              # Single value
  subnet_ids = module.vpc.public_subnet_ids   # List value
}

13.4 Module Composition — Building in Layers

Real infrastructure is layered. Each module depends on the layer below it. This creates a dependency chain where changes flow upward — changing the VPC triggers re-evaluation of EKS and everything above it.

Anihpj Infrastructure Stack — 4-Layer Module Tower
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                      │
│  LAYER 4: APPLICATION (modules/app/)                                  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  🌐 kubernetes_deployment.jobpost                               │ │
│  │  🌐 kubernetes_service.jobpost (LoadBalancer)                   │ │
│  │  Inputs: cluster_endpoint, rds_hostname, secret_arns            │ │
│  │  Outputs: lb_dns_name, app_url                                  │ │
│  └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                             │ depends on                              │
│  LAYER 3: COMPUTE (modules/eks/)                                     │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ☸️ aws_eks_cluster.anihpj (v1.28)                             │ │
│  │  ☸️ aws_eks_node_group.main (t3.medium × 3)                    │ │
│  │  Inputs: vpc_id, subnet_ids, cluster_version                    │ │
│  │  Outputs: cluster_endpoint, ca_cert, oidc_provider              │ │
│  └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                             │ depends on                              │
│  LAYER 2: NETWORK (modules/vpc/)                                     │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  🔗 aws_vpc.main, subnets, NAT, IGW, route tables             │ │
│  │  Inputs: vpc_cidr, public_subnets, private_subnets              │ │
│  │  Outputs: vpc_id, public_subnet_ids, private_subnet_ids         │ │
│  └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                             │ depends on                              │
│  LAYER 1: FOUNDATION (modules/foundation/)                           │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  🏗️ S3 bucket (state), DynamoDB (locks), KMS (encryption)     │ │
│  │  Outputs: state_bucket_name, lock_table_name                    │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                      │
│  🔑 RULE: Each layer depends on the layer below                      │
│  🔑 Changes to VPC trigger re-evaluation of ALL layers above         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Module Composition Pitfalls

(1) Circular dependencies: Module A depends on Module B which depends on Module A — Terraform will error. (2) Too many layers: 4-5 layers is the sweet spot; beyond that, plan times slow down. (3) Hardcoded references: Always use outputs — never hardcode IDs from one module into another.

🔀 Provider Passing — When Modules Need Different Providers

Child modules inherit providers from the root by default. But what if you need a module to use a different region or account?

Default: Inherited Provider
# Root: default provider = us-east-1
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }

module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" }
# VPC module automatically uses us-east-1
Override: Aliased Provider
# Root: two providers
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1"; alias = "virginia" }
provider "aws" { region = "us-west-2"; alias = "oregon" }

module "dr_vpc" {
  source    = "./modules/vpc"
  providers = { aws = aws.oregon }  # Override!
}

🔑 This is exam Pattern 3: providers = { aws = aws.ALIAS } in the module block. Essential for multi-region and multi-account deployments.

Module Versioning — Semantic Versioning for Infrastructure
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MODULE VERSIONING: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH                                 │
│                                                                      │
│  version = "~> 1.2"  → >= 1.2.0, < 2.0.0  (minor updates OK)       │
│  version = ">= 2.0, < 3.0" → Any 2.x (explicit range)               │
│  version = "1.0.0"  → EXACTLY 1.0.0 (pinned, no updates)            │
│                                                                      │
│  VERSION    WHAT CHANGES                BREAKING?                     │
│  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│  v1.0.0     Initial release             N/A                          │
│  v1.1.0     New features, backward compat ❌ Minor                    │
│  v1.1.1     Bug fixes only               ❌ Patch                    │
│  v2.0.0     Breaking changes (removed     ✅ MAJOR — read CHANGELOG! │
│             args, renamed outputs)                                    │
│                                                                      │
│  ANIHPJ USAGE:                                                        │
│  module "vpc" {                                                      │
│    source  = "github.com/anihpj/terraform-aws-vpc"                   │
│    version = "~> 1.5"  # Accept 1.5.x, 1.6.x, but NOT 2.x          │
│  }                                                                   │
│                                                                      │
│  🔑 EXAM: Major version bump (1.x → 2.x) = BREAKING CHANGES!        │
│     Always check CHANGELOG before upgrading major versions.          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔴 WITHOUT Modules — Raw Resources (Anti-Pattern)
# Every environment copy-pastes 40+ lines
# dev/main.tf:
resource "aws_vpc" "dev" { cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" }
resource "aws_subnet" "dev_pub_1a" { ... }
resource "aws_subnet" "dev_pub_1b" { ... }
resource "aws_subnet" "dev_priv_1a" { ... }
# ... 35 more resources ...

# staging/main.tf: COPY-PASTE the same 40 lines!
# prod/main.tf: COPY-PASTE again!

# RESULT: 120 lines of duplicate code
# If VPC design changes → update 3 files
🟢 WITH Modules — Clean Abstraction
# modules/vpc/ contains the 40 lines ONCE

# dev/main.tf: 5 lines
module "vpc" { source = "../modules/vpc"
  name = "dev"; cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" }

# staging/main.tf: 5 lines
module "vpc" { source = "../modules/vpc"
  name = "staging"; cidr = "10.1.0.0/16" }

# prod/main.tf: 5 lines
module "vpc" { source = "../modules/vpc"
  name = "prod"; cidr = "10.2.0.0/16" }

# RESULT: 120 lines → 15 lines. One change fixes all.
🧪 Module Exam Patterns — What the Exam Tests
🔹 Pattern 1"How do you reference a module's output?" → Answer: module.NAME.OUTPUT (e.g., module.vpc.vpc_id)
🔹 Pattern 2"Where can modules come from?" → Answer: Local path, Registry, GitHub, S3, Bitbucket, HTTP URLs, Terraform Cloud private registry
🔹 Pattern 3"How do you pass a provider to a module?" → Answer: providers = { aws = aws.us-east-1 } in the module block (for aliased providers)
🔹 Pattern 4"What is the ROOT module?" → Answer: Every Terraform working directory IS a root module (the directory where terraform init is run)
🔹 Pattern 5"Where do child modules get their providers?" → Answer: Inherited from root UNLESS explicitly overridden with the providers argument

Chapter 13 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is a Terraform module and how does it differ from a resource?
Show Answer
Answer

A module is a container for multiple resources that are used together. A resource manages a single cloud object (one EC2, one VPC). A module groups many resources (VPC + subnets + NAT + routes) into one reusable unit. Every Terraform directory is a root module.

Explanation

Modules enable reuse, organization, and encapsulation. Instead of copying 50 lines of VPC code into every environment, you call module "vpc" {} and pass parameters. The root module is the directory where terraform init runs; child modules are called via module blocks.

Q2
How do you access a module's output value from the root module?
Show Answer
Answer

module.NAME.OUTPUT_NAME. Example: module.vpc.vpc_id returns the VPC ID from the vpc module.

module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" }
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id  # ← accessing module output
}
Explanation

The syntax is always module.LOCAL_NAME.OUTPUT_NAME. The local name is what you put after module in the block (e.g., module "vpc"). The output name must exist in the module's outputs.tf. This is one of the most tested patterns on the exam.

Q3
List at least 4 valid sources for Terraform modules.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Local path: "./modules/vpc"
2. Public Registry: "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
3. GitHub: "github.com/anihpj/terraform-aws-vpc"
4. S3: "s3::https://s3.amazonaws.com/bucket/vpc.zip"
Also: Private Registry, Bitbucket, GitLab, HTTP URLs, GCS buckets.

Explanation

The exam may ask "which of the following are valid module sources?" — all of the above are valid. Terraform supports local paths, registries (public and private), and any Git-based source. S3/GCS sources must point to zip/tar archives.

Q4
What is the root module and where does it get its name?
Show Answer
Answer

The root module is the working directory where you run terraform init. Every Terraform configuration has exactly one root module. It has no explicit name — it IS the root.

Explanation

This is a common exam trick question. The root module isn't declared with a module block — it's defined by the directory itself. All .tf files in the root directory belong to the root module. Child modules are called FROM the root module.

Q5
Your VPC module exposes vpc_id and public_subnet_ids as outputs. How do you use both in an EKS cluster resource?
Show Answer
Answer
module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" }

resource "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  vpc_id     = module.vpc.vpc_id
  subnet_ids = module.vpc.public_subnet_ids
}
Explanation

Each output is accessed individually with module.NAME.OUTPUT. You can also reference the entire module output as an object: module.vpc is an object with .vpc_id and .public_subnet_ids attributes. You could pass it whole: vpc_config = module.vpc.

Q6
Where do child modules get their provider configurations from?
Show Answer
Answer

Child modules inherit providers from the root module unless explicitly overridden. If the root has provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }, all child modules use it.

Explanation

To override a provider in a child module, use the providers argument: module "replica" { providers = { aws = aws.us-west-2 } }. This is tested when you need different regions or aliased providers in different modules.

Q7
What is module composition and why is layer ordering important?
Show Answer
Answer

Module composition is building infrastructure in layers where each layer depends on the one below. Foundation → Network → Compute → Application. Ordering matters because upper layers need outputs from lower layers (e.g., EKS needs VPC ID).

Explanation

Proper layering creates clear dependency chains. If VPC changes, Terraform knows to re-evaluate EKS and Application layers. Without layering, you risk creating resources before their dependencies exist, causing apply failures.

Q8
How do you version-pin a module from the Terraform Registry?
Show Answer
Answer
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"  # Accept 5.x, NOT 6.x
}
Explanation

~> 5.0 means >= 5.0.0 and < 6.0.0 — you get bug fixes and new features but no breaking changes. >= 4.0, < 5.0 is an explicit range. 5.0.0 is exact pinning. Always pin registry modules to avoid surprise breaking changes.

Q9
What files should every well-structured module contain?
Show Answer
Answer

Minimum: main.tf (resources), variables.tf (inputs), outputs.tf (outputs)
Recommended: README.md (documentation), versions.tf (provider requirements), examples/ (usage examples)

Explanation

The standard module structure makes modules discoverable and consistent. The Registry requires main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, and README.md. Examples help users understand how to call your module. Follow this convention for all modules.

Q10
What happens if you remove a module block from your root configuration?
Show Answer
Answer

All resources in that module will be DESTROYED. Terraform sees the module is no longer in the configuration and plans to delete everything it created.

Explanation

Removing a module call is equivalent to removing all its resources from .tf. Terraform's job is to make reality match config — if the module is gone from config, the resources must be gone from reality. Use terraform state rm first if you want to keep the resources but remove Terraform management.

Chapter 14: The Terraform Registry

The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) hosts 2,000+ community modules — battle-tested infrastructure patterns you can use instead of writing everything from scratch. Learning to find, evaluate, and use registry modules is a core professional skill.

🔑 Exam Focus

The exam tests: (1) finding and using registry modules, (2) version constraints (~>, >=, <), (3) knowing which modules to use for common tasks (VPC, EKS, RDS, security groups), and (4) evaluating module quality.

14.1 Public Registry — Don't Reinvent the Wheel

The public registry at registry.terraform.io contains thousands of free, verified modules. The most popular ones (terraform-aws-modules) have millions of downloads and are maintained by AWS and HashiCorp partners.

Checklist✅ Good Sign❌ Red Flag
Verified badgeHashiCorp partner badgeNo badge (not necessarily bad)
Downloads> 100K downloads< 1K downloads
Recent release< 6 months oldNo release in 12+ months
GitHub stars> 100 stars< 10 stars
Versionv1.0.0+ (stable)v0.x.x (unstable, no compatibility guarantee)
DocumentationClear README with examplesMinimal or missing docs
💡 Anihpj Recommended Registry Modules
terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws50M+ downloadsComplete VPC with subnets, NAT, routes
terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws20M+ downloadsEKS cluster + managed node groups
terraform-aws-modules/rds/aws10M+ downloadsRDS with all options
terraform-aws-modules/security-group/aws5M+ downloadsClean security group rules

14.2 Using Registry Modules for Anihpj

14.2a VPC Module (terraform-aws-modules/vpc)

Anihpj VPC using Registry Module
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.5"

  name = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"

  azs             = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
  public_subnets  = ["10.0.101.0/24", "10.0.102.0/24"]

  enable_nat_gateway   = true
  single_nat_gateway   = var.environment != "prod"  # Cost saving
  enable_dns_hostnames = true

  tags = { Project = "anihpj"; Environment = var.environment }
}

# Outputs available:
# module.vpc.vpc_id, module.vpc.public_subnets, module.vpc.private_subnets
# module.vpc.nat_public_ips, module.vpc.vpc_cidr_block

14.2b EKS Module (terraform-aws-modules/eks)

Anihpj EKS using Registry Module
module "eks" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws"
  version = "~> 20.0"

  cluster_name    = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
  cluster_version = "1.28"

  vpc_id     = module.vpc.vpc_id
  subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnets  # Nodes in private subnets

  eks_managed_node_groups = {
    main = {
      instance_types = ["t3.medium"]
      min_size       = 2
      max_size       = 6
      desired_size   = var.environment == "prod" ? 3 : 2
    }
  }

  tags = { Project = "anihpj"; Environment = var.environment }
}

# Outputs: module.eks.cluster_endpoint, module.eks.cluster_ca_certificate

14.2c RDS Module (terraform-aws-modules/rds)

Anihpj RDS using Registry Module
module "rds" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/rds/aws"
  version = "~> 6.5"

  identifier = "anihpj-jobpost-${var.environment}"
  engine     = "postgres"
  engine_version = "15.4"
  instance_class = var.environment == "prod" ? "db.t3.large" : "db.t3.small"

  db_name  = "jobpost"
  username = "jobpost_admin"
  port     = 5432

  vpc_security_group_ids = [module.security_group_rds.security_group_id]
  subnet_ids             = module.vpc.private_subnets

  backup_retention_period = var.environment == "prod" ? 35 : 7
  storage_encrypted       = true
  multi_az               = var.environment == "prod"
}

14.2d Security Group Module

Clean Security Groups with Registry Module
module "security_group_rds" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/security-group/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"

  name        = "anihpj-rds-${var.environment}"
  description = "RDS security group for jobpost database"
  vpc_id      = module.vpc.vpc_id

  ingress_with_cidr_blocks = [
    { from_port = 5432; to_port = 5432; protocol = "tcp"
      cidr_blocks = "10.0.0.0/16"; description = "PostgreSQL from VPC" }
  ]
  egress_rules = ["all-all"]
}

14.3 Version Constraints — Pinning for Safety

Module versions follow semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Pinning versions prevents surprise breaking changes.

ConstraintMeaningExampleAllows
version = "~> 1.2"Pessimistic: >= 1.2, < 2.0"~> 5.0"5.0.x, 5.1.x, ..., NOT 6.x
version = ">= 2.0, < 3.0"Explicit range">= 20.0, < 21.0"20.x.x only
version = "1.0.0"Exact pin"5.5.1"ONLY 5.5.1
⚠️ Version Bump = Breaking Changes

When a module goes from v1.x to v2.x, it's a MAJOR change — variables may be removed, outputs renamed, defaults changed. Always read the CHANGELOG before upgrading major versions. Use ~> to get safe minor/patch updates without breaking changes.

🏗️ Write Your Own Module When...
  • Your pattern is unique to your org
  • You need full control over defaults
  • Security/compliance requirements are strict
  • Registry modules are over-engineered for your need
  • You're building competitive advantage (core IP)

Example: Anihpj's custom EKS module with org-specific IAM roles, logging config, and node taints.

📦 Use Registry Module When...
  • Pattern is standard (VPC, RDS, SG)
  • Module is battle-tested (50M+ downloads)
  • You don't want to maintain boilerplate
  • Module has active maintainers + updates
  • You need something working FAST

Example: Using terraform-aws-modules/vpc for the standard VPC pattern everyone needs.

Chapter 14 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is the Terraform Registry and why should you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) is a public repository of 2,000+ community modules. You should use it to avoid reinventing common infrastructure patterns (VPC, EKS, RDS) — these modules are battle-tested, maintained, and used by thousands of organizations.

Explanation

The Registry solves the "not invented here" problem — why spend days writing a VPC module when a verified, production-tested one already exists? Registry modules save time, reduce bugs, and benefit from community maintenance. The exam expects you to know when to use Registry modules vs custom modules.

Q2
How do you evaluate whether a registry module is trustworthy?
Show Answer
Answer

Check: (1) Verified/HashiCorp partner badge, (2) Download count > 100K, (3) Recent release < 6 months, (4) v1.0.0+ (not v0.x), (5) Clear README with examples, (6) Active GitHub with >100 stars.

Explanation

The "verified" badge means HashiCorp has confirmed the publisher's identity. High download counts indicate widespread use and testing. Recent releases show active maintenance. v1.0.0+ means stable API with semantic versioning. A good README with complete examples means you can evaluate the module without digging through source code.

Q3
Write the module block to use terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws version 5.x for anihpj.
Show Answer
Answer
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"
  name    = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
  cidr    = "10.0.0.0/16"
  # ...
}
Explanation

The source follows the format NAMESPACE/NAME/PROVIDER for Registry modules. The version constraint uses ~> 5.0 to accept any 5.x version. Setting name and cidr are the minimum required inputs for this module. The registry page for each module lists all required and optional inputs.

Q4
What does version = "~> 5.0" mean?
Show Answer
Answer

>= 5.0.0 and < 6.0.0. Accepts 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.99.x — any 5.x version. Rejects 6.0.0 and above (potential breaking changes).

Explanation

The ~> operator (pessimistic constraint) locks the major version while allowing minor and patch updates. ~> 5.0 means "any version >= 5.0.0 but < 6.0.0." This is the recommended constraint for production modules — you get bug fixes and features without breaking changes.

Q5
Why should you avoid v0.x.x modules in production?
Show Answer
Answer

v0.x.x has no stability guarantees. The module author can make breaking changes in any minor/patch version. v1.0.0+ follows semantic versioning: breaking changes only in major versions. v0.5.1 → v0.6.0 could break your infrastructure without warning.

Explanation

Semantic versioning only applies from v1.0.0. In v0.x.x, the API is considered unstable — the maintainer signals "this module may change significantly." Production infrastructure should never depend on unstable APIs. Always pin to v1.0.0+ modules with ~> constraints for production.

Q6
Which registry module would you use for an EKS cluster and why?
Show Answer
Answer

terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws — 20M+ downloads, maintained by AWS partners, supports managed node groups, IRSA, and all EKS features.

Explanation

This module encapsulates the complex IAM roles, networking, and node configuration that EKS requires. Without it, setting up EKS requires 5+ IAM roles, security group rules, and node group configurations. The module abstracts all this complexity behind a clean interface — you provide cluster_name, vpc_id, subnet_ids, and it handles the rest.

Q7
What version constraint allows any version from 1.5 to 2.0 (excluding 2.0)?
Show Answer
Answer

version = "~> 1.5" (pessimistic) OR version = ">= 1.5, < 2.0" (explicit). Both achieve the same result — ~> is more concise.

Explanation

The pessimistic constraint ~> 1.5 locks the rightmost specified version component — in this case, the minor version. It means >= 1.5.0, < 2.0.0. For more complex constraints, use the explicit form: ">= 1.5, < 2.0, != 1.7.0".

Q8
How does the VPC module communicate its outputs to the EKS module?
Show Answer
Answer
module "eks" {
  vpc_id     = module.vpc.vpc_id
  subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnets
}
Explanation

Module outputs are accessed via module.NAME.OUTPUT. The VPC module's vpc_id and private_subnets outputs become the EKS module's inputs. This creates an implicit dependency — Terraform knows the EKS module must wait for the VPC module to complete. No depends_on needed.

Q9
What does the single_nat_gateway = true argument do in the VPC module?
Show Answer
Answer

Creates only ONE NAT Gateway (shared across AZs) instead of one per AZ. This saves ~$32/month per additional NAT Gateway. Use in non-production environments.

Explanation

By default, the VPC module creates one NAT Gateway per availability zone for high availability. If one AZ fails, the others still have internet access. In dev/staging, this HA is overkill — single_nat_gateway = true creates one shared NAT. The anihpj config uses this: single_nat_gateway = var.env != "prod" to save costs in non-prod.

Q10
What happens if the registry module you're using gets a new major version (e.g., v5 → v6) with breaking changes?
Show Answer
Answer

If you pinned with version = "~> 5.0", nothing happens — Terraform will not upgrade to v6. Your infrastructure is safe. If you used no version constraint, Terraform would download the latest (v6) on next terraform init -upgrade.

Explanation

Version pinning is your safety net against breaking changes. Without constraints, terraform init -upgrade downloads whatever's latest — potentially breaking your configuration. The lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl) records the exact version and checksum. Always pin major versions in production, and test upgrades in dev first.

Chapter 15: Writing Your Own Modules

After using registry modules, you'll inevitably need custom modules for your organization's specific patterns. Writing good modules requires discipline: clean structure, minimal interfaces, and thorough testing.

🔑 Exam Focus

The exam tests: (1) standard module structure, (2) designing good variable interfaces, (3) module testing approaches, and (4) publishing workflows. Expect questions about module file layout and variable design.

15.1 Module Structure Best Practices

Every well-structured module follows a standard layout. This consistency makes modules discoverable, maintainable, and publishable to the Registry.

📁 Required Files (Minimum)
modules/my-module/
├── main.tf        # Resources
├── variables.tf   # Input variables
└── outputs.tf     # Output values
📁 Recommended Files (Registry-Ready)
modules/my-module/
├── main.tf        # Resources
├── variables.tf   # Input variables
├── outputs.tf     # Output values
├── versions.tf    # Provider requirements
├── README.md      # Documentation
└── examples/      # Usage examples
    └── basic/
        └── main.tf
Module Design Principles
# PRINCIPLE 1: Minimal required inputs — maximize optional with defaults
variable "name" {
  type        = string
  description = "REQUIRED: Base name for all resources"
}
variable "instance_type" {
  type    = string
  default = "t3.medium"  # OPTIONAL: sensible default
}

# PRINCIPLE 2: Use for_each for flexible resource creation
variable "subnets" {
  type    = map(object({ cidr = string; az = string; public = optional(bool, true) }))
  default = {}  # No subnets by default — caller decides
}

# PRINCIPLE 3: Tag EVERYTHING
locals {
  tags = merge(var.tags, { Module = "vpc"; ManagedBy = "terraform" })
}

# PRINCIPLE 4: Output everything callers might need
output "vpc_id"              { value = aws_vpc.main.id }
output "public_subnet_ids"   { value = [for s in aws_subnet.public : s.id] }
output "private_subnet_ids"  { value = [for s in aws_subnet.private : s.id] }

15.2 Building the Anihpj EKS Module

Let's build a complete, production-ready EKS module from scratch. This module encapsulates: EKS cluster, managed node group, IAM roles, and networking configuration.

modules/eks/main.tf — Complete EKS Module
# ─── modules/eks/main.tf ───
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  name     = var.cluster_name
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.cluster.arn
  version  = var.cluster_version

  vpc_config {
    subnet_ids             = var.subnet_ids
    endpoint_private_access = true
    endpoint_public_access  = true
  }

  depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.cluster_AmazonEKSClusterPolicy]
}

resource "aws_eks_node_group" "main" {
  cluster_name    = aws_eks_cluster.main.name
  node_group_name = "${var.cluster_name}-nodes"
  node_role_arn   = aws_iam_role.node_group.arn
  subnet_ids      = var.subnet_ids

  scaling_config {
    desired_size = var.desired_size
    max_size     = var.max_size
    min_size     = var.min_size
  }

  instance_types = var.instance_types
}

# ─── modules/eks/variables.tf ───
variable "cluster_name"    { type = string }
variable "cluster_version" { type = string; default = "1.28" }
variable "subnet_ids"      { type = list(string) }
variable "instance_types"  { type = list(string); default = ["t3.medium"] }
variable "desired_size"    { type = number; default = 2 }
variable "min_size"        { type = number; default = 1 }
variable "max_size"        { type = number; default = 6 }
variable "tags"            { type = map(string); default = {} }

# ─── modules/eks/outputs.tf ───
output "cluster_endpoint"          { value = aws_eks_cluster.main.endpoint }
output "cluster_ca_certificate"    { value = aws_eks_cluster.main.certificate_authority[0].data }
output "cluster_name"              { value = aws_eks_cluster.main.name }
output "oidc_provider_arn"         { value = aws_eks_cluster.main.identity[0].oidc[0].issuer }
💡 Module Design Pattern: Sensible Defaults

Only require inputs that MUST be provided (cluster_name, subnet_ids). Everything else (cluster_version, instance_types, desired_size) has reasonable defaults. This minimizes the mental load on module users — they only specify what's unique to their environment.

15.3 Module Testing — Trust But Verify

Infrastructure code needs testing too. Terratest (Go-based) is the standard framework for testing Terraform modules. Test stages: init → apply → validate outputs → destroy.

Terratest Example — Testing the EKS Module
// File: test/eks_test.go
func TestEKSModule(t *testing.T) {
    terraformOptions := &terraform.Options{
        TerraformDir: "../examples/basic",
        Vars: map[string]interface{}{
            "cluster_name": "test-anihpj",
            "subnet_ids":   []string{"subnet-123", "subnet-456"},
        },
    }

    // Clean up after test
    defer terraform.Destroy(t, terraformOptions)

    // Init and apply
    terraform.InitAndApply(t, terraformOptions)

    // Validate outputs
    clusterEndpoint := terraform.Output(t, terraformOptions, "cluster_endpoint")
    assert.NotEmpty(t, clusterEndpoint)

    clusterName := terraform.Output(t, terraformOptions, "cluster_name")
    assert.Equal(t, "test-anihpj", clusterName)
}
Module Testing Pyramid
                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │  E2E Tests   │  ← Full deploy + app validation (slow, expensive)
                    │  (Apply to   │
                    │   real AWS)  │
                    └──────┬──────┘
                    ┌──────┴──────┐
                    │ Integration  │  ← Test module with dependencies (moderate)
                    │  Tests       │
                    └──────┬──────┘
                    ┌──────┴──────┐
                    │  Unit Tests  │  ← Validate logic, plan output (fast, cheap)
                    │  (terraform  │
                    │   validate,  │
                    │   fmt, plan) │
                    └─────────────┘

15.4 Publishing Modules — Sharing with Your Team and the World

Publishing a module makes it available to your team (private registry) or the community (public registry). The workflow is: Git tag → GitHub release → Registry sync.

Module Publishing Workflow
# 1. Ensure module follows standard structure
ls modules/anihpj-eks/
# main.tf  variables.tf  outputs.tf  README.md  examples/

# 2. Tag with semantic version
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0

# 3. Create GitHub release (with changelog)

# 4. Connect repo to Terraform Registry
# Go to registry.terraform.io → Publish → Module → Connect GitHub

# 5. Registry auto-detects new tags and publishes new versions!

# USAGE (after publishing):
module "eks" {
  source  = "anihpj/eks/aws"       # Public registry
  version = "~> 1.0"
  cluster_name = "anihpj-prod"
}
⚠️ Before Publishing Checklist

(1) All variables have description fields, (2) All outputs have description fields, (3) README has usage examples, (4) Version tag follows semver (v1.0.0 not 1.0), (5) versions.tf declares minimum provider versions, (6) Module has been tested with terraform validate and fmt.

Module Lifecycle — From Idea to Published
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     MODULE DEVELOPMENT LIFECYCLE                       │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐         │
│  │ 1. CODE  │──▶│ 2. TEST  │──▶│ 3. TAG   │──▶│ 4. PUBLISH│         │
│  │          │   │          │   │          │   │          │         │
│  │ Write    │   │ terraform│   │ git tag  │   │ Registry │         │
│  │ main.tf  │   │ validate │   │ v1.0.0   │   │ auto-    │         │
│  │ vars.tf  │   │ fmt      │   │ git push │   │ detects  │         │
│  │ outs.tf  │   │ plan     │   │ --tags   │   │ new tag  │         │
│  │ README   │   │ Terratest│   │          │   │          │         │
│  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘         │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 5. CONSUME: Users reference your module                       │   │
│  │ module "my_vpc" {                                             │   │
│  │   source  = "anihpj/vpc/aws"                                  │   │
│  │   version = "~> 1.0"                                          │   │
│  │ }                                                             │   │
│  │                                                               │   │
│  │ 6. ITERATE: Bug fix → git tag v1.0.1 → Registry auto-updates  │   │
│  │    New feature → git tag v1.1.0 → Users get it on next init   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.4 Terraform Test Framework — Testing Infrastructure as Code (TF 1.6+) 🆕

The terraform test command (introduced in Terraform 1.6) brings native testing to infrastructure code. Instead of manually running plan/apply to verify modules work, you write .tftest.hcl files that declare assertions about your infrastructure behavior.

Module Test Example — modules/s3/tests/basic.tftest.hcl
# File: modules/s3/tests/basic.tftest.hcl
# Tests run with: terraform test

run "basic_bucket" {
  command = plan  # plan or apply

  # Input variables for this test run
  variables {
    bucket_name = "anihpj-test-bucket"
    environment = "dev"
  }

  # Assertions on the plan output
  assert {
    condition     = aws_s3_bucket.main.bucket == "anihpj-test-bucket"
    error_message = "Bucket name does not match input variable"
  }

  assert {
    condition     = aws_s3_bucket.main.tags.Environment == "dev"
    error_message = "Environment tag was not set correctly"
  }
}

run "versioning_enabled" {
  command = plan
  variables {
    bucket_name      = "test-versioned"
    enable_versioning = true
  }

  assert {
    condition     = aws_s3_bucket.main.versioning[0].enabled == true
    error_message = "Versioning should be enabled when enable_versioning=true"
  }
}

run "apply_and_destroy" {
  command = apply  # Actually creates resources to test

  variables {
    bucket_name = "anihpj-integration-test-${random_string.suffix.result}"
  }

  # Module outputs can be verified
  assert {
    condition     = output.bucket_arn != ""
    error_message = "Bucket ARN should not be empty after creation"
  }
}

# Run: $ terraform test
# PASS: basic_bucket (plan) — 2 assertions passed
# PASS: versioning_enabled (plan) — 1 assertion passed
# PASS: apply_and_destroy (apply) — 1 assertion passed
# All 3 tests passed!
🧪
Why Terraform Test Matters

Before TF 1.6, testing modules meant: (1) apply to a sandbox account, (2) manually verify resources, (3) destroy. This was slow, expensive, and rarely done. Native testing makes module verification as easy as terraform test — tests run in seconds (plan mode) and cost nothing. This is a paradigm shift for infrastructure quality.

📋
Test File Convention

Test files use .tftest.hcl extension and live in a tests/ directory within the module. Each run block is an independent test scenario with its own variables, providers, and assertions. Tests can run in plan mode (fast, no resources created) or apply mode (creates real resources, then destroys them).

💡 Exam Relevance

The Terraform Authoring Professional exam tests module quality and testing patterns. While terraform test itself may not be directly tested (it was introduced in TF 1.6 and the exam may lag), understanding testing methodology — writing modules that are testable, with clear interfaces and verifiable outputs — IS tested. Know that tests belong in a tests/ directory and use .tftest.hcl extension.

Chapter 15 — Practice Questions

Q1
What are the minimum required files for a well-structured module?
Show Answer
Answer

main.tf (resources), variables.tf (inputs), outputs.tf (outputs). For registry publication, also README.md and versions.tf.

Explanation

These three files form the standard module interface: main.tf defines what the module creates, variables.tf declares what callers can customize, and outputs.tf exposes what callers need to reference. The exam expects you to know this structure — if asked to "create a module," these three files are the answer.

Q2
What's the principle of "minimal surface area" in module design?
Show Answer
Answer

Require as few inputs as possible. Only make variables required when there's no sensible default. Everything else should have a reasonable default value. This makes modules easier to use and harder to misuse.

Explanation

Think of modules like API design: fewer required parameters = easier adoption. A VPC module that requires only cidr_block and defaults everything else (AZs, subnets, NAT) is much more usable than one requiring 20 inputs. The "sensible defaults" pattern lets beginners get started quickly while experts can override everything.

Q3
Write a complete variables.tf for a simple S3 bucket module.
Show Answer
Answer
variable "bucket_name" {
  type        = string
  description = "REQUIRED: Globally unique bucket name"
}
variable "environment" {
  type        = string
  default     = "dev"
}
variable "versioning" {
  type        = bool
  default     = true
}
variable "tags" {
  type        = map(string)
  default     = {}
}
Explanation

Notice the pattern: only bucket_name is required (no default). Everything else has sensible defaults. The description field documents each variable for the Registry. Required variables should have descriptions starting with "REQUIRED:" to stand out in auto-generated docs.

Q4
What framework is commonly used to test Terraform modules?
Show Answer
Answer

Terratest — a Go library that provides helpers for terraform init, apply, output, and destroy in automated tests. It runs against real cloud resources and validates outputs.

Explanation

Terratest is the industry standard for Terraform module testing. Unlike terraform validate (which only checks syntax), Terratest deploys real infrastructure, validates it works, and destroys it — all in CI. The exam may ask about testing approaches: Terratest = integration/E2E testing against real cloud resources.

Q5
What are the three stages of the module testing pyramid?
Show Answer
Answer

Unit tests: terraform validate, fmt, plan (fast, cheap). Integration tests: Test module with real dependencies. E2E tests: Full deploy + app validation against real cloud (slow, expensive).

Explanation

The testing pyramid applies to Terraform too: run many fast/cheap unit tests (fmt, validate), fewer integration tests (deploy to a sandbox account), and fewest E2E tests (full production-like deployment). CI/CD should run unit tests on every PR, integration on staging, and E2E before major releases.

Q6
How do you publish a module to the Terraform Registry?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Standard structure (main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, README.md), (2) Tag with semver (git tag v1.0.0), (3) Push tag, (4) Connect GitHub repo to Registry. The Registry auto-detects new tags.

Explanation

The Registry uses webhooks to detect new semantic version tags pushed to your GitHub repository. Within minutes of pushing v1.0.0, the module appears on registry.terraform.io with auto-generated documentation from your variables.tf descriptions. The module name must be terraform-PROVIDER-NAME format.

Q7
What naming convention should custom modules follow?
Show Answer
Answer

terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>. Examples: terraform-aws-vpc, terraform-aws-eks. This convention is required for publishing to the public registry.

Explanation

The naming convention terraform-PROVIDER-NAME is required by the Registry for automatic provider detection. If you name your module my-awesome-vpc, the Registry won't know it's an AWS module. The PROVIDER portion must match a provider on the Registry (aws, gcp, azurerm, kubernetes, etc.).

Q8
Your EKS module has 3 required and 5 optional variables. How do you communicate this to users?
Show Answer
Answer

Use description fields: prefix required ones with "REQUIRED:" and optional ones with their default behavior. In README, use an inputs table. The Registry auto-generates this from your variables.tf.

Explanation

The Registry reads your variables.tf and auto-generates an inputs/outputs table on the module page. Well-written descriptions become documentation. The convention of prefixing descriptions with "REQUIRED:" for mandatory variables is a community best practice that makes your module instantly scannable.

Q9
What goes in versions.tf and why is it important?
Show Answer
Answer
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.3"
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws"; version = ">= 5.0" }
  }
}
Explanation

versions.tf is a Terraform convention (not a required name) for the terraform {} block. It declares minimum versions so users get clear errors if they're on incompatible versions. "Module X requires Terraform >= 1.3, but you're on 1.2" is much better than a cryptic syntax error.

Q10
You've tested your module locally. What's the publish workflow with semantic versioning?
Show Answer
Answer
terraform fmt -recursive && terraform validate
git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0
# Create GitHub release with changelog
# Registry auto-detects and publishes
Explanation

The publish workflow: (1) Ensure code is formatted and valid, (2) Create a semantic version tag (v1.0.0), (3) Push the tag (not just the commit), (4) Create a GitHub release describing changes. Within minutes, the Registry detects the new tag and makes the module available. Users can then pin with version = "~> 1.0".
