🟡 Part 6: Provisioners & Advanced WorkflowsChapters 16-17

Chapter 16: Provisioners — Last Resort Configuration

Provisioners run scripts during resource creation or destruction. They're Terraform's escape hatch — a way to do things the provider doesn't support. But they come with serious limitations: no state tracking, no idempotency guarantees, and no drift detection. Think of them as the tool of last resort.

🔑 Key Exam Insight

The exam tests: (1) knowing when NOT to use provisioners, (2) local-exec vs remote-exec, (3) when = destroy for cleanup, and (4) on_failure = continue. The #1 exam trap: choosing a provisioner when user_data, Packer, or a provider resource would work better.

16.1 When to Use (and NOT Use) Provisioners

Provisioners exist because sometimes you need to run a command that no provider supports. But they should be your last option, not your first.

Provisioner Decision Tree — Should You Use One?
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  "I need to configure something after resource creation"          │
│                          │                                        │
│           ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐                        │
│           ▼              ▼              ▼                        │
│    ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────┐                 │
│    │ Provider │  │ Can I    │  │ Does the     │                 │
│    │ supports │  │ use      │  │ provider     │                 │
│    │ it?      │  │ user_data│  │ have a       │                 │
│    │          │  │ ?        │  │ resource?    │                 │
│    └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └──────┬───────┘                 │
│         │ YES         │ YES            │ YES                     │
│         ▼             ▼                ▼                        │
│    ✅ USE IT     ✅ USE          ✅ USE RESOURCE                 │
│                  USER_DATA                                       │
│                                                                  │
│         NO               NO              NO                      │
│         │                │               │                       │
│         └────────────────┼───────────────┘                       │
│                          ▼                                       │
│                   ┌──────────────┐                               │
│                   │ ⚠️ LAST      │                               │
│                   │ RESORT:      │                               │
│                   │ Provisioner! │                               │
│                   └──────────────┘                               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
✅ Valid Use Cases
  • Register cluster with ArgoCD after EKS creation
  • Run kubectl apply for initial K8s manifests
  • Deregister from monitoring during destroy
  • Call an API the provider doesn't support
❌ Anti-Patterns
  • Configure a web server → Use user_data or Packer
  • Install packages → Use a pre-baked AMI
  • Manage app config → Use K8s ConfigMaps
  • Anything needing idempotency
Configuration Priority Ladder — What to Use BEFORE a Provisioner
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BEST                                                             │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │ 1. PROVIDER RESOURCE — Does the provider have a resource?    ││
│  │    Example: aws_iam_role instead of aws CLI provisioner      ││
│  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 2. USER_DATA / CLOUD-INIT — Can you pass a startup script?  ││
│  │    Example: EC2 user_data instead of remote-exec             ││
│  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 3. PRE-BAKED IMAGE (PACKER) — Build an AMI with everything  ││
│  │    Example: Packer AMI with Docker pre-installed             ││
│  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 4. CONFIG MGMT (ANSIBLE/CHEF) — Post-boot configuration     ││
│  │    Example: Ansible playbook after EC2 is running            ││
│  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 5. PROVISIONER — LAST RESORT ⚠️                             ││
│  │    Only when options 1-4 are impossible                      ││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│  WORST                                                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔑 The exam WILL test this priority. If a question asks "how to configure a server" and lists provider resource, user_data, Packer, and provisioner — answer in this order.

16.2 local-exec — Run on Your Machine

local-exec runs commands on the machine executing Terraform (your laptop or CI runner). It has full access to your local tools, credentials, and network.

local-exec — Anihpj Post-EKS Automation
# After EKS cluster creation, register with ArgoCD + apply manifests
resource "null_resource" "post_eks_setup" {
  depends_on = [aws_eks_cluster.anihpj]
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = <<-EOT
      aws eks update-kubeconfig --name anihpj-${var.environment} --region us-east-1
      argocd cluster add anihpj-${var.environment}
      kubectl apply -f ${path.module}/manifests/jobpost-namespace.yaml
      kubectl apply -f ${path.module}/manifests/jobpost-deployment.yaml
      echo "EKS cluster anihpj-${var.environment} ready!"
    EOT
    interpreter = ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
  }
}

# Trigger a webhook after resource creation
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" { bucket = "anihpj-assets-${var.environment}" }
resource "null_resource" "notify" {
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "curl -X POST ${var.slack_webhook} -d '{\"text\":\"Bucket ${aws_s3_bucket.assets.bucket} created\"}'"
  }
}

16.3 remote-exec — Run on a Remote Machine

remote-exec runs scripts on a newly created resource (EC2, VM) via SSH or WinRM. It requires a connection block specifying how to connect.

remote-exec — Bootstrap an Anihpj CI Runner
resource "aws_instance" "ci_runner" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type = "t3.medium"
  key_name      = aws_key_pair.ci.key_name

  connection {
    type        = "ssh"
    user        = "ubuntu"
    private_key = file("~/.ssh/anihpj-ci.pem")
    host        = self.public_ip
    timeout     = "5m"
  }

  provisioner "remote-exec" {
    inline = [
      "sudo apt-get update",
      "sudo apt-get install -y docker.io docker-compose",
      "sudo usermod -aG docker ubuntu",
      "sudo systemctl enable docker",
      "echo 'CI runner ready!' | sudo tee /etc/motd",
    ]
  }
}

# connection block fields:
# type = "ssh"|"winrm"  |  user = ssh user  |  private_key = path
# host = self.public_ip  |  port = 22/5986   |  timeout = "5m"

16.4 Provisioner Failures and Handling

OptionBehaviorWhen to Use
on_failure = continueApply succeeds even if provisioner failsOptional tasks (notifications, logging)
on_failure = failApply fails, resource is taintedCritical setup that MUST succeed
when = destroyRuns during terraform destroyCleanup: deregister monitoring, remove DNS
when = createRuns after resource creationNormal post-creation setup
Destroy-Time + Failure Handling
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    when       = destroy
    command    = "curl -X DELETE https://monitoring/api/nodes/${self.private_ip}"
    on_failure = continue  # Don't block destroy if API is down
  }
  provisioner "remote-exec" {
    inline = ["sudo systemctl start nginx"]
    # on_failure defaults to "fail" — taints resource if nginx fails
  }
}
⚠️ 5 Reasons NOT to Use Provisioners in Production

(1) No state tracking — can't detect drift, (2) Not idempotent — re-running may error, (3) Slows down apply — re-runs every time, (4) Poor error handling — taints resources on failure, (5) Hard to test — scripts aren't validated like .tf code.

Featurelocal-execremote-exec
Runs WHERE?YOUR machine (laptop/CI runner)REMOTE resource (EC2/VM)
Connection?NONE (local)SSH or WinRM required
Best Forkubectl apply, API calls, register servicesBootstrap scripts, install agents, configure apps
Anihpj ExampleRegister EKS with ArgoCD after creationInstall CloudWatch agent on new EC2
Cloud API Access✅ Has access (your credentials)❌ May not (needs IAM role)

🔑 Exam: local-exec for CI/CD tasks, remote-exec for bootstrapping. Both are last-resort tools!

🧪 Provisioner Exam Traps — The Exam Loves These
❌ TRAP 1"Use remote-exec to configure the web server" → ✅ FIX: Use user_data, cloud-init, or pre-baked AMI. Provisioners have NO STATE — can't detect drift.
❌ TRAP 2"Run provisioner to install packages" → ✅ FIX: Use Packer to build a custom AMI. Provisioners make terraform apply SLOW and unreliable.
✅ TRAP 3"Use when=destroy provisioner for cleanup" → ✅ CORRECT! Cleanup scripts (deregister monitoring, remove DNS) ARE a valid use case.

🔑 RULE: Provisioners = LAST RESORT. Use only when the provider doesn't support what you need AND there's no better alternative.

Provisioner Execution Lifecycle — When Exactly Do They Run?
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  terraform apply SEQUENCE:                                            │
│                                                                      │
│  1. REFRESH STATE (read current cloud state)                         │
│  2. BUILD DEPENDENCY GRAPH                                           │
│  3. CREATE/UPDATE RESOURCES (in dependency order)                    │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│     │ For EACH resource being CREATED:                            │ │
│     │   3a. AWS API: Create the resource (e.g., EC2 instance)     │ │
│     │   3b. WAIT for resource to be "ready" (status checks)       │ │
│     │   3c. RUN create-time provisioners (local-exec/remote-exec) │ │
│     │   3d. Resource is marked as "created" in state              │ │
│     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│  4. WRITE STATE                                                     │
│                                                                      │
│  terraform destroy SEQUENCE:                                         │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │   1. RUN destroy-time provisioners (when = destroy)            │  │
│  │   2. AWS API: Delete the resource                             │  │
│  │   3. Remove resource from state                                │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                      │
│  ⚠️  KEY INSIGHT: Provisioners run AFTER the resource is created    │
│     but BEFORE state is written. If provisioner fails:               │
│     → Resource is TAINTED (marked for recreation on next apply)     │
│     → State is NOT written (resource exists in AWS but not in state) │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 16 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is a provisioner and when should you use one?
Show Answer
Answer

A script runner during resource create/destroy. Use as last resort — only when the provider lacks support AND no better alternative exists (user_data, Packer, Ansible).

Explanation

Exam trap: "configure a web server" → answer is user_data/Packer, NEVER provisioner. Provisioners have no state, aren't idempotent, and slow down applies.

Q2
Where does local-exec run?
Show Answer
Answer

On the machine running Terraform (laptop, CI runner, TFC agent). Has access to your local tools and credentials.

Explanation

local-exec executes commands on the Terraform host — your laptop, CI/CD runner, or Terraform Cloud agent. This means it has access to your local shell, AWS CLI, kubectl, and any other tools installed. Use it for client-side tasks like updating kubeconfig, running migrations, or triggering webhooks.

Q3
What does the connection block configure?
Show Answer
Answer

SSH/WinRM connection for remote-exec: type, user, private_key/password, host (usually self.public_ip), port, timeout.

Explanation

The connection block tells Terraform how to connect to a remote machine for remote-exec. It's required before any remote-exec provisioner. Common pattern: host = self.public_ip for EC2 instances. SSH is the most common type; WinRM is used for Windows instances.

Q4
How to run a provisioner during terraform destroy?
Show Answer
Answer
provisioner "local-exec" { when = destroy; command = "cleanup.sh" }
Explanation

The when = destroy argument runs the provisioner during resource deletion instead of creation. Common uses: deregistering from service discovery, cleaning up DNS records, or sending decommission notifications. Without when = destroy, provisioners only run during creation.

Q5
What does on_failure = continue do?
Show Answer
Answer

Apply succeeds even if provisioner fails. Resource is NOT tainted. Use for optional tasks where failure shouldn't block deployment.

Explanation

By default (on_failure = fail), a failed provisioner taints the resource and stops the apply. on_failure = continue logs the error but continues — the resource is marked as successfully created. Use this for best-effort tasks like sending notifications or running optional health checks.

Q6
Why shouldn't you use provisioners to configure a web server?
Show Answer
Answer

No state tracking, not idempotent, slow. Use user_data (cloud-init), Packer (pre-baked AMI), or Ansible/Chef instead.

Explanation

Provisioners run a script once. If someone changes the server config manually, Terraform won't detect or fix it — there's no state tracking for provisioner effects. user_data runs cloud-init which is idempotent. Packer bakes config into the AMI so every instance is identical. Both are superior alternatives.

Q7
Write local-exec to update kubeconfig after EKS creation.
Show Answer
Answer
provisioner "local-exec" {
  command = "aws eks update-kubeconfig --name ${aws_eks_cluster.main.name} --region us-east-1"
}
Explanation

This is one of the few legitimate uses of local-exec — updating a client-side config file that Terraform can't manage as a resource. After EKS cluster creation, you need to update kubeconfig before kubectl commands work. This runs on YOUR machine, not the cluster.

Q8
What happens when a provisioner fails with default settings?
Show Answer
Answer

Resource is tainted — destroyed and recreated on next apply. The current apply fails.

Explanation

A tainted resource means "this resource might be in a bad state." On the next terraform apply, Terraform will destroy and recreate it. This ensures the provisioner gets a fresh chance to run. If you're sure the resource is fine despite the provisioner failure, use terraform untaint to remove the mark.

Q9
Valid when argument values?
Show Answer
Answer

when = create (default) or when = destroy.

Explanation

Only two values are valid: create (runs during resource creation) and destroy (runs before resource deletion). There's no when = update — provisioners only run at creation time (unless you use triggers with null_resource). For ongoing configuration management, use a dedicated CM tool.

Q10
Most important limitation of provisioners?
Show Answer
Answer

No state tracking. Terraform doesn't record provisioner effects. Manual changes won't be detected or fixed, unlike provider resources which track state.

Explanation

This is THE fundamental limitation. Provider resources write their state after every apply — Terraform knows every attribute. Provisioners just run a script and move on — Terraform has no idea what the script did. If someone manually changes what the script configured, Terraform will never detect or fix it. This makes provisioners unsuitable for any ongoing configuration.

Chapter 17: Data Sources, External Providers & Null Resources

Beyond basic resources, Terraform provides advanced mechanisms for reading external data, calling external programs, and triggering actions without managing a real resource. These patterns are essential for real-world workflows.

🔑 Exam Focus

The exam tests: (1) data source chaining and lifecycle, (2) external data source limitations, (3) null_resource with triggers, and (4) terraform_data (TF 1.4+) as the modern replacement.

17.1 Advanced Data Source Patterns

Data sources read existing infrastructure at plan time. They cannot depend on resources being created in the same apply — unless you use depends_on.

Data Source Lifecycle — When They Execute
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                  │
│  terraform plan:                                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Read ALL data sources (from existing infrastructure)   │   │
│  │ 2. Compute desired state from .tf files                   │   │
│  │ 3. Diff actual (from data sources) vs desired (.tf)       │   │
│  │ 4. Show plan                                              │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                  │
│  terraform apply:                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Read data sources AGAIN (values may have changed!)     │   │
│  │ 2. Create/update resources                                │   │
│  │ 3. Write state                                            │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                  │
│  ⚠️  Data sources execute BEFORE resource creation               │
│     → Can't read resources being created in the SAME apply       │
│     → Use depends_on to force ordering if needed                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Data Source Chaining — Anihpj EKS Setup
# Chain: AMI → Subnets → Security Group → EC2
data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" {
  most_recent = true
  filter { name = "name"; values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd/ubuntu-jammy-22.04-*"] }
  owners = ["099720109477"]  # Canonical
}

data "aws_subnets" "private" {
  filter { name = "vpc-id"; values = [module.vpc.vpc_id] }
  filter { name = "tag:Tier"; values = ["private"] }
}

data "aws_security_group" "rds_sg" {
  filter { name = "group-name"; values = ["anihpj-rds-${var.environment}"] }
}

# Use chained data sources in a resource
resource "aws_instance" "bastion" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  subnet_id     = data.aws_subnets.private.ids[0]
  vpc_security_group_ids = [data.aws_security_group.rds_sg.id]
}
📖 Data Source (READ only)
data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" {
  most_recent = true
  owners = ["099720109477"]
}

Reads existing infrastructure. Runs at plan AND apply time. Cannot create or modify anything. Result is read-only reference stored in state.

🔧 Resource (CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE)
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type = "t3.medium"
}

Manages real cloud resources. Runs at apply time. Creates, updates, or destroys infrastructure. Fully tracked in state with drift detection.

17.2 The external Data Source — Call External Programs

The external data source runs an external program and reads JSON from its stdout. This lets you incorporate data from scripts, APIs, or tools that don't have Terraform providers.

external Data Source — Python Script + Terraform
# File: generate_id.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, sys, hashlib, datetime
input_data = json.load(sys.stdin)
unique_id = hashlib.md5(f"{input_data['env']}-{datetime.datetime.now()}".encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
print(json.dumps({"id": unique_id}))

# File: main.tf
data "external" "unique_id" {
  program = ["python3", "${path.module}/generate_id.py"]
  query   = { env = var.environment }
}

# Use the generated ID
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "unique" {
  bucket = "anihpj-${var.environment}-${data.external.unique_id.result.id}"
}

# ⚠️  LIMITATIONS:
# • Program must output valid JSON to stdout
# • Program is re-run on EVERY plan/apply (SLOW!)
# • No built-in caching or state tracking
⚠️ external Data Source Limitations

The external program runs on every plan and apply — there's no caching. If the program is slow, Terraform is slow. Also, the program must accept JSON on stdin and output JSON on stdout. Any stderr output is logged but ignored. Use sparingly — prefer native providers or http data source for API calls.

17.3 null_resource — Provisioner Without a Resource

null_resource behaves like a resource but manages nothing. Its purpose: to run provisioners that aren't tied to a real resource, especially with triggers that force re-execution when values change.

17.3a The triggers Pattern — Rerun When Values Change

null_resource triggers — K8s ConfigMap Watcher
# PROBLEM: When a ConfigMap changes, pods need to restart to pick up new config
# null_resource triggers can detect changes and trigger a rolling restart

resource "kubernetes_config_map" "app_config" {
  metadata { name = "jobpost-config" }
  data = { DATABASE_URL = "postgres://${aws_db_instance.jobpost.address}:5432/jobpost" }
}

resource "null_resource" "restart_pods" {
  triggers = {
    # Re-run when ConfigMap data changes
    config_hash = sha256(jsonencode(kubernetes_config_map.app_config.data))
  }

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = <<-EOT
      kubectl rollout restart deployment/jobpost -n ${var.environment}
      echo "Restarted jobpost pods due to config change"
    EOT
  }
}

17.3b local-exec with null_resource

null_resource + local-exec — Post-Apply Automation
resource "null_resource" "anihpj_health_check" {
  depends_on = [aws_eks_node_group.main]

  triggers = {
    # Re-run if cluster endpoint or node count changes
    endpoint = aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.endpoint
    nodes    = aws_eks_node_group.main.scaling_config[0].desired_size
  }

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = <<-EOT
      echo "Waiting for EKS nodes to be Ready..."
      kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready nodes --all --timeout=300s
      echo "All nodes Ready! Running smoke test..."
      curl -f https://${aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.endpoint}/healthz && echo "OK" || echo "FAIL"
    EOT
  }
}

17.4 terraform_data — The Modern Replacement (TF 1.4+)

terraform_data is the managed replacement for null_resource. It's a first-class managed resource that integrates better with the dependency graph.

🔴 null_resource (Legacy)
resource "null_resource" "example" {
  triggers = {
    hash = sha256(var.value)
  }
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "echo trigger fired"
  }
}

❌ Still works but considered legacy
❌ Requires null provider

🟢 terraform_data (TF 1.4+)
resource "terraform_data" "example" {
  triggers_replace = {
    hash = sha256(var.value)
  }
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "echo trigger fired"
  }
}

✅ Built-in — no extra provider
✅ triggers_replace is explicit about behavior

💡 When to Use terraform_data vs null_resource

Use terraform_data for new projects (TF 1.4+). The key difference: terraform_data.triggers_replace explicitly signals "changing this replaces the resource" — clearer intent than null_resource.triggers. Both support provisioners, but terraform_data is the future.

17.4 terraform_data — The Modern Replacement for null_resource (TF 1.4+) 🆕

The terraform_data managed resource (built-in, no provider needed) replaces null_resource as the standard way to store values, trigger replacements, and run provisioners without managing a real cloud resource.

terraform_data — Three Core Patterns
# PATTERN 1: Store arbitrary data with managed lifecycle
resource "terraform_data" "config" {
  input = {
    environment = var.environment
    version     = var.app_version
    timestamp   = timestamp()
  }
}
# Access: terraform_data.config.output.environment

# PATTERN 2: Trigger replacement from plain values
variable "revision" { default = 1 }
resource "terraform_data" "replacement" {
  input = var.revision
}
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  lifecycle {
    replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.replacement]
    # ↑ When var.revision changes → terraform_data replaces → EC2 replaces
  }
}

# PATTERN 3: Run provisioners without a real resource
resource "terraform_data" "bootstrap" {
  triggers_replace = [
    aws_instance.web.id,
    aws_instance.database.id
  ]
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "bootstrap-hosts.sh"
  }
}
# When web or database ID changes → bootstrap re-runs
Featurenull_resourceterraform_data (TF 1.4+)
Provider needed?✅ Yes (hashicorp/null)❌ No (built-in)
Trigger mechanismtriggers (map)triggers_replace (list)
Data storage❌ No✅ Yes (input → output)
replace_triggered_by support❌ No✅ Yes
Future direction⚠ Deprecated direction✅ Recommended for new code

Chapter 17 — Practice Questions

Q1
When do data sources execute in the Terraform lifecycle?
Show Answer
Answer

At plan time (to build the plan) and again at apply time (to get current values). They cannot read resources being created in the same apply unless you use depends_on.

Explanation

Data sources read twice: once during plan to determine what changes are needed, and once during apply to get fresh values. This means a data source that depends on a resource being created in the same apply WILL fail unless you explicitly add depends_on. This is a common exam pattern.

Q2
What does the external data source do?
Show Answer
Answer

Runs an external program, reads JSON from stdout, and exposes the result as a data source. Useful for scripts or tools without Terraform providers. Runs every plan/apply — no caching.

Explanation

The external data source is an escape hatch: if no Terraform provider exists for your API, write a script that outputs JSON, and Terraform can read it. Caveats: it runs on EVERY plan/apply (can be slow), the program must be available on the Terraform host, and the output MUST be valid JSON.

# Script: get_ami_id.sh (Python/bash/any language)
#!/bin/bash
# Reads stdin: {"region":"us-east-1","name":"ubuntu-jammy"}
# Must output JSON to stdout:
echo '{"ami_id":"ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0","created":"2024-01-15"}'

# Terraform usage:
data "external" "latest_ami" {
  program = ["bash", "${path.module}/get_ami_id.sh"]
  query = {
    region = "us-east-1"
    name   = "ubuntu-jammy"
  }
}

# Access results:
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami = data.external.latest_ami.result.ami_id
  #     ↑ .result is a map of all JSON keys
  tags = { Created = data.external.latest_ami.result.created }
}

# ⚠ Runs EVERY plan/apply — can be VERY slow
# ⚠ Script must be on Terraform host (not on remote machine)
# ⚠ Output MUST be valid JSON — any other output = ERROR
Q3
What is a null_resource and when would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

A resource that manages nothing — used to run provisioners not tied to a real resource, especially with triggers to force re-execution when values change.

Explanation

null_resource is a "do-nothing" resource that exists only to run provisioners. Common pattern: trigger a kubectl rollout restart when a ConfigMap changes. Without null_resource, you'd need to attach the provisioner to a real resource that might not be the one you want to change. Note: terraform_data (TF 1.4+) is the modern replacement.

Q4
How do triggers work in null_resource?
Show Answer
Answer

When any trigger value changes, the null_resource is destroyed and recreated, re-running its provisioners. This forces a provisioner to re-execute when something changes.

Explanation

Triggers are a map of arbitrary key-value pairs. Terraform computes a hash of all trigger values. When the hash changes (any value changed), the null_resource is replaced, running its create provisioner again. This is how you implement "run this command whenever X changes" in Terraform.

Q5
Write a null_resource that restarts pods when ConfigMap data changes.
Show Answer
Answer
resource "null_resource" "restart" {
  triggers = { config_hash = sha256(jsonencode(kubernetes_config_map.app.data)) }
  provisioner "local-exec" { command = "kubectl rollout restart deploy/jobpost" }
}
Explanation

This is the classic pattern: hash the ConfigMap data with sha256(). When the ConfigMap changes, the hash changes, the null_resource is replaced, and the provisioner runs — restarting pods to pick up the new config. Without triggers, the provisioner would only run once at initial creation.

Q6
What is terraform_data and when was it introduced?
Show Answer
Answer

TF 1.4+ managed replacement for null_resource. Uses triggers_replace instead of triggers. Built-in resource — no extra provider needed.

Explanation

terraform_data is HashiCorp's answer to "null_resource requires an extra provider just for triggers." It's a built-in managed resource type that does the same thing but is cleaner and more explicit. If you see terraform_data in exam questions, know it requires TF ≥ 1.4.

Q7
What format must external data source programs output?
Show Answer
Answer

Valid JSON on stdout. Input is read from stdin (also JSON). Stderr is logged but ignored. Any other output format causes an error.

Explanation

The external program receives a JSON object via stdin (containing the query map from the data source block) and must output a JSON object to stdout. The keys in the output JSON become the data source's attributes. This is a strict contract — if your script outputs plain text or invalid JSON, Terraform errors.

Q8
Can a data source read a resource being created in the same apply?
Show Answer
Answer

Not by default — data sources execute before resource creation. To force ordering, use depends_on on the data source referencing the resource being created.

Explanation

Data sources execute BEFORE any resources are created in the apply phase. If you need to read a resource being created in the SAME apply, add depends_on. Without this, the data source will error.

# ❌ FAILS — data source reads BEFORE EKS is created
data "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  name = aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.name  # EKS not created yet!
}

# ✅ WORKS — depends_on forces data source to wait
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" {
  name     = "anihpj-prod"
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.cluster.arn
  vpc_config { subnet_ids = module.vpc.public_subnet_ids }
}

data "aws_eks_cluster" "main" {
  name       = aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.name
  depends_on = [aws_eks_cluster.anihpj]  # WAIT for creation
}

# Now you can use cluster data in dependent resources:
resource "kubernetes_namespace" "jobpost" {
  metadata { name = "jobpost" }
}
# The K8s provider now has valid endpoint/cert/token from data source

# 🎯 PATTERN: Resource → depends_on → Data Source → Resource
Q9
What's the difference between null_resource.triggers and terraform_data.triggers_replace?
Show Answer
Answer

Functionally identical, but triggers_replace is more explicit about behavior. Both replace the resource when trigger values change. terraform_data is the modern, built-in replacement.

Explanation

The naming difference is intentional: triggers could be misinterpreted as "triggers an action," while triggers_replace makes it crystal clear — changing these values replaces the resource. For new code, prefer terraform_data with triggers_replace. The exam may test this naming distinction for TF 1.4+.

Q10
What is data source chaining and why is it useful?
Show Answer
Answer

Using one data source's output as another's input: data.aws_ami → data.aws_subnet → resource. Reads all necessary information from existing infrastructure before creating new resources.

Explanation

Data source chaining eliminates hardcoded IDs. Instead of writing subnet_id = "subnet-abc123", you chain: look up VPC by tag → get subnets in that VPC → use the first one. This makes your configuration portable across accounts and regions. The exam tests this pattern — never hardcode resource IDs.

  • local-exec = runs on your machine
  • remote-exec = runs on remote via SSH/WinRM

  • on_failure=continue for non-critical tasks
  • No state tracking = can't detect drift
📊 Ch 17: Data & Null Resources

🔴 Part 7: Terraform Cloud & EnterpriseChapters 18-20

Chapter 18: Terraform Cloud — Remote Execution

Terraform Cloud (TFC) moves plan and apply execution from your laptop to remote infrastructure. It provides centralized state, team collaboration, policy enforcement via Sentinel, cost estimation, and full audit trails. Think of it as "Terraform as a Service" — the engine runs in the cloud, you just push code.

🔑 Key Exam Insight

The exam tests: (1) CLI vs TFC workflow differences, (2) workspace types (VCS/CLI/API), (3) Sentinel policy levels, and (4) run triggers for cross-workspace dependencies. Know that TFC never exposes secrets to developer laptops during plan/apply.

18.1 Terraform Cloud vs CLI — Why Go Remote? 🎯

TFC fundamentally changes where Terraform executes. Instead of running terraform plan on your laptop (with your credentials), TFC runs everything in managed cloud runners with injected secrets.

CLI vs Terraform Cloud — Architecture Comparison
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LOCAL CLI WORKFLOW (laptop-based):                                │
│  ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ LAPTOP  │───▶│ TERRAFORM│───▶│  STATE   │───▶│   AWS    │   │
│  │ (.tf)   │    │  BINARY  │    │  (S3)    │    │   API    │   │
│  │         │    │ (local)  │    │          │    │          │   │
│  │ ⚠️ CPU  │    │ ⚠️ Token │    │          │    │          │   │
│  │ ⚠️ Net  │    │  on disk │    │          │    │          │   │
│  └─────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘   │
│                                                                  │
│  TERRAFORM CLOUD WORKFLOW (remote execution):                     │
│  ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ LAPTOP  │───▶│  TFC     │───▶│ MANAGED  │───▶│   AWS    │   │
│  │ git push│    │  RUNNER  │    │  STATE   │    │   API    │   │
│  │         │    │ (cloud)  │    │ (TFC)    │    │          │   │
│  │ ✅ Only │    │ ✅ Never │    │ ✅ Auto  │    │ ✅ IAM   │   │
│  │ git!    │    │ on laptop│    │ encrypted│    │ role     │   │
│  └─────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘   │
│                                                                  │
│  KEY DIFFERENCES:                                                │
│  • Secrets NEVER touch developer laptops in TFC                  │
│  • TFC provides audit log (who ran what, when)                   │
│  • TFC enforces Sentinel policies BEFORE apply                   │
│  • TFC supports cost estimation on every plan                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔐 Security

TFC: Credentials injected at runtime, never on dev laptops. CLI: Credentials in ~/.aws or env vars on every workstation.

📋 Audit

TFC: Full audit log of every plan/apply. CLI: No centralized audit (rely on git history).

🛡️ Policy

TFC: Sentinel policies enforced before apply. CLI: Manual review (or pre-commit hooks).

18.2 Workspaces in Terraform Cloud

TFC workspaces come in three flavors, each suited for different workflows:

TypeTriggerBest For
VCS-DrivenGit push/PR → auto planGitOps workflow (plan on PR, apply on merge)
CLI-Driventerraform apply (executed remotely)Developers used to CLI but want remote execution
API-DrivenREST API callsFull automation, CI/CD integration, external triggers
TFC CLI-Driven Workflow
# Login to Terraform Cloud
$ terraform login
# Opens browser → generate API token → paste into terminal

# Configure TFC backend
# File: backend.tf
terraform {
  cloud {
    organization = "anihpj"
    workspaces { name = "anihpj-production" }
  }
}

# Now every command runs REMOTELY:
$ terraform plan    # Runs in TFC, shows output locally
$ terraform apply   # Runs in TFC with Sentinel policy checks
📝 VCS-Driven (GitOps)

Trigger: Git push/PR
Plan: Automatic on PR
Apply: On merge to branch
Best for: Teams using GitOps review workflows

💻 CLI-Driven (Remote Ops)

Trigger: terraform apply
Plan: Runs remotely, output streamed
Apply: After Sentinel check
Best for: Devs wanting CLI feel with TFC security

18.3 Sentinel — Policy as Code 🎯

Sentinel is HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework. It enforces rules BEFORE infrastructure changes go live — blocking non-compliant changes at the plan stage.

Sentinel Policy Enforcement Levels
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🔴 HARD-MANDATORY (DENY)                                         │
│  "S3 buckets MUST have encryption enabled"                        │
│  "EBS volumes MUST be encrypted with KMS"                         │
│  RESULT: ❌ Plan BLOCKED. Cannot proceed.                        │
│  Use for: Security, compliance, regulatory requirements           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  🟡 SOFT-MANDATORY (OVERRIDE ALLOWED)                             │
│  "EC2 instances SHOULD use t3 family"                             │
│  "RDS SHOULD have Multi-AZ enabled"                               │
│  RESULT: ⚠️ Warning + override with justification                │
│  Use for: Best practices, cost optimization                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  🟢 ADVISORY (WARN ONLY)                                          │
│  "Consider using gp3 volumes (cheaper + faster)"                  │
│  "Tags missing: consider adding CostCenter tag"                   │
│  RESULT: ℹ️ Info message. No action needed.                      │
│  Use for: Suggestions, reminders, documentation                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Hard-Mandatory: S3 Encryption

Sentinel Policy — Deny Unencrypted S3
# File: enforce-s3-encryption.sentinel
import "tfplan/v2" as tfplan

s3_buckets = filter tfplan.resource_changes as _, rc {
    rc.type is "aws_s3_bucket" and rc.change.actions includes "create"
}

main = rule {
    all s3_buckets as _, bucket {
        bucket.change.after.server_side_encryption_configuration is not null
    }
}

Soft-Mandatory: Instance Type Guard

Warns when non-t3 instances are used but allows override with justification.

Advisory: Tag Checker

Reminds teams to add CostCenter and Owner tags — informational only.

🛡️ Anihpj Sentinel Policies — Production Requirements
🔴 HardS3 buckets must have: encryption + block_public_access enabled
🟡 SoftRDS instances should have: deletion_protection = true, Multi-AZ in prod
🟢 AdvisoryResources should have: CostCenter, Owner tags; consider gp3 volumes

18.4 Cost Estimation — Financial Guardrails 🎯

Terraform Cloud's cost estimation shows the financial impact of infrastructure changes BEFORE you apply them. This is a Domain 6 exam topic — know what it covers, what it doesn't, and how to interpret its output.

Cost Estimation in the Plan Workflow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  COST ESTIMATION LIFECYCLE                                         │
│                                                                   │
│  terraform plan ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │  1. Plan calculates resource changes (create/update/destroy)│  │
│  │  2. TFC queries pricing API for each resource              │  │
│  │  3. Computes: Current monthly cost → Projected monthly cost │  │
│  │  4. Shows delta: +$361.14 (increase) or -$150.00 (decrease)│  │
│  │  5. Per-resource breakdown in plan output                  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                   │
│  SUPPORTED: Compute (EC2, EKS), Storage (S3, EBS), Database (RDS) │
│  NOT SUPPORTED: Custom resources, 3rd-party providers, IAM, VPC   │
│                                                                   │
│  🎯 EXAM NOTE: Cost estimation works on SPECULATIVE PLANS too!    │
│  PR shows "this change will add $842/month" before merge.         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Cost Estimation Output (Anihpj Example)
Plan: 3 to add, 2 to change, 0 to destroy.

Cost Estimation:
  Resources: 5 of 12 estimated
  Current monthly cost:    $842.31
  Proposed monthly cost:  $1,203.45
  Monthly delta:          +$361.14 (42.9% increase)

  Resource changes (largest deltas):
    aws_db_instance.jobpost    +$280.00  (t3.small → t3.large upgrade)
    aws_nat_gateway.secondary  +$81.14   (new NAT GW for DR region)
    aws_eks_cluster.anihpj      +$0.00   (no change — $0.10/hr already)

⚠️  Cost threshold exceeded: +$361.14 > $200/month org limit
    Requires justification to proceed (Sentinel soft-mandatory)
🔑 Exam Tips — Cost Estimation
  • Cost estimation is TFC-only — not available in CLI (OSS)
  • It uses list prices, not your negotiated AWS discount
  • Does NOT include: data transfer, API request costs, reserved instance discounts
  • Can be paired with Sentinel: "Block if monthly increase > $500"
  • Enabled per-organization in TFC Settings → Cost Estimation

18.5 Run Triggers — Cross-Workspace Dependencies

When workspace A successfully applies, it can trigger workspace B to run. This creates infrastructure deployment pipelines.

Anihpj Run Trigger Chain
┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐     ┌────────────┐
│  VPC WS    │────▶│  EKS WS    │────▶│  APP WS    │
│ (network)  │     │ (compute)  │     │ (deploy)   │
│            │     │            │     │            │
│ Creates:   │     │ Creates:   │     │ Creates:   │
│ VPC, subs  │     │ EKS, nodes │     │ K8s deploy │
└────────────┘     └────────────┘     └────────────┘
       │                  │                  │
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
  Output:            Output:            Output:
  vpc_id             cluster_endpoint   lb_dns_name

FLOW: VPC apply ✅ → triggers EKS plan → EKS apply ✅
      → triggers APP plan → APP apply ✅

18.6 Terraform Cloud Agents — Self-Hosted Runners 🎯

TFC Agents let you run plan/apply on your own infrastructure instead of TFC's managed runners. Essential for: private data centers, air-gapped environments, or when you need to access resources inside a VPC.

🔑 Exam Relevance

Domain 6 tests: when to use TFC Agents vs managed runners, agent pool configuration, and agent token management. Know that agents are the bridge between TFC and private infrastructure.

18.7 Sentinel Policy Deep Dive — Writing Production Policies 🎯

Beyond the three enforcement levels, Sentinel policies use imports (tfplan/v2, tfstate/v2, tfconfig/v2) to inspect every aspect of your Terraform configuration and planned changes.

Sentinel Policy — Block Public S3 Buckets
# File: block-public-s3.sentinel
import "tfplan/v2" as tfplan

# Get all S3 buckets being created or updated
s3_buckets = filter tfplan.resource_changes as _, rc {
    rc.type is "aws_s3_bucket" and
    rc.change.actions not contains "delete"
}

# HARD-MANDATORY: No public access
block_public = rule {
    all s3_buckets as _, bucket {
        bucket.change.after.block_public_acls is true and
        bucket.change.after.block_public_policy is true and
        bucket.change.after.ignore_public_acls is true and
        bucket.change.after.restrict_public_buckets is true
    }
}

# Main rule
main = rule { block_public else false }
Sentinel Policy — Enforce Instance Types (Cost Control)
# File: restrict-instance-types.sentinel
import "tfplan/v2" as tfplan

allowed_types = ["t3.small", "t3.medium", "t3.large", "m5.large"]

ec2_instances = filter tfplan.resource_changes as _, rc {
    rc.type is "aws_instance" and
    rc.change.actions contains "create"
}

# SOFT-MANDATORY: Warn if non-standard instance type
instance_type_check = rule {
    all ec2_instances as _, instance {
        instance.change.after.instance_type in allowed_types
    }
}

main = rule { instance_type_check else false }
Sentinel Policy — Require Tags (Advisory)
# File: require-tags.sentinel
import "tfplan/v2" as tfplan

required_tags = ["Project", "Environment", "Owner", "CostCenter"]

tagged_resources = filter tfplan.resource_changes as _, rc {
    rc.change.actions contains "create" and
    rc.change.actions not contains "delete"
}

# ADVISORY: Check each resource has all required tags
tag_check = rule {
    all tagged_resources as _, resource {
        all required_tags as tag {
            resource.change.after.tags contains tag
        }
    }
}

main = rule { tag_check else false }

Chapter 18 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is the key security advantage of Terraform Cloud over local CLI?
Show Answer
Answer

Secrets/credentials never touch developer laptops. TFC injects them at runtime into the plan/apply execution environment on managed cloud infrastructure.

Explanation

With local CLI, every developer needs AWS credentials on their machine — a security risk if a laptop is compromised. With TFC, credentials live in workspace variables (encrypted at rest) and are injected only during plan/apply. Developers see plan output but never the actual secret values.

Q2
What are the three TFC workspace types?
Show Answer
Answer

VCS-Driven (Git triggers plan), CLI-Driven (remote execution), API-Driven (REST automation).

Explanation

VCS-Driven is the GitOps model — push to Git, TFC plans automatically. CLI-Driven is for teams that want remote execution but trigger manually. API-Driven is for fully automated pipelines that use the TFC REST API. The exam expects you to know when to use each type.

Q3
What are the three Sentinel policy enforcement levels?
Show Answer
Answer

Hard-Mandatory (deny), Soft-Mandatory (override with justification), Advisory (warn only).

Explanation

Sentinel policies enforce organizational rules. Hard-mandatory blocks the apply entirely — no exceptions. Soft-mandatory can be overridden but requires a justification message (auditable). Advisory only warns — the apply continues regardless. Know this distinction for the exam.

Q4
What does TFC cost estimation show?
Show Answer
Answer

Monthly cost, delta (increase/decrease), and per-resource cost breakdown in plan output. Supports major AWS/GCP/Azure resources.

Explanation

Cost estimation runs during the plan phase and shows the financial impact BEFORE you apply. If you're adding 10 EC2 instances, you'll see the estimated monthly cost increase. This helps prevent surprise cloud bills. Not all resources are supported — it covers the most common compute, storage, and database resources.

Q5
What is a run trigger in TFC?
Show Answer
Answer

A cross-workspace dependency: when workspace A successfully applies, it triggers workspace B to run. Used for infrastructure pipelines (VPC → EKS → App).

Explanation

Run triggers create infrastructure pipelines in TFC without external CI/CD. Example: the "networking" workspace creates VPC/subnets. When it finishes, the "compute" workspace (EKS) runs automatically because it needs the VPC ID. This is Terraform Cloud's native orchestration mechanism.

Q6
Which Sentinel level for "S3 must have encryption"?
Show Answer
Answer

Hard-Mandatory — security requirements must never be violated. Plan is blocked if any S3 bucket lacks encryption.

Explanation

Security policies like encryption, public access blocking, and IAM restrictions should always be hard-mandatory. There's no legitimate reason to create an unencrypted S3 bucket in production. Cost policies ("instances must be < $500/month") might be soft-mandatory. Naming conventions might be advisory.

Q7
How does VCS-driven workspace trigger a plan?
Show Answer
Answer

Git push or PR triggers an automatic plan. Speculative plan on PR, apply on merge to the configured branch. Standard GitOps workflow.

Explanation

When you connect a VCS-driven workspace to GitHub/GitLab, TFC registers a webhook. Every push triggers a plan. PRs trigger speculative plans ("what would happen if we merged this?"). When the PR merges to the target branch, TFC applies. No manual CLI commands needed.

Q8
What command logs you into Terraform Cloud from CLI?
Show Answer
Answer

terraform login — opens browser for API token generation, stores the token locally for remote execution.

Explanation

terraform login authenticates your CLI with Terraform Cloud. It opens a browser to app.terraform.io where you generate an API token. The token is stored in ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json. After login, terraform plan runs remotely on TFC instead of locally.

Q9
Where does Terraform RUN in TFC CLI-driven mode?
Show Answer
Answer

On TFC's managed cloud runners, not your laptop. Your CLI sends commands to TFC; TFC executes and streams output back.

Explanation

Remote execution means the heavy lifting happens on TFC infrastructure. Your laptop just sends the command and displays output. Benefits: consistent execution environment, no local credentials needed, works even if your laptop goes to sleep mid-apply. The exam tests this architectural difference.

Q10
TFC provides audit logs. What do they track?
Show Answer
Answer

Who ran what, when, with what result. Every plan, apply, and policy check is logged with user identity, timestamp, and outcome.

Explanation

Audit logs are essential for compliance (SOC2, HIPAA). They answer: who applied the change to production at 3 AM? What was the plan output? Which Sentinel policies passed/failed? This is a key differentiator from local CLI where there's no centralized audit trail.

Chapter 19: Team Management & RBAC

Terraform Cloud provides organizational structures for managing teams, permissions, and shared configuration across workspaces. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) ensures the right people have the right access.

19.1 Organizations and Teams

An Organization is the top-level container for workspaces, teams, policies, and variable sets. Teams group users with specific permissions.

Anihpj Org Structure — Teams → Workspaces
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ORGANIZATION: anihpj                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  TEAM: platform-eng (Admin)                                  │ │
│  │  Permissions: Full access to ALL workspaces                  │ │
│  │  Members: Alice, Bob                                         │ │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │  TEAM: devs (Write)                                          │ │
│  │  Permissions: Write to dev/staging, Read to prod             │ │
│  │  Members: Charlie, Diana, 8 developers                       │ │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │  TEAM: ops (Admin)                                           │ │
│  │  Permissions: Full access to prod, Read to dev/staging       │ │
│  │  Members: Eve, Frank                                         │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

19.2 Workspace Permissions

PermissionCan Do
ReadView workspace, see plan outputs, read state
PlanQueue plans (Read + trigger plan runs)
WriteApply plans, edit variables, lock/unlock workspace
AdminManage workspace settings, delete workspace, manage team access

19.3 Variable Sets — Share Across Workspaces

Variable Set Scoping
# Global: Applied to ALL workspaces
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID     = var.aws_key       # Every workspace gets this
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = var.aws_secret    # (marked as sensitive)

# Scoped by workspace name
vpc_cidr   = "10.0.0.0/16"     # Applies to workspaces matching "*-networking"
env        = "prod"             # Applies to workspaces matching "anihpj-production"

# Precedence: Workspace-specific > Scoped > Global

19.4 RBAC Design Philosophy — Why It Matters for Infrastructure

RBAC isn't just about permissions — it's about preventing disasters. In infrastructure management, the blast radius of a mistake is proportional to the permissions of the person making it. Terraform Cloud's RBAC model is designed around the principle of least privilege: give people exactly the permissions they need, nothing more.

The RBAC Hierarchy — How Permissions Flow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  TERRAFORM CLOUD RBAC MODEL                   │
  │                                                               │
  │  ORGANIZATION: anihpj                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                     TEAMS                                │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐              │ │
  │  │  │platform  │  │  devs    │  │   ops    │              │ │
  │  │  │(Admin)   │  │(Write)   │  │(Admin)   │              │ │
  │  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘              │ │
  │  │       │             │             │                      │ │
  │  │       ▼             ▼             ▼                      │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
  │  │  │                WORKSPACES                        │   │ │
  │  │  │  ┌─────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │   │ │
  │  │  │  │  dev    │  │ staging  │  │     prod       │  │   │ │
  │  │  │  │platform:│  │platform: │  │  platform:     │  │   │ │
  │  │  │  │ Admin   │  │ Admin    │  │  Admin         │  │   │ │
  │  │  │  │ devs:   │  │ devs:    │  │  devs: Read    │  │   │ │
  │  │  │  │ Write   │  │ Write    │  │  ops: Admin    │  │   │ │
  │  │  │  └─────────┘  └──────────┘  └────────────────┘  │   │ │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🎯 PRINCIPLE: Same TEAM, different permissions per WORKSPACE.
  🎯 devs get Write on dev/staging but Read-only on production.
  🎯 ops team gets Admin on production, Read on dev.
🔐
Least Privilege in Practice

A junior developer should be able to create resources in dev but should NEVER be able to touch production. TFC enforces this through per-workspace team permissions. Even if someone accidentally runs terraform destroy, they can't destroy production if they only have Read access. This isn't just good practice — it's a compliance requirement for SOC2, HIPAA, and PCI.

👥
Separation of Duties

The person who WRITES infrastructure code should not be the same person who APPROVES production changes. TFC enables this through: (1) developers have Write on dev (can experiment freely), (2) PR reviews enforce code review by seniors, (3) only ops/SRE team has Admin on production. This two-person rule prevents single points of failure — no one person can deploy to production alone.

Chapter 19 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is a TFC Organization?
Show Answer
Answer

Top-level container for workspaces, teams, policies, and variable sets. Groups everything for one company or project.

Explanation

Think of an Organization like a GitHub organization — it's the namespace that contains all your workspaces, teams, and policies. Everything in TFC lives under an Organization. You can have multiple Organizations for different business units or environments.

Q2
What are the four workspace permission levels?
Show Answer
Answer

Read (view), Plan (queue plans), Write (apply + edit vars), Admin (manage settings + delete).

Explanation

Permissions are cumulative: Write includes Plan, Plan includes Read. Most developers need Write on dev and Read on prod. Only senior engineers should have Admin on production workspaces. This is the standard least-privilege model tested on the exam.

Q3
How do variable sets differ from workspace-specific variables?
Show Answer
Answer

Variable sets apply to multiple workspaces (globally or scoped). Workspace-specific vars apply to one workspace only. Precedence: Workspace > Scoped > Global.

Explanation

Variable sets eliminate repetition: instead of setting AWS credentials on 50 workspaces, create one global variable set. If a workspace needs different credentials, set a workspace-specific variable — it overrides the global one. The precedence chain ensures specific overrides always win.

Q4
Which permission allows applying plans?
Show Answer
Answer

Write — allows applying plans, editing variables, and locking/unlocking workspaces.

Explanation

Write is the first level that can actually CHANGE infrastructure. Read and Plan are read-only. The exam may test: "A developer needs to apply plans to dev but only view prod. What permissions?" Answer: Write on dev workspace, Read on prod workspace.

Q5
How share AWS credentials across all workspaces?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a Global Variable Set with AWS credentials (marked sensitive). All workspaces inherit them.

Explanation

Instead of adding AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID to every workspace, create it once as a global variable set. Mark credentials as sensitive so they're encrypted and hidden. Use environment variable category (not terraform variable) so they're set as env vars during plan/apply.

Q6
Can a team have different permissions on different workspaces?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. A team can be Admin on dev workspaces and Read-only on prod workspaces.

Explanation

This is the recommended pattern: the "developers" team gets Write/Admin on dev workspaces and Read on production. The "ops" team gets Admin on everything. This enforces separation of duties — developers can experiment in dev but can't accidentally modify production.

Q7
Difference between teams and organizations in TFC?
Show Answer
Answer

Organization = container for everything. Team = group of users with specific permissions.

Explanation

One organization can have many teams. Teams can have different permissions on different workspaces. Users belong to teams. This three-level hierarchy (Org → Team → Workspace) with per-workspace permissions is TFC's RBAC model.

Q8
How scope a variable set to specific workspaces?
Show Answer
Answer

By workspace name pattern (e.g., "*-production") or tag. Only matching workspaces receive the variables.

Explanation

Scoping prevents production variables from leaking to dev. Example: create a variable set scoped to "*-production" containing production database credentials. Dev workspaces won't see these. Use tags for more flexible scoping beyond name patterns.

Q9
What permission is needed to delete a workspace?
Show Answer
Answer

Admin — the highest level. Only Admins can manage settings and delete workspaces.

Explanation

Workspace deletion is destructive — it can optionally delete the state file and all run history. This is why only Admin can do it. Write can apply plans but can't delete the workspace itself. This tiered permission model prevents accidental destruction.

Q10
Variable precedence: workspace-specific vs global variable set?
Show Answer
Answer

Workspace-specific wins. Order: Workspace > Scoped variable set > Global variable set.

Explanation

Think of it as a specificity cascade, like CSS. The most specific setting (workspace) overrides the least specific (global). This lets you set global defaults while allowing specific workspaces to customize values. The exam may test: "If global says t3.small and workspace says t3.large, what applies?"

Chapter 20: Private Registry & API Automation

Terraform Cloud provides a private module registry for sharing modules within your organization and a REST API for full automation of workspace management, runs, and integrations.

20.1 Private Module Registry

Host modules visible only to your organization. Integrates with GitHub — tag a release, and the registry automatically publishes the new version.

Private Module Usage
# Instead of public registry:
# source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"

# Use your organization's private module:
module "vpc" {
  source  = "app.terraform.io/anihpj/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 2.0"
  name    = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
}

# Publishing workflow:
# 1. Tag release: git tag v2.0.0 && git push --tags
# 2. Registry auto-detects and publishes v2.0.0
# 3. Teams can immediately use version = "~> 2.0"

20.2 Why a Private Registry? — Enterprise Module Management

Organizations quickly accumulate dozens of custom modules — VPC patterns, EKS configurations, database setups, monitoring stacks. Without a central registry, these modules scatter across Git repositories, S3 buckets, and local directories. The private registry solves this by providing a single source of truth for all internal modules.

🏢
Governance

Control who can publish modules and which versions are approved for production use. Enforce semantic versioning and maintain a changelog for every release.

🔍
Discoverability

Teams can browse the registry, read auto-generated documentation, and see usage examples — without digging through Git repos or asking around.

🔄
Automated Publishing

Connect to GitHub. Tag a release with v1.2.0 → registry auto-publishes. No manual uploads, no S3 sync scripts. Git tags ARE the release mechanism.

20.3 Terraform Cloud API — Full Automation

The TFC REST API enables programmatic management of every aspect of Terraform Cloud — workspaces, runs, variables, teams, and policies. This is how large organizations integrate Terraform into their existing platforms and portals.

TFC API — Common Automation Patterns
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PATTERN 1: CREATE WORKSPACE VIA API                          │
  │  POST /api/v2/organizations/anihpj/workspaces                 │
  │  { "data": { "attributes": { "name": "anihpj-prod" } } }     │
  │  → Creates workspace programmatically (CI/CD or portal)       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  PATTERN 2: TRIGGER RUN VIA API                               │
  │  POST /api/v2/runs                                            │
  │  { "data": { "attributes": { "is-destroy": false } } }       │
  │  → Triggers plan+apply without CLI or VCS                     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  PATTERN 3: QUERY STATE VIA API                               │
  │  GET /api/v2/workspaces/ws-abc123/current-state-version       │
  │  → Read outputs programmatically (DNS, IPs, endpoints)        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  PATTERN 4: MANAGE VARIABLES VIA API                          │
  │  POST /api/v2/workspaces/ws-abc123/vars                       │
  │  → Set Terraform/env variables without UI clicks              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  AUTHENTICATION: Bearer token via TFC_API_TOKEN env var
  BASE URL: https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/

20.2 Terraform Cloud API

TFC API — Key Endpoints
# API Token Types:
# • User Token     — Personal, tied to your account
# • Team Token     — Shared by entire team (CI/CD use)
# • Organization Token — Org-wide automation

# Trigger a run
curl -X POST https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/runs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TFC_TOKEN" \
  -d '{ "data": { "attributes": { "message": "Triggered by CI" },
    "relationships": { "workspace": { "data": { "id": "ws-abc123" } } } } }'

# List workspaces
curl https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/organizations/anihpj/workspaces \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TFC_TOKEN"

# Create/update variables
curl -X POST https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/workspaces/ws-abc123/vars \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TFC_TOKEN" \
  -d '{ "data": { "type": "vars", "attributes": { "key": "instance_count",
    "value": "3", "category": "terraform", "sensitive": false } } }'

20.3 CI/CD Integration

GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions Workflow
name: Terraform
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  terraform:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
      - uses: hashicorp/terraform-plan-comment@v1  # Comment plan on PR

GitLab CI

Same workflow: validate → plan → apply stages in .gitlab-ci.yml with TFC backend.

Jenkins Pipeline

Declarative pipeline with terraform validate → plan → manual approval → apply stages.

Chapter 20 — Practice Questions

Q1
What is the TFC Private Registry?
Show Answer
Answer

An organization-internal module registry. Modules visible only to org members, integrated with GitHub for auto-publishing on git tags.

Explanation

Unlike the public registry (visible to everyone), the private registry hosts modules exclusively for your organization. This lets you share proprietary infrastructure patterns internally without exposing them publicly. Works with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps.

Q2
How do you publish a new module version?
Show Answer
Answer

git tag v1.0.0 && git push --tags — the registry auto-detects the tag and publishes the version.

Explanation

Publishing is fully automated: push a semantic version tag, and the private registry detects it via webhook. Within minutes, the new version appears in the registry. No manual upload, no API calls. The module name must follow terraform-PROVIDER-NAME format even for private modules.

Q3
What TFC API endpoint triggers a run?
Show Answer
Answer

POST /api/v2/runs with workspace ID. Requires bearer token with appropriate permissions.

Explanation

The TFC API lets you automate everything you can do in the UI. Triggering a run via API is common in CI/CD pipelines where an external system (Jenkins, GitHub Actions) decides WHEN to run Terraform, but TFC executes the actual plan/apply in a secure, audited environment.

Q4
What GitHub Action is used for Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3 — installs Terraform CLI in GitHub Actions. hashicorp/terraform-plan-comment adds plan output as PR comment.

Explanation

The setup-terraform action installs a specific Terraform version in the CI runner. The plan-comment action takes plan output and posts it as a PR comment — reviewers can see exactly what infrastructure changes the PR will cause without running Terraform themselves.

Q5
What are the three API token types in TFC?
Show Answer
Answer

User (personal), Team (shared), Organization (org-wide). Each has different permission scopes.

Explanation

User tokens inherit your personal permissions. Team tokens have the team's permissions and survive when members leave. Organization tokens have broad access — use sparingly. For CI/CD, Team tokens are recommended because they're not tied to an individual.

Q6
What's a typical CI/CD pipeline for Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

fmt -check → validate → plan → manual approval → apply. Plan runs on PR, apply on merge.

Explanation

This pipeline catches issues at multiple stages: fmt catches style issues, validate catches syntax errors, plan shows the impact, manual approval provides a human gate. The apply step only runs after merge to main — this ensures every production change has been reviewed.

Q7
How does TFC API authentication work?
Show Answer
Answer

Bearer token in Authorization header. Tokens generated in TFC under User Settings → Tokens.

Explanation

All TFC API requests use bearer token authentication. Generate tokens in the TFC UI. Store them securely — treat them like passwords. For CI/CD, inject the token via GitHub Secrets or equivalent. Never commit tokens to Git.

Q8
Can the TFC private registry host modules from GitLab?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. Supports GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps as VCS providers.

Explanation

The private registry integrates with all major VCS providers. When you connect a repository, TFC registers a webhook to detect new tags. This VCS-agnostic design means your module workflow stays the same regardless of which Git platform your organization uses.

Q9
What are typical Jenkins Terraform pipeline stages?
Show Answer
Answer

Checkout → Validate → Plan → Manual Approval → Apply.

Explanation

Jenkins pipelines mirror the same pattern as any CI/CD: validate syntax, preview changes, get human approval, apply. The manual approval step is critical — it's the gate between "here's what will change" and "make it happen." This prevents fully automated production changes.

Q10
How do you create variables via the TFC API?
Show Answer
Answer
curl -X POST https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/workspaces/WS_ID/vars \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"data":{"type":"vars","attributes":{"key":"name","value":"val","category":"terraform"}}}'
Explanation

The TFC API allows programmatic variable management — essential for automation. The category field must be terraform (HCL variables) or env (environment variables). Mark sensitive variables with "sensitive": true — they can be written but never read back via API.
