Chapter 21: Infrastructure Design Patterns

Production infrastructure requires thoughtful design: how to organize environments, deploy across regions, manage multiple AWS accounts, and enforce consistent tagging. These patterns separate production-grade Terraform from proof-of-concept.

🔑 Key Exam Insight

The exam tests: (1) environment strategies (directories vs workspaces vs Terragrunt), (2) multi-region provider aliases, (3) multi-account assume-role patterns, and (4) tagging strategies. Know when to use each approach based on team size and complexity.

21.1 Environment Management Strategies

Directory-per-Environment

Each environment is a separate directory with its own .tf files and state. Best for configurations that differ significantly per environment.

envs/dev/main.tf    →  s3://tfstate/dev/terraform.tfstate
envs/staging/main.tf → s3://tfstate/staging/terraform.tfstate
envs/prod/main.tf   →  s3://tfstate/prod/terraform.tfstate

Workspace-per-Environment

Same .tf files, different workspaces. Best for environments that are nearly identical.

terraform workspace select dev     # → s3://tfstate/env:/dev/state
terraform workspace select prod    # → s3://tfstate/env:/prod/state

Terragrunt (DRY Terraform)

Terragrunt wraps Terraform to keep configurations DRY across environments. It auto-generates backend configs and enables module reuse without copy-paste.

21.2 Multi-Region Deployments

Multi-Region Anihpj — Provider Alias Pattern
# providers.tf
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }           # DEFAULT (primary)
provider "aws" { alias = "eu"; region = "eu-west-1" }  # ALIAS (DR)

# ┌── us-east-1 (PRIMARY) ──┐  ┌── eu-west-1 (DR) ──────┐
# │ 🌎 Virginia, USA        │  │ 🌍 Ireland, Europe      │
# │  EKS active, RDS primary│  │  EKS standby, RDS read  │
# └─────────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets_us" {
  bucket = "anihpj-assets-us"  # Default provider (us-east-1)
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets_eu" {
  provider = aws.eu              # Aliased provider!
  bucket   = "anihpj-assets-eu"
}

21.3 Multi-Account Architecture (AWS Organizations)

Separate AWS accounts for dev, staging, and prod. Use assume_role in the provider block so a single Terraform configuration can deploy to multiple accounts.

Assume Role Pattern
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1"; assume_role { role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/tf-deploy" } }

21.4 Infrastructure Tagging Strategy

Anihpj Tag Hierarchy
# LEVEL 1: default_tags — AUTO on ALL resources
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1"
  default_tags { tags = { Project="anihpj"; ManagedBy="terraform"; Owner="platform-team"; CostCenter="eng-123" } }
}
# LEVEL 2: local.common_tags — MERGE with resource
locals { common_tags = { Environment=var.environment; App="jobpost" } }
# LEVEL 3: resource tags — OVERRIDE if needed
# FINAL TAGS = Level1 ∪ Level2 ∪ Level3

21.5 Design Decision Framework — Choosing the Right Pattern

Infrastructure design isn't one-size-fits-all. The right pattern depends on your team size, compliance requirements, and operational maturity. Here's how to think about these decisions:

Environment Strategy Decision Tree
  START: Need multiple environments (dev, staging, prod)?
  │
  ├─ Are environments NEARLY IDENTICAL?
  │   YES → Workspace-per-Environment (simple, same .tf files)
  │   │      Example: 3 environments that differ only in instance sizes
  │   │
  │   NO → Do you need DIFFERENT BACKENDS per env?
  │          YES → Directory-per-Environment (full isolation)
  │          │      Example: dev uses local state, prod uses S3+DynamoDB
  │          │
  │          NO → Do you need 5+ environments?
  │                 YES → Terragrunt (DRY at scale)
  │                 │      Example: 10 microservices × 3 envs = 30 configs
  │                 │
  │                 NO → Directory-per-Environment (still recommended)
  │
  └─ Do you need separate AWS ACCOUNTS?
       YES → Directory-per-Environment + assume_role
       │      Each dir has different assume_role ARN per account
       │
       NO → Single account with directory-per-environment isolation

  ANIHPJ CHOICE: Directories + assume_role for multi-account
  Reason: Different configurations, strict isolation, compliance
🏗️
When to Use Workspaces

Small teams (2-5 engineers), 2-3 environments that are nearly identical, no compliance requirements for environment isolation. Workspaces are simple but share the same backend, credentials, and IAM — a mistake in one workspace can affect all of them. The HashiCorp-recommended approach for production is directories, not workspaces.

🔐
When to Use Multi-Account

Any production workload should use separate AWS accounts per environment. Benefits: (1) blast radius — dev can't affect prod, (2) billing — separate invoices per env, (3) IAM — completely isolated permissions, (4) compliance — auditors can verify prod isolation. Terraform enables this with assume_role — one config deploys to all accounts.

21.6 Provider Debugging & Troubleshooting 🎯

Provider issues are the most common source of Terraform failures. Knowing how to debug them quickly separates exam-passers from exam-failers. This section covers TF_LOG-based debugging, lock file troubleshooting, and provider authentication diagnostics — all directly tested in Domain 5.

TF_LOG — Terraform's Built-In Debugger

When Terraform fails with a cryptic error, TF_LOG is your first diagnostic tool. It controls the verbosity of Terraform's internal logging across all providers and the core engine.

TF_LOG Levels — From Quiet to Noisy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TF_LOG LEVELS (set via environment variable)                      │
│                                                                   │
│  TF_LOG=TRACE    🔍🔍🔍  Most verbose — shows every API call,     │
│                          HTTP request/response bodies, timing      │
│                          Use: Debugging provider API failures      │
│  TF_LOG=DEBUG    🔍🔍    Shows internal decisions, graph building  │
│                          Use: Understanding plan/apply logic       │
│  TF_LOG=INFO     🔍      Shows major milestones, provider versions │
│                          Use: Confirm provider loading, versions   │
│  TF_LOG=WARN     ⚠️      Shows warnings only (default for some)    │
│  TF_LOG=ERROR    ❌      Shows errors only                         │
│                                                                   │
│  TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log  — Write logs to file (recommended!) │
│  TF_LOG_CORE=DEBUG           — Debug core only, not providers     │
│  TF_LOG_PROVIDER_AWS=TRACE   — Debug AWS provider specifically    │
│                                                                   │
│  🎯 EXAM TIP: TF_LOG=TRACE logs full HTTP bodies including        │
│  credentials! NEVER use TRACE in CI/CD — use DEBUG at most.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TF_LOG Debugging Examples
# DEBUG: Provider failing to authenticate
$ TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2>&1 | grep -i "aws.*error"
# Shows detailed AWS API error with request ID for AWS Support

# TRACE: See every API call Terraform makes
$ TF_LOG=TRACE TF_LOG_PATH=./trace.log terraform plan
# ⚠️ trace.log WILL contain credentials in plain text!

# Core-only debug (skip provider noise)
$ TF_LOG_CORE=DEBUG terraform plan
# Shows: graph building, state processing, plan generation

# Single provider debug
$ TF_LOG_PROVIDER_AWS=TRACE terraform plan
# Shows: every AWS API call, retry logic, credential chain resolution

# Common debugging patterns:
$ TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform init 2>&1 | grep -i "error\|failed\|timeout"
$ TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2>&1 | grep "aws_s3\|permission\|AccessDenied"
$ TF_LOG=TRACE terraform apply 2>&1 | grep "HTTP/[0-9]"

.terraform.lock.hcl — Provider Version Lock Troubleshooting

The lock file ensures every team member uses the exact same provider version. When it breaks, deployments stop. Know these scenarios cold for the exam.

Lock File Conflict Resolution
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCENARIO 1: "Lock file already exists" on new platform           │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  CAUSE: Lock file was generated on Linux, you're on Mac/Windows   │
│  FIX:   terraform init -upgrade    # Regenerate for all platforms │
│         OR: terraform providers lock -platform=darwin_amd64       │
│                                                                   │
│  SCENARIO 2: "Provider hashes do not match"                       │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  CAUSE: Someone updated providers without updating lock file      │
│  FIX:   terraform init -upgrade    # Refresh lock file            │
│         OR: Manually update version constraint + terraform init   │
│                                                                   │
│  SCENARIO 3: Lock file missing from Git                           │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  CAUSE: .gitignore excludes .terraform.lock.hcl                   │
│  FIX:   git add .terraform.lock.hcl && git commit                 │
│         ⚠️ LOCK FILE MUST BE COMMITTED TO GIT!                   │
│                                                                   │
│  SCENARIO 4: terraform providers mirror (air-gapped)              │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  USE:   terraform providers mirror /path/to/local/mirror          │
│         # Creates a local mirror with all platforms               │
│         # Then: provider_installation { filesystem_mirror {...} } │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Lock File Commands — Exam Essentials
# View what's locked
$ cat .terraform.lock.hcl          # Shows provider versions + hashes

# Regenerate lock file (new platform or updated providers)
$ terraform init -upgrade          # Re-downloads + re-locks ALL providers
$ terraform providers lock         # Lock WITHOUT upgrading

# Add a specific platform to lock file
$ terraform providers lock -platform=linux_arm64

# Mirror for air-gapped environments
$ terraform providers mirror /mnt/tf-providers/

# Check lock file consistency
$ terraform providers schema -json | head -20

Provider Authentication Troubleshooting

Provider authentication failures are the #1 reason terraform plan fails. Know the credential resolution chain and how to debug each step.

AWS Provider Credential Resolution Chain
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HOW TERRAFORM FINDS AWS CREDENTIALS (checked in ORDER):           │
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ 1. Static credentials in provider block                      │ │
│  │    provider "aws" { access_key="..."; secret_key="..." }     │ │
│  │    ⚠️ NEVER USE — commits secrets to Git!                   │ │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ 2. Environment variables                                     │ │
│  │    export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA...                          │ │
│  │    export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...                          │ │
│  │    export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=...  (if using STS)              │ │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ 3. Shared credentials file (~/.aws/credentials)              │ │
│  │    [default]                                                 │ │
│  │    aws_access_key_id=AKIA...                                 │ │
│  │    Can use profiles: provider "aws" { profile = "anihpj" }   │ │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ 4. IAM Role (EC2 instance profile / EKS IRSA)                │ │
│  │    Automatically assumed when running on AWS infra           │ │
│  │    ✅ BEST OPTION — no credentials to manage!               │ │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ 5. Web Identity (OIDC — GitHub Actions → AWS)                │ │
│  │    No long-lived secrets. GitHub OIDC → STS → temp creds     │ │
│  │    ✅ RECOMMENDED FOR CI/CD                                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                   │
│  DEBUGGING AUTH FAILURES:                                         │
│  $ TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2>&1 | grep -i "cred\|auth\|403"  │
│  $ aws sts get-caller-identity    # Who am I?                    │
│  $ echo $AWS_PROFILE              # Which profile?               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Provider Version Constraint Debugging

Version constraint problems cause silent failures or upgrade issues. Master these patterns:

ConstraintMeaningWhen to Use
version = "~> 5.0"≥ 5.0, < 6.0 (minor only)Production — safe upgrades
version = ">= 5.0, < 6.0"Any 5.xExplicit range for clarity
version = "5.32.1"EXACT pin (⚠️ too strict)Only during incident response
terraform { required_version = ">= 1.5" }Min Terraform binary versionEvery root module should have this

Common Provider Errors & Fixes — Exam Quick Reference

🔴
Error: "Provider not found"

Fix: terraform init — provider wasn't downloaded. Check required_providers block has correct source.

🔴
Error: "Signature does not match"

Fix: terraform init -upgrade — lock file hashes are stale. Provider was re-released with same version.

🔴
Error: "AccessDenied" from AWS

Fix: Check aws sts get-caller-identity. Verify IAM permissions for the resource. Check SCPs (Service Control Policies).

🔴
Error: "Rate limit exceeded"

Fix: Reduce -parallelism=5. Add retry logic. For AWS: request service quota increase.

🟡
Warning: "Provider produced inconsistent result"

Fix: Provider bug. Upgrade to latest patch. Add lifecycle ignore_changes for problematic attributes.

🟡
Error: "dial tcp: i/o timeout"

Fix: Network issue reaching provider API. Check proxy settings, VPC endpoints, firewall rules. Use HTTPS_PROXY if behind corporate proxy.

Chapter 21 — Practice Questions

Q1
Directories vs workspaces for environments?
Show Answer
Answer

Directories: Configs differ, strict isolation, 4+ envs. Workspaces: Configs nearly identical, 2-3 envs. Anihpj uses directories.

Explanation

Directory-per-environment is the industry standard because it provides complete isolation — separate state files, separate backends, separate IAM permissions. Workspaces share the same backend and credentials, making them unsuitable for production isolation. The exam tests this distinction.

Q2
How deploy identical resources to multiple AWS regions?
Show Answer
Answer

Use provider aliases: provider "aws" { alias = "eu"; region = "eu-west-1" } then provider = aws.eu.

Explanation

Provider aliases are the standard pattern for multi-region deployments. The default provider (no alias) handles the primary region. Aliased providers handle additional regions. Combine with for_each over a set of regions to create identical resources everywhere. This is tested in Domain 5 (Providers).

Q3
How does default_tags on the provider work?
Show Answer
Answer

Auto-applies specified tags to ALL resources created by that provider. Individual resource tags merge with and can override default_tags.

Explanation

default_tags is the cleanest way to ensure every resource gets baseline tags (Project, Owner, CostCenter). Per-resource tags are merged on top — if both define Environment, the resource-level value wins. This eliminates the need to call merge() on every single resource.

Q4
What is the assume_role pattern for multi-account?
Show Answer
Answer
provider "aws" { assume_role { role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/NAME" } }
Explanation

Assume role lets a central "hub" account deploy resources into "spoke" accounts without managing credentials per account. The hub account's IAM role is trusted by the spoke accounts. This is the AWS Organizations best practice and is tested on the exam.

Q5
What does Terragrunt do?
Show Answer
Answer

Wraps Terraform to keep configs DRY. Auto-generates backend configs, enables module reuse, reduces copy-paste across environments.

Explanation

Terragrunt solves Terraform's "not DRY" problem: you have the same backend config, provider config, and variable values across environments. Terragrunt auto-generates these, so you write configuration once and inherit it. It's not an official HashiCorp tool, but it's widely used and may appear in exam scenarios.

Q6
What 4 mandatory tags should every resource have?
Show Answer
Answer

Project, Environment, Owner, CostCenter.

Explanation

These four tags enable cost allocation, ownership tracking, and environment identification. Use default_tags for Project/Owner/CostCenter (same everywhere). Use per-environment variable for Environment (different per env). This is a production best practice tested on the exam.

Q7
How handle DR with Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

Deploy to secondary region using provider aliases. Route53 failover between regions. Keep state accessible across regions.

Explanation

DR patterns: active-passive (standby in secondary region), active-active (both regions serve traffic), pilot light (minimal infra in secondary, scale up during failover). Terraform enables all three by deploying identical configuration to multiple regions. State should be in a globally accessible backend (S3 cross-region replication).

Q8
How does tag inheritance work across levels?
Show Answer
Answer

Provider default_tags → auto-applied base. local.common_tags merged via merge(). Resource tags → final override.

Explanation

The tag hierarchy: (1) default_tags set the baseline, (2) locals provide environment-specific additions, (3) resource-level tags override everything. Use merge(local.common_tags, {Component = "special"}) at the resource level. This ensures consistency while allowing exceptions.

Q9
Benefits of separate AWS accounts per environment?
Show Answer
Answer

Blast radius containment, independent billing, strict IAM isolation, compliance separation. Dev mistake can't affect production.

Explanation

Multi-account is the AWS Well-Architected best practice. Each environment gets its own account with isolated IAM, networking, and billing. Terraform can deploy across accounts using assume_role. This is the gold standard for production security — tested in Domain 5 and Domain 3.

Q10
Auto-stop dev resources at night using tags?
Show Answer
Answer

Tag resources Environment=dev; AutoStop=true. Lambda/AWS Instance Scheduler stops at 8 PM, starts at 7 AM — ~60% savings.

Explanation

Tag-driven automation is a cost optimization pattern: Terraform applies tags, an external system (Lambda, Instance Scheduler) reads them and takes action. This is a practical exam pattern — Terraform manages the tags, the operational tool acts on them. Non-production resources should never run 24/7.

Chapter 22: Security and Compliance

Security in Terraform means protecting secrets, securing state files, enforcing policies before deployment, and maintaining audit trails. A single leaked state file can expose your entire infrastructure.

22.1 Secrets Management 🎯

Where Secrets LIVE (and DON'T LIVE)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ✅ WHERE TO STORE:               ❌ WHERE NEVER TO STORE:        │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐     │
│  │ AWS Secrets Manager    │      │ .tf FILES (git!)       │     │
│  │ (encrypted, rotated)   │      │ ❌ NEVER hardcode!     │     │
│  └────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘     │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐     │
│  │ SSM Parameter Store    │      │ .tfvars (if not         │     │
│  │ (SecureString)         │      │ gitignored!) ❌ NEVER!  │     │
│  └────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘     │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐     │
│  │ HashiCorp Vault        │      │ .tfstate (unencrypted)  │     │
│  │ (enterprise secrets)   │      │ ❌ contains ALL attrs!  │     │
│  └────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘     │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐                                      │
│  │ TF_VAR_* env vars      │     ANIHPJ PATTERN:                  │
│  │ ✅ OK for CI/CD        │     AWS Secrets Manager →            │
│  └────────────────────────┘     data source → K8s Secret         │
│                                  Secret NEVER touches laptop!    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

AWS Secrets Manager

data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" {
  secret_id = "anihpj/${var.environment}/db-password"
}
locals { db_pass = jsondecode(data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db.secret_string)["password"] }

SSM Parameter Store

SecureString parameters for simpler secrets. data.aws_ssm_parameter.db_pass.

HashiCorp Vault

Enterprise-grade secrets with the Vault provider: vault_generic_secret data source.

Environment Variables

TF_VAR_db_password=secret — acceptable for CI/CD but never for local dev without care.

What NEVER to Do

❌ Hardcode in .tf files ❌ Commit .tfvars with secrets ❌ Store unencrypted in state. Secrets in git = immediate rotation required.

22.2 State File Security

🛡️ 6 State File Security Must-Haves

1. Encryption at rest (SSE-S3/KMS) 2. Block public access 3. Enable versioning + MFA delete 4. Least privilege IAM 5. Never share state files 6. Enable CloudTrail logging on the bucket.

🧪 Secrets Handling — Exam Security Patterns
Q: Where store DB passwords?AWS Secrets Manager / SSM / Vault. NEVER in .tf, .tfvars, or state!
Q: What does sensitive=true do?Suppresses display in plan/apply. Does NOT prevent storage in STATE.
Q: How to protect state file?Encrypt at rest, IAM access, versioning + MFA delete, block public access.
Q: Committed .tfvars with secrets?Rotate credentials IMMEDIATELY. Scrub with git-filter-repo. Add pre-commit scanning.

22.3 Policy as Code (Sentinel / OPA)

Pre-deployment enforcement: block non-compliant resources before creation. Example policies: S3 must have encryption, EBS must be KMS-encrypted, EKS must use private endpoints, RDS must have deletion protection.

22.4 Audit Logging and Compliance

Audit trail: Git commit → TFC run → CloudTrail API call → audit log. Every infrastructure change is traceable end-to-end.

22.5 Ephemeral Values — Secrets That Never Touch State (TF 1.9+) 🆕

Ephemeral values are the most secure way to handle secrets in Terraform. Unlike sensitive = true (which still stores values in state), ephemeral values are never written to state or plan files. They exist only in memory during apply and are gone immediately after.

Secret Handling Comparison — Sensitive vs Ephemeral
  SENSITIVE = TRUE:                     EPHEMERAL (TF 1.9+):
  ┌──────────┐                          ┌──────────┐
  │ Variable │                          │ Variable │
  │ password │                          │ password │
  └────┬─────┘                          └────┬─────┘
       │                                     │
       ▼                                     ▼
  ┌──────────┐                          ┌──────────┐
  │  STATE   │ ← PERSISTED (encrypted)  │  MEMORY  │ ← NEVER persisted
  │  FILE    │    Value still exists!   │  ONLY    │    Gone after apply
  └──────────┘                          └──────────┘
       │
       ▼
  ⚠ Accessible via terraform show
  ⚠ Copied to every team member
  ⚠ In CI/CD logs if state is read

  EPHEMERAL GUARANTEES:
  ✅ Never in state file (terraform.tfstate)
  ✅ Never in plan output (terraform plan)
  ✅ Never in terraform show output
  ✅ Never in terraform output (even with -json)
  ✅ Gone from memory after apply completes
Ephemeral Values — Usage Pattern
# OLD WAY (sensitive — still in state):
variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true  # Hidden from display, BUT IN STATE
}

# NEW WAY (ephemeral — TF 1.9+, NEVER in state):
# Uses ephemeral resources and write-only attributes
# Example: aws_db_instance password is a write-only attribute
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  # password is write-only — set once, never readable from state
  password = var.db_password  # Value flows through but isn't stored
}

# SECURITY HIERARCHY:
# 🥇 Ephemeral values (TF 1.9+) — NEVER persisted, best security
# 🥈 Secrets Manager at runtime — retrieved fresh each apply
# 🥉 sensitive = true — hidden but in state (adequate for most)
# ❌ Plain text in .tf/.tfvars — NEVER acceptable
📖 Exam Note

Ephemeral values are TF 1.9+ and may not be directly tested on the current exam version. However, understanding the security hierarchy — ephemeral > runtime retrieval > sensitive masking > plain text — is essential exam knowledge. The exam WILL test that sensitive = true does NOT remove values from state.

Chapter 22 — Practice Questions

Q1
Where should you NEVER store database passwords?
Show Answer
Answer

NEVER in .tf files, .tfvars, or plaintext in state files. Use AWS Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, or HashiCorp Vault.

Explanation

Secrets in .tf files get committed to Git — permanent exposure. Even in gitignored .tfvars, they sit on disk. State files contain ALL resource attributes including passwords. Always use a dedicated secrets manager and retrieve values at runtime via data sources.

# ❌ NEVER: Hardcoded password in .tf
resource "aws_db_instance" "bad" {
  password = "SuperSecret123!"  # Committed to Git forever!
}

# ❌ AVOID: Password in .tfvars (even if gitignored)
# terraform.tfvars:
# db_password = "SuperSecret123!"  # Sits on developer machines

# ✅ BEST: AWS Secrets Manager
data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" {
  secret_id = "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456:secret:anihpj/db"
}
locals {
  db_creds = jsondecode(data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db.secret_string)
}
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  username = local.db_creds.username
  password = local.db_creds.password  # Never touches .tf or Git
}

# ✅ GOOD: SSM Parameter Store (for simpler values)
data "aws_ssm_parameter" "db_pass" {
  name = "/anihpj/prod/db/password"
  with_decryption = true
}
# Use: data.aws_ssm_parameter.db_pass.value
Q2
What does sensitive = true actually protect?
Show Answer
Answer

Suppresses display in plan/apply. Does NOT prevent storage in state — state still contains the value. Must encrypt state at rest.

Explanation

Sensitive is a display mask, not encryption. The value is still written to state in plaintext (though the state file itself may be encrypted at rest on S3). For true secret protection, don't put secrets in variables at all — retrieve them at runtime from Secrets Manager or Vault.

# variables.tf
variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true  # ✅ Hidden from plan/apply display
}

# Plan output:
#   + db_password = (sensitive value)  ← MASKED in CLI

# BUT — state file STILL contains it:
# terraform.tfstate:
# {
#   "resources": [{
#     "instances": [{
#       "attributes": {
#         "password": "SuperSecret123!"  ← PLAINTEXT in state!
#       }
#     }]
#   }]
# }

# PROTECTION: Encrypt state at rest
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket  = "anihpj-tf-state"
    key     = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    encrypt = true  # SSE-S3 encryption at rest
    # OR use KMS for customer-managed keys:
    # kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:..."
  }
}

# ⚠ sensitive = true is a DISPLAY mask, not encryption
# ⚠ State ALWAYS contains secrets — encrypt your backend!
Q3
What are 6 state file security requirements?
Show Answer
Answer

Encryption, block public access, versioning, MFA delete, least privilege IAM, CloudTrail logging.

Explanation

State is the most sensitive file in your Terraform workflow — it contains every resource ID, attribute, and secret in plaintext. These 6 protections are the minimum baseline. Without them, a single misconfigured S3 bucket policy could expose your entire infrastructure to the internet.

Q4
What if you accidentally commit .tfvars with secrets?
Show Answer
Answer

Rotate credentials IMMEDIATELY. Scrub with git-filter-repo. Add *.tfvars to .gitignore + pre-commit scanning.

Explanation

Deleting the file and committing "removed secrets" doesn't help — the secret is still in Git history. You must: (1) rotate the actual credential, (2) use git-filter-repo to purge history, (3) force-push (notify team first!), and (4) add pre-commit hooks to prevent recurrence.

Q5
How does Secrets Manager integrate with Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version reads secrets at plan/apply time. The value flows to resources without touching developer machines.

Explanation

The data source retrieves the secret during plan and apply. The secret is never stored in .tf files or .tfvars — it goes directly from Secrets Manager to the resource. This is the recommended pattern for production secrets: the developer never sees the actual value.

# 1. Store secret in AWS Secrets Manager (manual or via Terraform)
# Secret name: anihpj/prod/database
# Secret value: {"username":"admin","password":"s3cur3P@ss!"}

# 2. Read secret in Terraform (NO value in .tf files)
data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db_creds" {
  secret_id = "anihpj/prod/database"
}

# 3. Parse JSON and use
locals {
  db_config = jsondecode(
    data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db_creds.secret_string
  )
}

# 4. Use in resources — secret never touches your machine
resource "aws_db_instance" "jobpost" {
  identifier     = "anihpj-prod-db"
  engine         = "postgres"
  engine_version = "16.3"
  instance_class = "db.t3.medium"

  username = local.db_config.username  # "admin"
  password = local.db_config.password  # "s3cur3P@ss!"
}

# 🔐 Flow: AWS Secrets Manager → Terraform data source → Resource
# 🔐 Developer NEVER sees the actual password
# 🔐 No secrets in .tf, .tfvars, Git, or developer machines
Q6
What Sentinel policies for anihpj production?
Show Answer
Answer

S3 encryption + block public access. EBS KMS encryption. EKS private endpoint only. RDS deletion protection + Multi-AZ. All hard-mandatory.

Explanation

Sentinel policies enforce security requirements before deployment. Hard-mandatory means the plan is BLOCKED if violated — no exceptions. These four policies cover the most common cloud security misconfigurations. The exam may ask which enforcement level to use for specific requirements.

Q7
What makes a complete Terraform audit trail?
Show Answer
Answer

Git commit → TFC run log → CloudTrail API call → State file change. End-to-end traceability of every infrastructure modification.

Explanation

A complete audit trail answers: who changed the code (Git), who approved it (PR review), who applied it (TFC run), what API calls were made (CloudTrail), and what the result was (state file diff). This chain is essential for SOC2, HIPAA, and PCI compliance.

Q8
Secrets Manager vs SSM Parameter Store?
Show Answer
Answer

Secrets Manager: auto-rotation, cross-account, higher cost. SSM: simpler, free standard params, no auto-rotation. Both support SecureString.

Explanation

For database passwords that need rotation, use Secrets Manager. For simple configuration values or feature flags, use SSM Parameter Store. The exam may present a scenario and ask which service to use — the key discriminator is whether auto-rotation is needed.

Q9
Environment variables for secrets in production?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes for CI/CD (TF_VAR_db_password). CI system injects from its own secrets manager. Never hardcode in pipeline YAML.

Explanation

CI/CD systems like GitHub Actions have built-in secrets management. Use ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }} in GitHub Actions to inject TF_VAR_db_password at runtime. The secret never appears in logs or pipeline definitions. This is acceptable for production if the CI system is properly secured.

Q10
Why is MFA delete important on state buckets?
Show Answer
Answer

Prevents accidental/malicious deletion of state file versions. Even with admin credentials, MFA is required to delete. Critical against ransomware.

Explanation

MFA delete adds a second factor requirement for deleting object versions. If an attacker compromises admin credentials, they still can't permanently delete state without physical access to the MFA device. Combined with versioning, this means you can always recover from accidental or malicious deletions.

Chapter 23: Performance and Scalability

As infrastructure grows, plan and apply times can slow dramatically. Optimizing parallelism, splitting state files, and understanding the dependency graph keeps Terraform fast at scale.

23.1 Large Infrastructure Optimization

Performance Tuning
# Increase parallelism (default=10)
terraform apply -parallelism=20

# Target specific resources (use sparingly!)
terraform apply -target=aws_eks_cluster.anihpj

# Skip refresh for faster plan (risky in production!)
terraform plan -refresh=false

# Limit resource count in plan output
terraform plan -parallelism=30 | head -100

23.2 Large State Files

State files > 1MB slow down every operation. Split state by module boundary.

State Split Strategy — Anihpj by Layer
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MONOLITHIC (SLOW):             SPLIT (FAST):                     │
│  ┌────────────────────┐        ┌──────────┐  s3://tfstate/       │
│  │ ONE state file     │        │ VPC      │  networking/state    │
│  │ 200+ resources     │        ├──────────┤  s3://tfstate/       │
│  │ Plan: 3-5 min      │        │ EKS      │  compute/state       │
│  │ Apply: 10+ min     │        ├──────────┤  s3://tfstate/       │
│  │ ONE failure blocks │        │ RDS      │  database/state      │
│  │ EVERYTHING         │        ├──────────┤  s3://tfstate/       │
│  └────────────────────┘        │ Apps     │  application/state   │
│                                └──────────┘                       │
│  INDEPENDENT: Each layer can be planned/applied separately       │
│  FASTER: 4 small plans < 1 giant plan                            │
│  SAFER: VPC change doesn't touch EKS/RDS/Apps                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

23.3 Dependency Graph Optimization

Minimize explicit depends_on — let Terraform's implicit graph handle ordering. Visualize with terraform graph | dot -Tpng > graph.png. Independent resources run concurrently; unnecessary dependencies serialize them.

23.4 Performance Tuning Decision Matrix

⚡
Parallelism

-parallelism=N (default 10). Increase for large plans with many independent resources. AWS safe range: 20-30. GCP/Azure: test at 15-20 first. Monitor for API throttling and dial down if needed.

📦
State Splitting

Split by module boundary when state exceeds 1MB or plan > 2 min. Each split gets its own state file + backend config. Use terraform_remote_state to share outputs.

🔍
Refresh Control

-refresh=false skips API calls for drift detection — plan becomes instant. Only safe in CI/CD where you're certain nothing changed externally. Never use in production apply.

🎯
Targeting

-target=RESOURCE limits scope to one resource + deps. Emergency only. Creates state inconsistency risk. Prefer state splitting for routine isolation.

🔗
Depends_on

Minimize explicit depends_on — each one is a serialization barrier. Let implicit graph handle 95% of ordering. Only use when Terraform can't infer the dependency.

📊
Graph Analysis

terraform graph | dot -Tpng > graph.png. Identify serial chains (slow), isolated subgraphs (split candidates), and bottlenecks (many dependents = critical path).

23.5 Parallelism vs API Throttling — Finding the Sweet Spot

Parallelism Impact on Plan/Apply Speed
  PARALLELISM 10 (default):         PARALLELISM 30 (optimized):
  ┌────────────────────────┐       ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ 10 concurrent API calls│       │ 30 concurrent API calls│
  │ ████████████░░░░░░░░░░ │       │ ██████████████████████ │
  │ Plan: 3-5 min          │       │ Plan: 1-2 min ⚡       │
  │ Safe: no throttling    │       │ Safe: under AWS limits │
  └────────────────────────┘       └────────────────────────┘

  PARALLELISM 100 (excessive):
  ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ 100 concurrent calls   │
  │ ████████████████████████│
  │ ██ THROTTLED ██████████│ ← AWS API returns 429 errors
  │ ██ RETRY     ██████████│ ← Terraform retries
  │ ██ SLOWER    ██████████│ ← Actually takes LONGER!
  │ Plan: 8-10 min (retries)│
  └────────────────────────┘

  AWS API RATE LIMITS (per region):
  EC2: ~50 calls/sec    S3: ~5,000 PUTs/sec
  RDS: ~20 calls/sec    IAM: ~20 calls/sec
  EKS: ~10 calls/sec    DynamoDB: Unlimited (on-demand)

  SWEET SPOT: -parallelism=20-30 for mixed AWS resources

23.6 State File Size Impact

State SizeResourcesRead TimePlan TimeRecommendation
< 100 KB< 50< 100ms< 30 sec✅ No action needed
100 KB - 1 MB50-200100-500ms30 sec - 2 min🟡 Monitor growth
1 MB - 5 MB200-5000.5-2 sec2-5 min🟠 Consider splitting
> 5 MB> 500> 2 sec> 5 min🔴 Split immediately

Chapter 23 — Practice Questions

Q1
How speed up a plan with 200+ resources?
Show Answer
Answer

terraform plan -parallelism=30. Higher parallelism speeds API calls. Also -refresh=false (risky — skips drift detection).

Explanation

Plan gets slower with more resources because Terraform refreshes each one via API calls. Increasing parallelism lets more API calls happen simultaneously. Default is 10. AWS can typically handle 20-30 without throttling. Skipping refresh makes plan instant but misses drift — only use in CI/CD where you're confident nothing changed.

Q2
When should you split state files?
Show Answer
Answer

When state exceeds ~1MB or plan/apply slow. Split by module: VPC, EKS, RDS, Apps — each with independent state.

Explanation

State splitting is like database sharding — smaller files are faster to read/write/parse. The natural boundary is modules: networking team owns VPC state, platform team owns EKS state, app team owns app state. Each can plan/apply independently. Use terraform_remote_state to share outputs between them.

Q3
Why minimize depends_on?
Show Answer
Answer

Unnecessary depends_on serializes resource creation. Let Terraform's implicit dependency graph handle ordering for maximum parallelism.

Explanation

Every depends_on is an explicit serialization point — it tells Terraform "don't parallelize these." Terraform's implicit graph already handles 95% of dependencies correctly from resource references. Adding unnecessary depends_on reduces parallelism and makes plans/applies slower.

Q4
What does terraform graph do?
Show Answer
Answer

Outputs dependency graph in DOT format. terraform graph | dot -Tpng > graph.png for visualization.

Explanation

The graph shows every resource and its dependencies. Look for: serial chains (no parallelism possible), isolated subgraphs (can be split to separate state), and cycles (must fix). This visual tool is invaluable for understanding why your plan is slow and where to optimize.

Q5
When is -target appropriate?
Show Answer
Answer

Emergency fixes only. It bypasses dependency ordering — use sparingly. Prefer splitting state files for routine isolation.

Explanation

-target is a surgical tool, not a workflow. It tells Terraform "only care about this resource and its dependencies." After using target, your state may be inconsistent — other resources that should have been updated weren't. For routine work, split state by module boundary instead.

Q6
How does state file size affect performance?
Show Answer
Answer

Large state slows everything: plan, apply, refresh, state list. Reading/writing/parsing JSON is O(n). Split state to keep files small.

Explanation

A 5MB state file with 500 resources takes significantly longer to process than five 1MB files with 100 resources each. Every plan/apply reads the entire state file. Splitting by module boundary gives you both performance and organizational benefits — different teams can work independently.

Q7
Risk of -refresh=false?
Show Answer
Answer

Terraform plans using stale state — may miss manual changes, creating incorrect plans. Only use when certain nothing changed.

Explanation

Refresh queries cloud APIs for every resource. Skipping it means Terraform assumes nothing changed since the last apply. If someone manually deleted a security group, Terraform won't detect it and may create resources referencing a non-existent SG. Use -refresh=false only in controlled CI/CD pipelines.

Q8
How do modules help with performance?
Show Answer
Answer

Modules create natural state boundaries. Each module can be split to its own state file for independent plans and applies.

Explanation

Modules are the natural unit of state splitting. A module for VPC, one for EKS, one for RDS — each can be managed independently. Changes to EKS don't require refreshing VPC resources. This is the foundation of scalable Terraform in large organizations.

Q9
What happens if parallelism is too high?
Show Answer
Answer

Cloud API rate limiting — too many simultaneous calls get throttled. Sweet spot: 20-30 for AWS. Test for your account limits.

Explanation

AWS APIs have rate limits: EC2 allows ~50 calls/second per region. If you set -parallelism=100 with 100 EC2 instances, you'll hit throttling — some calls will fail and Terraform will retry, actually making things SLOWER. Monitor CloudTrail for throttling errors and adjust parallelism down if needed.

Q10
How visualize infrastructure dependency graph?
Show Answer
Answer

terraform graph | dot -Tpng > infra.png. Visual graph of all resources and dependencies.

Explanation

The graph visualization shows: resource nodes, dependency arrows, parallelizable groups (unconnected nodes), and bottlenecks (nodes many others depend on). Use it to explain architecture to stakeholders, debug why plan takes so long, and identify candidates for state splitting.

🔴 Part 9: Terraform + Kubernetes — IaC Meets Container OrchestrationChapters 24-26

Chapter 24: The Kubernetes Provider

Terraform can manage not just the infrastructure that hosts Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS), but also the resources inside the cluster — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and even Helm charts. This unifies infrastructure and application deployment under one tool.

24.1 Kubernetes Provider Configuration 🎯

EKS Authentication — The Standard Pattern
# Fetch EKS auth token
data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "anihpj" {
  name = module.eks.cluster_name
}

# Configure K8s provider to talk to EKS
provider "kubernetes" {
  host                   = module.eks.cluster_endpoint
  cluster_ca_certificate = base64decode(module.eks.certificate_authority_data)
  token                  = data.aws_eks_cluster_auth.anihpj.token
}

# For multiple clusters (dev + prod), use aliases:
provider "kubernetes" {
  alias                  = "prod"
  host                   = module.eks_prod.cluster_endpoint
  cluster_ca_certificate = base64decode(module.eks_prod.certificate_authority_data)
  token                  = data.aws_eks_cluster_auth.prod.token
}

24.2 Managing K8s Resources with Terraform

K8s ResourceTerraform ResourcePurpose
Namespacekubernetes_namespaceIsolate dev/staging/prod
Deploymentkubernetes_deploymentDeploy the jobpost Django app
Servicekubernetes_serviceExpose as LoadBalancer (ALB)
ConfigMapkubernetes_config_mapExternalize Django settings
Secretkubernetes_secretDB passwords, API keys
Ingresskubernetes_ingress_v1Route external traffic

24.3 The Helm Provider 🎯

Helm + Terraform — Deploy Monitoring Stack
provider "helm" {
  kubernetes {
    host                   = module.eks.cluster_endpoint
    token                  = data.aws_eks_cluster_auth.anihpj.token
    cluster_ca_certificate = base64decode(module.eks.certificate_authority_data)
  }
}

resource "helm_release" "prometheus" {
  name       = "prometheus"
  repository = "https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts"
  chart      = "kube-prometheus-stack"
  namespace  = "monitoring"
  set { name = "grafana.adminPassword"; value = var.grafana_password }
}

resource "helm_release" "ingress_nginx" {
  name       = "ingress-nginx"
  repository = "https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx"
  chart      = "ingress-nginx"
  namespace  = "ingress"
  set { name = "controller.service.type"; value = "LoadBalancer" }
}

24.4 Deploying jobpost to EKS — Complete Walkthrough

Jobpost K8s Deployment — Dependency Chain
Step 1: kubernetes_namespace.jobpost          ← Creates namespace
Step 2: kubernetes_secret.db_password +       ← Run in PARALLEL
        kubernetes_config_map.django_settings
Step 3: kubernetes_deployment.jobpost          ← Depends on 1+2
        Pulls: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v2.4.1
Step 4: kubernetes_service.jobpost             ← Depends on deployment
        Type: LoadBalancer → AWS ALB
Step 5: kubernetes_ingress_v1.jobpost          ← Depends on service
        Host: jobpost.anihpj.com

⏱️  ~5-8 min (EKS already exists) — ALL in one terraform apply!
Complete jobpost K8s Terraform Code
resource "kubernetes_namespace" "jobpost" { metadata { name = "jobpost" } }

resource "kubernetes_config_map" "django_settings" {
  metadata { name = "django-settings"; namespace = "jobpost" }
  data = { DJANGO_DEBUG = "False"; DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS = "jobpost.anihpj.com" }
}

data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db_password" { secret_id = "anihpj/rds/password" }
resource "kubernetes_secret" "db_password" {
  metadata { name = "db-password"; namespace = "jobpost" }
  data = { DB_PASSWORD = data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db_password.secret_string }
}

resource "kubernetes_deployment" "jobpost" {
  metadata { name = "jobpost"; namespace = "jobpost" }
  spec {
    replicas = 3; selector { match_labels = { app = "jobpost" } }
    template {
      metadata { labels = { app = "jobpost" } }
      spec { container {
        image = "ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v2.4.1"; name = "jobpost"; port { container_port = 8000 }
        env_from { config_map_ref { name = "django-settings" }; secret_ref { name = "db-password" } }
      } }
    }
  }
}

resource "kubernetes_service" "jobpost" {
  metadata { name = "jobpost"; namespace = "jobpost" }
  spec { type = "LoadBalancer"; selector = { app = "jobpost" }; port { port = 80; target_port = 8000 } }
}

Chapter 24 — Practice Questions

Q1
How authenticate K8s provider to EKS?
Show Answer
Answer

Use data.aws_eks_cluster_auth for token, pass host, cluster_ca_certificate, and token to provider.

Explanation

After EKS creation, two data sources provide everything needed: aws_eks_cluster gives endpoint and CA cert, aws_eks_cluster_auth generates a short-lived IAM token.

# 1. Create EKS cluster (AWS provider)
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" {
  name     = "anihpj-${var.environment}"
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.cluster.arn
  vpc_config {
    subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnet_ids
  }
}

# 2. Read cluster endpoint + CA cert (AWS provider)
data "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" {
  name       = aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.name
  depends_on = [aws_eks_cluster.anihpj]
}

# 3. Generate auth token (AWS provider)
data "aws_eks_cluster_auth" "anihpj" {
  name       = aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.name
  depends_on = [aws_eks_cluster.anihpj]
}

# 4. Configure K8s provider with all three values
provider "kubernetes" {
  host                   = data.aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.endpoint
  cluster_ca_certificate = base64decode(data.aws_eks_cluster.anihpj.certificate_authority[0].data)
  token                  = data.aws_eks_cluster_auth.anihpj.token
}

# Now K8s resources can be created:
resource "kubernetes_namespace" "jobpost" {
  metadata { name = "jobpost" }
}

# 🔐 No static credentials! Token auto-refreshes each plan/apply
# 🔐 Token lasts ~15 min — more than enough for a terraform run
Q2
What Terraform resource creates a K8s Deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

kubernetes_deployment. Manages replicas, container images, env vars, and resource limits — like a YAML manifest but in HCL.

Explanation

The Kubernetes provider translates HCL into K8s API calls. Instead of kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml, you write HCL. Benefits: Terraform tracks state, forces consistency, and can reference cloud resources directly (like ECR image URLs or RDS endpoints).

Q3
How install a Helm chart with Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

helm_release resource with chart, repository, and set {} for values. Example: nginx-ingress, Prometheus, cert-manager.

Explanation

Helm charts package complex K8s applications. The Helm provider manages chart lifecycle — install, upgrade, rollback — as Terraform resources. set {} blocks override default values. Charts can come from any Helm repository, not just the official one.

Q4
Correct order for deploying jobpost resources?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Namespace → 2. Secret + ConfigMap → 3. Deployment → 4. Service → 5. Ingress. Terraform handles ordering via implicit deps.

Explanation

Order matters: the Deployment references the Namespace, Secret, and ConfigMap, so Terraform creates those first. The Service references the Deployment's labels. The Ingress references the Service. Terraform builds this dependency chain automatically from resource references.

Q5
How pass AWS Secrets Manager passwords to K8s?
Show Answer
Answer

Read with data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version → pass to kubernetes_secret.data. Secret never touches developer machine.

Explanation

This creates a secure pipeline: AWS Secrets Manager (encrypted) → Terraform data source (in-memory) → Kubernetes Secret (etcd encrypted). At no point is the secret written to a file or displayed in logs.

# AWS Secrets Manager (created once, manually or via Terraform)
# Secret: anihpj/prod/database
# Value: {"username":"admin","password":"s3cur3P@ss!","host":"rds.xxx"}

# 1. Read secret from AWS (NO value in .tf files)
data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" {
  secret_id = "anihpj/prod/database"
}

locals {
  db = jsondecode(data.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.db.secret_string)
}

# 2. Create K8s Secret (value flows directly — never on disk)
resource "kubernetes_secret" "db" {
  metadata {
    name      = "db-credentials"
    namespace = kubernetes_namespace.jobpost.metadata[0].name
  }
  data = {
    DB_USERNAME = local.db.username
    DB_PASSWORD = local.db.password
    DB_HOST     = local.db.host
  }
}

# 3. K8s Deployment consumes via env vars
resource "kubernetes_deployment" "jobpost" {
  metadata { name = "jobpost"; namespace = "jobpost" }
  spec {
    template {
      spec {
        container {
          image = "ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:latest"
          name  = "jobpost"
          env {
            name = "DB_PASSWORD"
            value_from {
              secret_key_ref {
                name = kubernetes_secret.db.metadata[0].name
                key  = "DB_PASSWORD"
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

# 🔐 AWS Secrets Manager → Terraform → K8s Secret → Pod env
# 🔐 Secret NEVER in .tf, .tfvars, Git, or developer terminal
Q6
What K8s resource types can Terraform manage?
Show Answer
Answer

Namespace, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, DaemonSet, StatefulSet, Job, CronJob, RBAC, HPA, PVC, and more.

Explanation

The Kubernetes provider covers virtually all K8s resource types. This means you can manage your entire K8s configuration — from cluster creation to application deployment — in a single Terraform workflow. No need to switch between Terraform and kubectl.

Q7
Manage multiple K8s clusters with Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

Provider aliases: provider "kubernetes" { alias = "prod"; ... } then provider = kubernetes.prod in resources.

Explanation

Same pattern as multi-region AWS: each provider alias points to a different cluster. Resources use the default provider unless provider = kubernetes.alias_name is specified. This lets one Terraform config manage dev/staging/prod clusters simultaneously.

Q8
What does kubernetes_config_map replace?
Show Answer
Answer

Replaces YAML ConfigMap manifests. Define in HCL alongside infrastructure instead of separate kubectl apply commands.

Explanation

Managing ConfigMaps in Terraform means your app configuration is version-controlled alongside your infrastructure. When you update a ConfigMap value, Terraform plans the change, you review it, and apply it — just like any infrastructure change. No more forgotten kubectl apply commands.

Q9
How does helm_release.set override chart values?
Show Answer
Answer

set { name = "replicaCount"; value = "5" } overrides chart defaults. Equivalent to helm install --set replicaCount=5.

Explanation

Each set {} block overrides one chart value. For complex values, use values = [file("values.yaml")] instead. Values set via Terraform take precedence over the chart's default values.yaml. This lets you customize charts for your environment without forking them.

Q10
Why use Terraform for K8s instead of kubectl?
Show Answer
Answer

Single workflow: EKS + K8s apps in one terraform apply. State tracks everything. Secrets flow AWS → K8s without touching dev machines.

Explanation

The killer feature: you create the EKS cluster AND deploy apps in one command. Outputs from EKS (endpoint, CA) feed directly into the Kubernetes provider. Secrets from AWS Secrets Manager feed into K8s Secrets. No manual steps, no separate scripts, no credential handling — Terraform orchestrates the entire pipeline.

Chapter 25: GitOps with Terraform — The Anihpj Pipeline

GitOps applies the same version-control discipline to infrastructure that developers use for application code. Git is the single source of truth; PRs propose changes; merges apply them.

25.1 The GitOps Philosophy Applied to Terraform

Git as Single Source of Truth

All .tf files live in git. The state of the repo = the desired state of infrastructure. No manual changes allowed — if it's not in git, it doesn't exist.

PR = Proposed Change, Merge = Apply

Open a PR → Terraform plan runs automatically → review plan output → merge → Terraform apply runs. The PR is the change request; the merge is the approval.

Drift Detection

Continuous speculative plans detect when reality has diverged from git. If someone changes a security group manually, the next plan shows the discrepancy.

25.2 GitHub Actions — Complete CI/CD Pipeline 🎯

GitHub Actions provides free CI minutes for public repos. The workflow below implements the full Terraform CI/CD pattern: format → validate → plan → review → apply. This is directly tested in Domain 3 (Collaborative Workflows).

.github/workflows/terraform-ci.yml — PR Checks
name: "Terraform CI"
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "terraform/**"
      - "terraform/**/*.tf"
      - "terraform/**/*.tfvars"

env:
  AWS_REGION: us-east-1

jobs:
  terraform-plan:
    name: "Terraform Plan"
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
      id-token: write  # For OIDC to AWS (no secrets!)

    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: terraform/envs/prod

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with:
          terraform_version: "1.7"
          cli_config_credentials_token: ${{ secrets.TFC_TOKEN }}

      - name: Configure AWS Credentials (OIDC)
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-actions-tf
          aws-region: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}

      - name: Terraform Format Check
        id: fmt
        run: terraform fmt -recursive -check -diff
        continue-on-error: true

      - name: Terraform Init
        id: init
        run: terraform init

      - name: Terraform Validate
        id: validate
        run: terraform validate -no-color
        continue-on-error: true

      - name: Terraform Plan
        id: plan
        run: |
          terraform plan -no-color -input=false \
            -out=tfplan \
            -detailed-exitcode
        continue-on-error: true

      - name: Post Plan to PR
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        with:
          script: |
            const plan = `${{ steps.plan.outputs.stdout }}`;
            const truncated = plan.length > 60000
              ? plan.substring(0, 60000) + "\n...(truncated)"
              : plan;
            github.rest.issues.createComment({...})
.github/workflows/terraform-apply.yml — Merge Deploy
name: "Terraform Apply"
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "terraform/**"

jobs:
  terraform-apply:
    name: "Terraform Apply"
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production  # Requires approval in GitHub!
    defaults: { run: { working-directory: terraform/envs/prod } }

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init
      - name: Terraform Apply
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false tfplan
        # tfplan from PR plan step (uploaded as artifact)
Complete GitHub Actions + TFC Pipeline Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DEVELOPER          GITHUB ACTIONS          TERRAFORM CLOUD        │
│                                                                   │
│  1. git push ──────▶ PR opened                                     │
│                      │                                            │
│  2.                  ├─ fmt -check ──────▶ ✅ / ❌                │
│                      ├─ validate ────────▶ ✅ / ❌                │
│                      ├─ plan ────────────▶ Plan output            │
│                      │                    │                       │
│  3.                  └─ Post plan as      │                       │
│                         PR comment ◀──────┘                       │
│                                                                   │
│  4. Review plan ◀──────────────────── PR shows +create/-destroy   │
│     in PR comment                                                 │
│                                                                   │
│  5. Approve + Merge ──────────────────▶ Push to main              │
│                                          │                        │
│  6.                                      ├─ init                  │
│                                          ├─ apply ───────────────▶│
│                                          │  ┌──────────────────┐  │
│  7.                                      │  │ Sentinel checks  │  │
│                                          │  │ Cost estimation  │  │
│  8.                                      │  └──────────────────┘  │
│                                          │  Apply infrastructure   │
│  9.  🎉 Done! ◀──────────────────────────┘  changes to AWS        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔐
OIDC — No Secrets Required

GitHub Actions uses OIDC to authenticate to AWS without storing long-lived credentials. GitHub's OIDC provider issues a JWT, AWS STS exchanges it for temporary credentials. No AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in GitHub Secrets. This is the modern, secure pattern for cloud CI/CD.

🛡️
Environment Protection Rules

GitHub Environments let you require: (1) manual approval before apply, (2) specific reviewers, (3) deployment branches only. Add environment: production to your apply job — no one deploys to production without explicit approval.

25.3 Atlantis — Self-Hosted GitOps Automation 🎯

Atlantis is an open-source tool that listens to GitHub/GitLab webhooks and runs terraform plan and terraform apply as PR comments. It provides locking to prevent concurrent applies on the same directory.

Atlantis — repo-config.yaml
# File: atlantis.yaml (in repo root)
version: 3
automerge: false
parallel_plan: true
parallel_apply: false

projects:
  - name: anihpj-network
    dir: terraform/envs/prod/network
    workspace: prod
    autoplan:
      when_modified: ["*.tf", "*.tfvars"]
      enabled: true
    apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable]

  - name: anihpj-compute
    dir: terraform/envs/prod/compute
    workspace: prod
    autoplan:
      when_modified: ["*.tf", "*.tfvars"]
      enabled: true
    apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable]

  - name: anihpj-app
    dir: terraform/envs/prod/app
    workspace: prod
    autoplan:
      when_modified: ["*.tf", "*.tfvars"]
      enabled: true
    apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable]
Atlantis Workflow — PR-Driven Infrastructure
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ATLANTIS WORKFLOW                                                │
│                                                                   │
│  1. Developer opens PR ──────▶ Atlantis webhook fires             │
│  2. Atlantis runs:                                                │
│     $ terraform plan -out=tfplan                                  │
│     → Posts plan output as PR comment                             │
│                                                                   │
│  3. Reviewer comments: "atlantis plan"                            │
│     → Re-runs plan (re-check)                                     │
│                                                                   │
│  4. Reviewer comments: "atlantis apply"                           │
│     → Atlantis checks: ✅ PR approved? ✅ Branch mergeable?       │
│     → Acquires LOCK on directory (prevents concurrent applies)    │
│     → Runs: terraform apply tfplan                                │
│     → Posts: "Apply complete! 🎉"                                 │
│     → Releases LOCK                                               │
│                                                                   │

│  🔒 LOCKING: Only one apply per directory at a time               │
│  💬 COMMENT-DRIVEN: No CI config needed, just PR comments         │
│  📋 AUDIT: Every plan and apply is a PR comment (searchable!)     │
│  🏠 SELF-HOSTED: Atlantis runs in YOUR infrastructure             │

25.4 The Full Anihpj CI/CD Pipeline

End-to-End Anihpj Pipeline
1. Developer pushes .tf change ──────────────────────────────────┐
2. GitHub Actions: fmt -check, validate                           │
3. PR opened → TFC speculative plan ──────────────────────────┐  │
4. Plan output → PR comment                                    │  │
5. Code review → Approve → Merge                               │  │
6. TFC apply (auto-triggered on merge)                         │  │
7. Infrastructure updated (EKS, RDS, etc.)                     │  │
8. K8s manifests updated → ArgoCD syncs                        │  │
9. jobpost v2.0 now running on new infrastructure! 🎉          │  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

25.5 GitHub Actions Workflow for Terraform CI

GitHub Actions provides free CI minutes for public repos. The workflow below runs on every PR — formatting check, validation, and plan — before any human reviews the code.

.github/workflows/terraform-ci.yml
name: "Terraform CI"
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "terraform/**"       # Only trigger on .tf changes
      - "terraform/**/*.tf"
      - "terraform/**/*.tfvars"

jobs:
  terraform:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults: { run: { working-directory: terraform/envs/prod } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with: { terraform_version: "1.7" }

      - name: Terraform Format Check
        run: terraform fmt -recursive -check -diff

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend=false  # No remote state for CI

      - name: Terraform Validate
        run: terraform validate

      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: |
          terraform plan -no-color -input=false \
            -out=plan.tfplan 2>&1 | tee plan.txt
        env:
          AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}

      - name: Post Plan as PR Comment
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require('fs');
            const plan = fs.readFileSync('terraform/envs/prod/plan.txt','utf8');
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: `### Terraform Plan\n\`\`\`\n${plan}\n\`\`\``
            });
💡 CI Pipeline Best Practices
  • Fail fast: Format check first (fastest), validate second, plan last (slowest — requires cloud creds)
  • No remote state in CI: Use -backend=false for init in PR checks to avoid state conflicts
  • Path filtering: Only trigger on terraform/** changes to avoid wasting CI minutes
  • Secrets via GitHub: Use ${{ secrets.NAME }} — never hardcode in workflow YAML

25.6 Atlantis Configuration

Atlantis uses an atlantis.yaml file at the repo root to define which directories contain Terraform configs, workflow customizations, and autoplan settings.

atlantis.yaml
version: 3
automerge: false       # Never auto-merge — always human review
parallel_plan: true    # Plan all projects in parallel
parallel_apply: false  # Apply sequentially (safer)

projects:
  # Dev environment — auto-plan on PR, auto-apply on merge
  - name: anihpj-dev
    dir: terraform/envs/dev
    workspace: dev
    autoplan:
      when_modified: ["*.tf", "*.tfvars"]
      enabled: true
    apply_requirements: [approved]  # Require PR approval

  # Staging — requires PR approval for apply
  - name: anihpj-staging
    dir: terraform/envs/staging
    workspace: staging
    autoplan:
      when_modified: ["*.tf", "*.tfvars"]
      enabled: true
    apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable]

  # Production — strict: requires PR approval + up-to-date branch
  - name: anihpj-prod
    dir: terraform/envs/prod
    workspace: prod
    autoplan:
      when_modified: ["*.tf", "*.tfvars"]
      enabled: true
    apply_requirements: [approved, mergeable, undiverged]
    # undiverged = branch MUST be up-to-date with base
apply_requirementsDescription
approvedPR must have at least one approval
mergeablePR must have no merge conflicts
undivergedBranch must be up-to-date with base branch
policies_passedAll policy checks (OPA/Sentinel) must pass

25.7 Pre-Commit Hooks — Catch Errors Before Push

Pre-commit hooks catch formatting issues and basic errors BEFORE they reach CI — saving time and CI minutes.

.pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/antonbabenko/pre-commit-terraform
    rev: v1.88.0
    hooks:
      - id: terraform_fmt          # Auto-format .tf files
      - id: terraform_validate     # Validate syntax
      - id: terraform_docs         # Auto-generate README.md
      - id: terraform_tflint       # Lint for best practices
      - id: terraform_tfsec        # Security scanning
        args: [--minimum-severity=HIGH]  # Block on HIGH/CRITICAL

  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v4.5.0
    hooks:
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: end-of-file-fixer
      - id: check-yaml
      - id: detect-aws-credentials   # Block AWS keys in code
      - id: detect-private-key       # Block private keys in code
🔒 Security Scanning is Critical

tfsec catches common misconfigurations: open S3 buckets, unencrypted RDS, public security groups. Run it as a pre-commit hook AND in CI. Set minimum severity to HIGH for pre-commit to avoid blocking on style warnings, but run full scan in CI.

25.8 Terraform Cloud VCS Integration

Terraform Cloud connects directly to GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket. When a PR is opened, TFC automatically runs a speculative plan. When the PR is merged, TFC applies the changes.
